title: Get Around Like Local
snippet: the complete guide to getting around china as a foreigner. airport transfers, high-speed trains, metro, buses, shared bikes, didi — everything you need to travel like a local.
text: 🚗 China Transport · 中国交通 Get Around Like a Local China's transport network is one of the most advanced in the world — but it can feel intimidating if you don't know the system. This guide covers everything you need, from the moment you land to your last day. ⏱ 9 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Foreign passport friendly Airport → Hotel → Every Transport Option → 1 How to Get to Your Hotel You've just landed. You're tired. Here's exactly how to get from the arrivals hall to your hotel — without getting scammed. ⚠️ First rule Ignore anyone in the arrivals hall who approaches you offering a "taxi" or "ride." These are unlicensed drivers who charge 3–5x the normal rate and sometimes take you to the wrong place. Use the app. Method Best For Cost (Approx.) How to Use 📱 Didi (Recommended) Most travelers — easiest, safest ¥60–150 (~$8–20 USD) Open Didi → set destination to hotel name in English. Wait in the 网约车 zone (ride-hailing pickup area). Share your hotel address in Chinese with the driver. Pay through the app — no cash needed. 🚇 Airport Metro Budget travelers, light luggage, hotel near metro ¥25–35 Look for 地铁 signs in arrivals. Most major airports (Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu, Guangzhou) have direct metro links to city centres. Buy a ticket at the machine — English available. 🚌 Airport Bus Heavy luggage, no rush, on a tight budget ¥20–35 Look for 机场巴士 signs outside arrivals. Fixed routes to major city hotels. Pay with cash or Alipay at the counter. Slower than metro but less hassle with luggage. 🏨 Hotel Shuttle International chain hotel guests Free–¥50 Check with your hotel before arrival — many international chains offer free airport pickup. Book at least 24 hours in advance. 💡 At your hotel Show your passport — hotels are legally required to register it. Some budget hotels don't accept foreign guests, so book international chains to be safe. Ask the front desk for the hotel's address in Chinese (useful for Didi). Connect to WiFi and test your VPN before heading out. 2 How Many Ways Can You Get Around China? China has built one of the world's most impressive transportation networks in just two decades. Here's a breakdown of every option available to travelers — from bullet trains that cross entire provinces in hours to shared bikes you unlock with a phone scan. 🚄 High-Speed Rail (高铁 Gāotiě) China's crown jewel. The world's largest high-speed rail network — over 40,000 km of track connecting every major city. Beijing to Shanghai in 4.5 hours. Trains run at 300–350 km/h, are almost always on time (average delay: under 1 minute), and are cleaner and more comfortable than most airlines. How to book: Use Trip.com (English, foreign cards accepted) or the 12306 app. Bring your passport and or use the foreigner e-ticket gate. Tip: Book 1–2 weeks ahead for popular routes like Beijing–Shanghai or during holidays. See the full High-Speed Train Guide → 🚇 Metro (地铁 Dìtiě) Every major city has a modern metro system — Beijing alone has 27 lines. Most ticket machines have English. You can also scan your Alipay or WeChat transport QR code directly at the gate (much faster). Fares are absurdly cheap: ¥3–15 per ride. Rush hours (7:30–9am and 5:30–7pm) get extremely crowded — avoid if possible. Stations are clean, well-signed, and have staff at 客服中心 (Customer Service) for questions. Tip: Use Amap to guide you between stations. See the full Metro Guide → 🚗 Didi (滴滴) — China's Uber Works in English. Set your pickup and destination in the app — it's about half the price of taxis in most Western countries. Most city rides cost ¥20–40 (~$3–6 USD). Send your driver a photo of your exact location if you're on a busy street. Copy-paste this to them: "我是外国人，不会讲中文" (I'm a foreigner, I can't speak Mandarin). Cheaper alternatives once you're comfortable: 曹操出行 and 花小猪. Avoid street taxis at airports and train stations — they often overcharge foreigners. See the full Didi Guide → 🚌 Public Bus (公交车 Gōngjiāochē) The cheapest way to get around — fares are ¥1–2 per ride. Buses cover areas the metro doesn't reach and are found in every Chinese city, from mega-cities to small towns. Pay with your Alipay or WeChat transport QR code, or get a physical bus card at any metro station. Use Amap(高德地图) to find routes — it shows real-time bus locations and estimated arrival times. Most big cities announce stops in both Chinese and English.See the full Bus Guide → 🚲 Shared Bikes (共享单车 Gòngxiǎng Dānchē) China's streets are filled with dockless bikes — you'll see blue (Hellobike 哈啰单车), yellow (Meituan Bike 美团单车), and green (Didi Bike) ones everywhere. Scan the QR code on the bike with Alipay or WeChat to unlock — no separate app needed. Cost: ¥1–3 per 30 minutes. Best for short trips under 3km, exploring neighborhoods, or getting from the metro to your final destination. Important: You must park in designated zones (look for painted rectangles on the pavement) or face a ¥5–20 fine. The app will show you where the nearest parking zone is.See the full Bike Guide → ✈️ Domestic Flights Best for very long distances (e.g., Beijing → Yunnan, Shanghai → Xinjiang). Book on Trip.com for English interface and foreign card support. Budget airlines include Xiamen Air, Shenzhen Airlines, and Juneyao Air. Arrive at least 2 hours before departure — security is thorough. Luggage: typically 20kg checked, 5kg carry-on. For distances under 1,000 km, the high-speed train is usually more worthy door-to-door when you factor in airport transfers and security. 🚕 Regular Taxis (出租车 Chūzūchē) Available everywhere but not recommended for foreigners unless you speak some Mandarin. Drivers rarely speak English, meters can be "broken" for tourists, and Didi is cheaper anyway. If you must take one, have your destination written in Chinese on your phone, insist on the meter (打表 dǎ biǎo), and take a photo of the license plate before getting in. 3 Smart City Navigation Tips Having the right tools and knowing a few insider tricks makes a huge difference. Here's what I tell every friend visiting China for the first time. 🗺️ Use Amap, Not Google Maps Google Maps data in China is inaccurate and outdated Amap → (高德地图) has real-time traffic, accurate walking paths, and indoor maps of malls and stations Switch to English in Settings — most labels will still show in Chinese, but menus become readable Works offline if you download city maps in advance 💳 One QR Code for Everything Your Alipay transport QR code works on metro, bus, and even some taxis in many cities No need to buy separate tickets or cards — just scan at the gate Set it up in Alipay: tap Transport (出行) → add your city's transit card Works in 300+ Chinese cities 📱 Save These Before You Leave WiFi Screenshot your hotel address in Chinese Download offline Amap for your cities Save a photo of your passport on your phone Bookmark your hotel's location on Amap ⏰ Avoid Rush Hour Metro rush: 7:30–9:00 AM and 5:30–7:00 PM — trains are packed shoulder-to-shoulder Road rush: 8:00–9:30 AM and 5:00–7:00 PM — Didi rides take 1.5–2x longer If you must travel during rush, the metro is faster than any car Weekend mornings before 10 AM are the quietest 📥 Get the Full PDF Guide A clean, printable version of this guide with all screenshots — perfect to keep on your phone for reference when you're in China. I'll also send you updates when Alipay changes its setup process. Send Me the PDF ✉️ ✅ Got it! Check your inbox — I'll send the PDF shortly. No spam. I read every email personally. Continue Getting Ready → 🆘 Emergency Contacts Important phone numbers and resources for travelers in China 🏥 Travel Insurance I bet the travel insurance worth every penny! 📶 Data Guide Get connected without the expensive hassle of international roaming 📚 All Guides → Everything you need before and after you land

title: Index
snippet: babysitter-level guide for foreigners: how to book tickets for the forbidden city, terracotta army, giant pandas & 99% of china's attractions via wechat/alipay mini-programs. spot official accounts, e
text: 🎟️ Before You Visit · 门票预约 How to Book Chinese Attraction Tickets on WeChat & Alipay In China, you don't "buy a ticket at the gate" — you reserve online with your passport number days in advance. This babysitter-level tutorial walks you through the whole flow on WeChat and Alipay mini-programs, with screenshots for every step. Master this and 99% of China's attractions are unlocked. ⏱ 12 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Passport-friendly 🎟️ Works for 99% of attractions 🔴 Read This First · China Ticket Reality You Almost Never Buy Tickets at the Gate China runs attractions on a real-name reservation system . Unlike Europe or the US, most popular spots in China don't sell walk-up tickets — you must book a timed slot online, with your passport, before you arrive. Here's what that means for you: 🪪 Passport is your ticket. Every booking asks for your passport number and name exactly as printed. No passport, no entry — even if you "have a ticket." 📉 Daily caps sell out fast. The Forbidden City releases only ~40,000 slots/day and they vanish in minutes. The Giant Panda Base morning session is gone by 8 AM. ⏰ Tickets drop on a schedule. Most spots open booking 7–8 days ahead at a fixed time (often 8 PM Beijing time). Miss it and you wait another day. 📱 It all happens inside WeChat or Alipay. Each attraction has its own "mini-program" — a tiny app-within-an-app. This guide teaches you how to find and use them. The Universal 4-Step Flow Every attraction uses the same basic dance. Learn it once, repeat everywhere. The 10 special spots in Part 4 only differ in when tickets drop — not how you book. 1 Find it Search the attraction's mini-program 2 Trust it Spot the official "Blue V" account 3 Fill it Enter passport number & name 4 Grab it Pick date, pay, screenshot QR 1 Find the Mini-Program A "mini-program" (小程序) is a lightweight app that lives inside WeChat or Alipay — no download needed. To book a ticket, you open the attraction's own mini-program and tap around. Here's how to find it: a In WeChat: from the chat list, either tap the search bar at the top , or pull down from the top of the screen to open the mini-program search. Type the attraction's official Chinese name (e.g. 故宫博物院). b In Alipay: tap the search bar on the home screen and type the attraction name + "预约" (reservation), e.g. 故宫 预约. c The official mini-program usually appears as the first result with a verified badge. Tap it to open. d Tip: once found, tap "⋯" → "Add to Favorites / 添加到我的小程序" so you can reopen it in one tap on booking day. 💡 Kat's Tip Search in Chinese , not English. "Forbidden City ticket" won't return anything — but 故宫博物院 will. If you can't type Chinese, copy the name from Part 4's table below and paste it into the search box. 2 Trust It — Spot the Official "Blue V" This is the step foreigners mess up most. Next to many search results you'll see a small blue badge (蓝V) — that means the account is officially verified . You want this one, not a reseller. a Look for the blue "V" or "认证" badge next to the account name. On WeChat it's a small blue circle-V; on Alipay it's a blue checkmark. b Tap the account → check the operator / 主体 . It should be the museum, scenic-area administration, or a government culture-tourism bureau — not a travel agency. c Avoid accounts that say "官方授权代理 / authorized agent" or show tour packages — those are third parties who mark up prices and may not guarantee entry. ⚠️ Watch Out Scam mini-programs exist. If the price looks 2–3× the official rate, or it asks for payment before showing your passport details, close it. Book only on the Blue-V official account — Part 4 lists the exact name for each top spot. 3 Fill In Your Passport Real-name booking means the ticket is tied to you . You'll add each visitor's passport info once, then reuse it. Get this right or you'll be turned away at the gate. a Tap "游客信息 / Add Visitor" and choose document type "护照 / Passport." b Enter your surname and given name exactly as printed on the passport , in Latin letters. If the form splits Surname / Given Name, put them in the right fields — don't mash your full name into one box. c Type your passport number carefully — no spaces, match the machine-readable zone at the bottom of the page. Double-check before submitting. d Add a phone number . If it demands a Chinese (+86) number, use your hotel's front desk number or a local SIM — see the eSIM guide. Some programs accept your home number with country code. e Save the visitor so you can re-select them on future bookings with one tap. 💡 Kat's Tip Add everyone in your group before ticket-drop time. On a hot drop (Forbidden City, Pandas), you won't have seconds to type passports — just tap the saved visitors and hit pay. 4 Book, Pay & Screenshot Now the actual grab. Many spots open a calendar a week ahead; you pick a date and a time slot, then pay. a Tap "预约购票 / Book Tickets," pick your date and time slot (morning/afternoon). Greyed-out slots are sold out. b Select your saved visitor(s), confirm the price, and pay via WeChat Pay or Alipay (foreign cards work if you set them up — see the payment guides). c On success, you'll get a reservation QR code / 预约码 . Screenshot it immediately and save it to your photo album — signal at the gate can be weak. d At entry: show the QR code + your physical passport . Staff scan both; the name must match. ⏰ The Grab Be online 2–3 minutes before the drop time (Part 4). The moment the clock hits, refresh the date and tap fast. For the Forbidden City and Pandas, the first 5 minutes decide everything. WeChat or Alipay? Use Both Good news: almost every attraction runs on both platforms, so you're not locked in. Set up payment on each before you fly. Here's the difference: 💬 WeChat 微信 · the all-rounder 🏛️ Best for government museums — the Forbidden City, National Museum, and most provincial museums run their primary mini-program here. 🔎 Find it: top search bar, or pull down from the chat list to open mini-program search. 💳 Pay with: WeChat Pay — link a foreign card or use the Tour Pass card. Setup guide linked below. 🌐 More English-friendly labels on many official museum programs than Alipay. 🅰️ Alipay 支付宝 · the aggregator 🎡 Best for scenic areas & aggregators — Great Wall sections, parks, and "景区预约" one-stop booking live here. 🔎 Find it: home-screen search bar; try name + "预约". There's also a "出行 / Travel" hub. 💳 Pay with: Alipay — foreign cards bind easily via the in-app "Tour Pass." Often smoothest for visitors. 🌐 Has a built-in English UI toggle — great if your Chinese is zero. 💡 Kat's Tip Install both apps and bind a card on each before landing. If one mini-program crashes during a ticket drop (it happens), you can jump to the other. Don't discover at 8 PM that only one is working. Top 10 Attractions: Booking Cheat-Sheet The 10 most-asked-about spots in China — and the ones with special, unforgiving rules . Search the exact Chinese name below (copy-paste it), look for the Blue V, and follow the drop time. Everything else in China books the same way — just a normal 7-day window. Attraction Official Mini-Program (search this) Book Ahead Tickets Drop At Key Rule / Passport Note Forbidden City ★ hardest 故宫博物院 · Beijing 故宫博物院 7 days 20:00 (8 PM) daily ~40k slots/day, gone in minutes. No on-site sales. Entry via Meridian Gate only. Book the main palace + optional treasure/garden tickets separately. National Museum ★ hardest 中国国家博物馆 · Beijing 国家博物馆 7 days 17:00 (5 PM) daily Free, but you MUST reserve. Slots vanish in seconds. Bring passport + reservation QR; bag check is strict. Terracotta Army ★ hard 秦始皇帝陵博物院 · Xi'an 秦始皇帝陵博物院 8 days ~ 17:00 (verify in-app) Official name covers both the pits and the mausoleum. One ticket, two sites, same day. Verify exact drop time in the program. Giant Panda Base ★ hard 成都大熊猫繁育研究基地 · Chengdu 成都大熊猫繁育研究基地 7 days Opens 07:30 gallery time Split morning / afternoon sessions; morning sells out first. Go early — pandas are most active before 10 AM. North gate = pandas, south gate = newborns. Badaling Great Wall ★ medium 八达岭长城 · Beijing 八达岭长城 7–10 days Rolling release Pick a time slot (avoid holiday peaks). Cable car + ticket are separate. Mutianyu is the easier, prettier alternative. Summer Palace ★ easy 颐和园 · Beijing 颐和园 7 days Rolling release Park entry + through-ticket (联票) for inner halls. Usually available — book the morning before. Temple of Heaven ★ easy 天坛公园 · Beijing 天坛公园 7 days Rolling release Cheap park ticket vs through-ticket (联票) for the Hall of Prayer. Easy to get — book same week. Shanghai Museum ★ medium 上海博物馆 · Shanghai 上海博物馆 7 days ~12:00 (verify in-app) Two buildings need separate reservations: the People's Square branch and the East (东馆) branch. Book both if you want both. Huaqing Palace ★ easy 华清宫 · Xi'an 华清宫 7 days Rolling release Often combined with Terracotta on a Xi'an day trip. Hot-spring heritage site; evening show needs a separate ticket. Zhangjiajie Forest Park ★ medium 张家界国家森林公园 · Hunan 张家界旅游 7 days Rolling release Multi-day pass (most visitors do 2–3 days). Pick your entry gate (East/West) — they're far apart. Cable cars separate. ⚠️ Drop times shift with season and holidays (National Day in Oct and Spring Festival are brutal — book the instant windows open). Always confirm the exact release time inside the official mini-program the day before. This table was verified August 2026. ℹ️ The Other 90% Lakes, city walls, gardens, temples, and most provincial museums simply open a 7-day calendar you can grab any time. Use the same four steps — you just won't be racing the clock. No need to memorize anything; copy the Chinese name, find the Blue V, book. Common Mistakes & FAQ The stuff that actually goes wrong for first-timers — and the questions I get every week. ⚠️ Mistake 1 · Name order flipped Surname and given name in the wrong boxes. The gate scanner matches your passport exactly — a mismatch = no entry. Always mirror the passport's Surname / Given name fields. ⚠️ Mistake 2 · Wrong phone number Some programs text a confirmation to a +86 number. If you only have a foreign number, use your hotel's front-desk number — they'll hold the message. Or grab a local eSIM (guide linked below). ⚠️ Mistake 3 · Paid but didn't screenshot Payment succeeded, you closed the app, and the gate has no signal. Always screenshot the reservation QR the second you see "成功." A saved image beats a spinning loader. ⚠️ Mistake 4 · Booked the wrong branch Shanghai Museum, the Pandas, and Zhangjiajie all have multiple entries/branches with separate reservations. Double-check which one you picked before paying. Can I just buy a ticket at the gate? ▼ For the top spots — almost never. The Forbidden City, National Museum, Terracotta Army, and Panda Base are reservation-only , no walk-up sales. Smaller parks may sell at the gate, but booking ahead is always safer and often cheaper. Don't gamble your one day in Beijing on a hope. Do foreigners really need to reserve, or is that just for locals? ▼ Everyone, including foreign passport holders, must reserve — the real-name system applies to all visitors. In fact, booking with a passport is often easier because you skip the domestic ID queue. Some spots even have a separate foreign-visitor channel. Passport number or name in Chinese — which do I enter? ▼ Enter your name in Latin letters exactly as on the passport (Surname / Given name in the right boxes), and your passport number with no spaces. Never enter a Chinese translation of your name — the scanner reads the machine-readable zone, so it must match the English on the document. Do I need to print or collect a physical ticket? ▼ No. Show the reservation QR on your phone + your physical passport . Staff scan both; that's your ticket. Keep the passport on you the whole visit — random checks happen. How many people can one WeChat/Alipay account book? ▼ You can add multiple saved visitors (family/friends) and book them all in one order — just enter each person's passport info in Step 3 first. Limits vary by

text: 🗺️ Essential Apps · Step 7 · 高德地图 How to Use Amap (高德地图) in China Your China Google Maps alternative — and one of the most useful apps to have once you land. ⏱ 4 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 🆓 Free, English mode available 💡 Kat's Tip Google Maps technically loads in China, but the data is so outdated it's almost useless — missing roads, wrong subway exits, restaurants that closed years ago. Amap is what I actually use every single day, and it's the one my friends thank me for the most. 1 Why You Need Amap in China Amap (高德地图, "Gaode Ditu") is China's most widely used map app — think Google Maps, but built for how China actually works: real-time subway data, accurate walking routes, and restaurant listings that are actually current. You don't need to learn every feature. Just these: • Search for places by name, even without knowing the Chinese characters • Get walking, driving, or public transit directions • Check bus and metro routes with ETA and estimated cost • Find restaurants, attractions, hotels, and yes — public toilets • Share or save a location to send to a friend or a driver Amap even has an AR walking mode — hold your phone up and it overlays directional arrows on the real street through your camera. It's a fun bonus, not something you need to figure out to survive your trip. 2 Before You Start 1 Download Amap before you fly — it's easiest from home wifi (see our VPN guide if you need Google Play access to work first). 2 Open Settings inside the app and switch the language to English — this makes menus, buttons, and most place names readable. 3 Make sure you have mobile data once you land — see our eSIM guide . 4 Allow location access when the app asks — it needs this to actually navigate you anywhere. 5 When searching, try the English name first — Amap recognizes most tourist spots, hotels, and chains. If nothing comes up, that's when you'll want the Chinese name (your hotel confirmation email usually has it). 3 How to Search for a Place 1 Tap the search bar at the top of the screen. 2 Type the name of the place — a landmark, hotel, restaurant, or even something generic like "coffee" or "pharmacy." 3 Amap will show a list of matching results with distance from your current location. 4 Tap a result to see its address, photos, opening hours, and how far it is from you. 4 How to Get Directions Once you've found your destination, tap the blue "Route" or "Directions" button. You'll see tabs across the top for: • Walking — best for short distances, shows sidewalks and pedestrian paths accurately • Public Transit — combines bus and metro, shown in the next step • Driving / Taxi — useful even if you're not driving, since it shows you the route a Didi or taxi driver would take, and roughly how long it should take 5 How to Use Amap for Public Transportation This is where Amap genuinely outperforms Google Maps in China. Tap the Public Transit tab after searching a destination, and it shows you: • Which metro line(s) or bus route(s) to take, including transfers • Which exit to use at the metro station (this alone saves you from surfacing on the wrong side of a huge intersection) • Estimated travel time and number of stops • Estimated cost of the trip • Live ETA for the next bus, if you're taking one For the actual mechanics of boarding and paying, check our Bus Guide or Metro Guide . 6 One Important Tip for Foreign Travelers • Save your hotel's Chinese name and address somewhere you can access offline — a screenshot works fine. • Before you head out, take a screenshot of your destination's location pin and address. • If a taxi or Didi driver looks confused, show them the Chinese address on your screen instead of trying to say it out loud. • Don't rely only on English place names — some smaller spots only show up if you search a rough Chinese name or use the pin location instead. ⚠️ Watch Out Amap's English mode is very good but not 100% complete — some restaurant names or small business listings stay in Chinese. That's normal, not a bug. Screenshotting is still your best backup plan. FAQ Do I need a Chinese phone number to use Amap? ▼ No. You can download and use Amap with any Apple ID or Google account and no Chinese phone number — it works as a straightforward map and navigation app without needing an account for basic search and directions. Does Amap work without internet? ▼ You can download offline maps for specific cities in advance, which is worth doing as a backup — but live directions, transit times, and ETAs need an internet connection. Is Amap better than Google Maps in China? ▼ For navigating inside mainland China, yes — Amap's data is far more current and complete, since it's the app hundreds of millions of local users actually rely on daily. Google Maps' China data is comparatively outdated and sparse. Can I use Amap outside of China? ▼ Amap's coverage is focused on mainland China. Stick with Google Maps or Apple Maps once you leave — Amap isn't built for international navigation. 📱 Get the Free Apps Cheat Sheet A printable one-pager covering Amap, Dianping, Alipay, WeChat, and Didi — exactly what to set up before you land. snippet: complete guide to arriving in china as a foreigner. immigration queues, arrival card, customs declaration, baggage claim, and what to do in your first hour after landing.
text: 🛃 After You Arrive · 入境指南 China Immigration & Arrival: What to Expect Step by Step Landing in China for the first time feels big. The airport signs are in Chinese, there are queues everywhere, and you're jet-lagged. Here's exactly what happens from the moment the plane lands to the moment you're in a taxi to your hotel — so there are no surprises. ⏱ 7 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Step-by-step with no gaps 💡 Pre-Fill Your Arrival Card Online China now lets you fill in your Arrival Card online up to 72 hours before landing — search "中国入境健康申报" or ask your airline. Skip the paper form on the plane and go straight to immigration. Huge time-saver. 1 On the Plane (Before Landing) 1 Flight attendants may distribute an Arrival Card (入境卡) — fill it in if given one (name, passport number, flight number, hotel address in China, purpose of visit) 2 Have your hotel address in Chinese ready — immigration may ask for it 3 Have your return or onward flight information accessible 4 Switch your phone to the China eSIM if you have one — it activates when you land 5 Keep your passport in your hand — you'll need it multiple times in the next hour 2 Immigration (入境检查) 1 Follow signs to 入境 (Immigration) — usually very well marked in English too 2 Join the 外国人 (Foreigners) queue — separate from Chinese citizens 3 At the booth, hand over your passport + Arrival Card 4 The officer will take your fingerprints and a photo — completely routine, don't be nervous 5 If asked questions, keep answers simple: purpose = tourism (旅游 lǚ yóu) (or whatever your purpose is), duration = your planned stay 6 They stamp your passport and hand it back — you're in China! YAYYY 🇨🇳 💡 What the Officer Might Ask "What is the purpose of your visit?" → "Tourism/Business trip/Study/Visit" / "How long will you stay?" → "[X] days" "Where are you staying?" → Show your hotel booking on your phone Officers are professional and used to 'foreigners'. Relax — this takes under 5 minutes. 3 Customs Declaration (海关申报) ✅ You Can Bring Up to ¥5,000 RMB cash without declaring Up to $5,000 USD equivalent in foreign currency Personal electronics (phone, laptop, camera) Power banks (must be under 20,000mAh and has a 3C (CCC) sign — check yours) Prescription medication (bring doctor's note) 200 cigarettes or 50 cigars 1.5 litres of alcohol ❌ Do NOT Bring Fresh fruit, vegetables, or meat products Dairy products More than ¥20,000 RMB cash without declaring Weapons or anything that looks like one Content that could be deemed politically sensitive Power banks over 20,000mAh or 100Wh Most travelers take the green "Nothing to Declare" channel. If you're unsure, use the red channel and ask — officers are helpful. 💡 Fresh Food Rule The "no fresh food" rule is strictly enforced. That banana you were eating on the plane? Finish it or throw it away before landing. Customs dogs are excellent and fines for undeclared food items start at ¥2,000. 4 Baggage Claim & Arrivals Hall 1 Follow signs to 行李提取 (Baggage Claim) 2 Check the departure board for your flight number and belt number 3 If your bag is lost or damaged: report it at the airline desk before leaving the baggage area — after you leave, claims become much harder 4 Exit through customs (green or red channel) into the Arrivals Hall 5 You're out! Now: ignore taxi touts (there are lots od spam), find the SIM counter if needed, then get your Didi or airport metro ⚠️ First 5 Minutes Outside Arrivals People WILL approach you offering taxis, rides, or help with luggage. They are not official. Better say "no thanks," and keep walking. Get your phone out, open Didi, and book your ride from the official ride-hailing zone (网约车区) — all airports have one, follow the signs. 5 Your First Hour Priority List 1 SIM / eSIM Activate your eSIM or buy a SIM — you need data NOW 2 VPN Connect to your VPN to access Instagram, WhatsApp etc. 3 Didi Book your ride to the hotel from the 网约车 zone 4 Hotel Check in, get their Chinese address card, ask and connect to Wi-Fi Next Steps → 🚗 Get a Didi From the airport to your hotel safely 🚇 Metro Guide Airport metro is often fastest and cheapest 📲 QR Payments How to pay for everything in China 📚 All Guides → Everything you need for your China trip

snippet: why travel insurance is essential for china, what to look for, recommended providers, and how much it costs. one hospital visit without insurance can cost $5,000+.
text: 🏥 Before You Fly · 旅行保险 Travel Insurance for China: What You Need and Why This is the step most travelers skip. Then something goes wrong and they wish they hadn't. A hospital visit in Beijing without insurance can cost ¥5,000–50,000 ($700–7,000 USD). Travel insurance costs about $3–8 per day. The math is obvious. ⏱ 6 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ From $3/day 1 Why Travel Insurance Matters China is generally a safe destination, but unexpected things can still happen. A sudden illness, an accident, a cancelled flight, or lost luggage can turn a smooth trip into an expensive headache. Travel insurance can help cover unexpected medical and travel costs, giving you one less thing to worry about while you're exploring China. You probably won't need it. But if you do, you'll be very glad you have it. 💰 Real Numbers Standard consultation at Beijing United Family Hospital: ¥800–2,000 Overnight hospital stay: ¥3,000–15,000 Appendectomy surgery: ¥30,000–80,000 Medical evacuation to home country: up to $150,000 USD 10-day travel insurance (World Nomads): ~$45 USD 2 What to Look For in Your Travel Insurance 🩺 Essential Coverage Emergency medical expenses: Look for a substantial medical coverage limit suitable for your trip. Emergency medical evacuation: Particularly important if you're travelling to remote areas or taking part in outdoor activities. 24/7 emergency assistance hotline: Ideally with English-language support. Hospital direct billing: Check whether the insurer can arrange direct payment or assistance with hospital bills. 👍 Good to have Trip cancellation/interruption Lost or stolen luggage (¥500 minimum cover) Passport/document replacement Missed connections Coverage for activities such as hiking or cycling 🔍 Check Before Buying Is China explicitly listed as a covered destination? Are pre-existing conditions covered? What's the deductible/excess per claim? Does it cover COVID-19 related cancellations? Does your credit card already include travel insurance? (Many do!) Are there restrictions based on your nationality, age, or trip length? ⚠️ Common Gaps Extreme sports often excluded — check if you're hiking or cycling Some policies don't cover trips over 30 days Pre-existing conditions often excluded without upgrade "Cancel for any reason" is usually a separate add-on 3 Recommended Providers 🌍 World Nomads — Best for adventurous travelers Covers adventure activities (hiking, cycling, water sports) that most standard policies exclude. Great for independent travelers. Can buy and extend online even mid-trip. Available in most countries. ✅ worldnomads.com — from ~$45 USD / 10 days. Covers most of what independent travelers need. 🛡️ SafetyWing — Best for long-term travelers Subscription-based ($49/4 weeks) — perfect if you're staying in China for a month or traveling through multiple Asian countries. Renews automatically, cancel any time. ✅ safetywing.com — very affordable for longer trips. Covers up to 30 days outside your home country per policy period. 🛜 EKTA — Best for straightforward travel coverage KAT'S PICK Flexible travel insurance for international trips, with coverage options for medical expenses, emergency assistance, trip disruptions, and more. A good option if you're looking for straightforward coverage for your China trip. ✅ ektainsurance.com — explore available plans and check coverage for your destination and travel dates. 🏢 Allianz Travel — Best comprehensive coverage More traditional travel insurer with very comprehensive medical coverage and excellent 24/7 support. Slightly more expensive but trusted by millions of travelers globally. ✅ allianztravelinsurance.com — good if you want a household-name insurer with deep pockets. 4 How to Use Your Insurance in China 1 Before travelling: save your policy number and the 24/7 emergency hotline in your phone contacts 2 Print or screenshot your insurance card — keep it in your wallet alongside your passport 3 When something happens: call your insurer's emergency line first — they'll guide you to the right hospital and can often arrange direct billing 4 Keep all receipts and medical reports — required for reimbursement claims 5 For international hospitals in China, show your insurance card at reception — many have direct billing arrangements 💡 Best International Hospitals in China Beijing: Beijing United Family Hospital (+86 10 5927-7000) Shanghai: Shanghai United Family Hospital (+86 21 2216-3900) Guangzhou: Guangzhou United Family Hospital (+86 20 2290-7600) Chengdu: Chengdu United Family Hospital (+86 28 6680-0888) These hospitals have English-speaking staff and are used to working with international insurance. snippet: how qr code payments work in china. scan with alipay or wechat — not your camera app. step-by-step guide for restaurants, shops, transport, and street food.
text: 📲 After You Arrive · 扫码支付 How to Pay with QR Codes in China This trips up almost every first-time visitor. When a vendor in China shows you a QR code, you do NOT scan it with your phone's camera app (sometimes it doesn't work). You open Alipay or WeChat and scan from inside the app. That one difference unlocks the entire payment system. ⏱ 5 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Works with foreign cards How to Pay → 📥 Download PDF 🔑 The One Thing to Remember Open Alipay or WeChat → tap Scan → point at QR code → done. NOT your camera app. NOT a QR scanner app. Alipay or WeChat only. 1 How to Scan and Pay (Alipay) 1 Open Alipay 2 Tap the Scan (扫一扫) icon at the top of the home screen 3 Point your camera at the vendor's QR code 4 Enter the amount if prompted (or it auto-fills) 5 Confirm with your fingerprint, face ID, or 6-digit PIN 6 A green ✅ and a success sound confirms payment — show the screen to the vendor 💡 WeChat Pay — Same Process Open WeChat → tap + (top right) → Scan → point at code → confirm. Identical experience. Use whichever app you prefer — both work everywhere. 2 When the Vendor Scans YOU Sometimes (especially at supermarkets and convenience stores) the vendor scans your QR code instead. Here's how: 1 Open Alipay → tap Pay/Collect or look for a barcode icon 2 A barcode and QR code appear on your screen 3 Hold your screen up to the vendor's scanner 4 You'll get a notification when the payment goes through ℹ️ Which Method When? You scan vendor's QR : (the most of time) Restaurants, market stalls, small shops, taxis, vending machines Vendor scans your QR : (the most of time) Supermarkets, convenience stores (7-Eleven, FamilyMart), pharmacies 3 Where You'll Use QR Payments 🍜 Restaurants Scan the table QR → digital menu appears → order and pay in one flow Or scan the payment QR at the counter Many restaurants : cash-free — QR or nothing If you're confused, show staff your Alipay scan screen — they'll guide you 🚇 Transport Metro: Open Alipay → click "transport" → get QR → scan at gate Bus: Same as metro — Alipay or WeChat transit QR Didi: Payment is automatic through the app after your ride (don't pay twice) Bike sharing: Scan the bike's QR with Alipay to unlock 🛍️ Shopping Street markets: vendor shows you QR on phone — you scan Supermarkets: self-checkout with Alipay or vendor scans your barcode Vending machines: scan the screen's QR with Alipay Tourist sites: tickets often sold via QR scan + WeChat mini-program 🏪 Convenience Stores 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Lawson all over China Open 24/7 — great for snacks, water, phone chargers Show your Alipay barcode at checkout English-labeled products available at larger branches 📲 Get the Free QR Payment Cheat Sheet One-page printable showing exactly how to pay at restaurants, shops, and transport — with screenshots. Keep it on your phone for your first week. Send Me the PDF ✉️ ✅ On its way! No spam. I reply personally. snippet: what's blocked in china, which vpns actually work in 2026, and how to set one up before you fly. google, instagram, whatsapp are all blocked — here's the honest guide.
text: 🌐 Before You Fly · 网络与VPN VPN for China: How to Stay Connected China's internet is different. Google, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube and hundreds of western sites are blocked. A VPN lets you use them normally — but there's one critical rule: download and test the VPN BEFORE you land in China. ⏱ 8 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Tested in China 🚨 The Most Important Rule You might not be able to download VPN apps from the App Store or Google Play once you're inside China — they're removed from the Chinese versions of these stores. Download, install, and TEST your VPN at home before your flight. This is the number one mistake first-time visitors make. 1 "Do I need a VPN in China?" Not necessarily to be honest. But if you rely heavily on Google services, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, or other services that may not be directly accessible from mainland China, it's worth planning your internet access before you arrive. 2 What's Blocked in China? China's internet filter (called the "Great Firewall") blocks thousands of foreign websites and apps. Here's what you need to know: 🚫 Blocked — doesn't work without a VPN 🔍 Google Search 📧 Gmail ▶️ YouTube 📸 Instagram 💬 WhatsApp 📘 Facebook 🐦 Twitter/X 👻 Snapchat 🎵 Spotify 🎬 Netflix 🗺️ Google Maps 🤖 ChatGPT 💼 LinkedIn 📰 BBC / NYT ✅ Works fine — no VPN needed 💬 WeChat 💳 Alipay 🗺️ Amap 🚗 Didi 🍽️ Dianping 🚄 Trip.com 🍎 iMessage 📱 Apple Maps ✈️ Booking.com 📺 TikTok (Chinese ver) 💡 Honest Reality Most of your day-to-day China life (maps, payments, food, transport) uses Chinese apps that work perfectly without a VPN. You'll only miss Instagram, WhatsApp, and Google. Once you're set up with the right apps, it's genuinely fine. 2 Which VPN Actually Works in China? A VPN stands for a virtual private network, what it's essentially doing is tricking the system. For example, when i set my location to the U.S. (while I am in China), I can access everything I would be able to access when I in the U.S.. 🛡️ ExpressVPN — Most reliable in China RECOMMENDED Consistently works in China even during politically sensitive periods. Servers in Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore are fastest for China. ~$8–13/month. 30-day money-back guarantee. ✅ expressvpn.com — Download before you fly. 🔒 NordVPN — Great value, very reliable Strong obfuscated servers that work well in China. Slightly slower than ExpressVPN but much cheaper on longer plans. ~$3–5/month on 2-year plans. ✅ nordvpn.com — Good budget option. ⚡ Surfshark — Best for multiple devices Unlimited simultaneous connections make it a great choice if you're travelling with multiple devices or sharing with family. Fast, easy to use, and often one of the more affordable options on longer plans. 💡 surfshark.com — Good value if you want to protect multiple devices with one subscription. ⚠️ On Legality VPN use by tourists in China is a legal grey area. Millions of foreign visitors use them every year without any issues. The Chinese government's enforcement focuses on VPN providers and businesses, not individual tourists using them for personal use. Use it sensibly — for personal browsing, not anything that would draw attention. 3 How to Set Up Your VPN Before Flying 1 Choose a VPN (ExpressVPN or NordVPN recommended) and sign up on their website 2 Download the app on ALL your devices — phone, tablet, laptop 3 Connect to a Hong Kong or Japan server to test — these are fastest from China 4 Open Google, Instagram, YouTube on your phone and your laptop (if you need to work on your laptop)— confirm everything works 5 Look for the VPN's "Stealth" or "Obfuscated" mode — enable it. This makes VPN traffic harder for the firewall to detect. 6 In China: connect to VPN → then open your apps. That's it. (you can always keep it open!) 💡 Backup Plan Download 2–3 VPN apps. The firewall occasionally blocks specific VPN servers. If one stops working, switch to another. Having a backup takes 5 minutes now and saves a lot of frustration later. text: 💳 Payment Guide · 支付宝设置 How to Set Up Alipay as a Foreigner China is almost entirely cashless — street food stalls, taxis, supermarkets, temples. Everything runs on QR codes. My friend Kory couldn't pay for dinner on her first night because she assumed her credit card would work. But the store waitress said 'Please use your Alipay to pay for your bill, we dont have the credit card machine'. Set this up before you fly and you'll never have that problem. ⏱ 5 min setup 📅 Updated July 2026 ✅ Works with Visa & Mastercard Start the Guide → 📥 Get your FREE offline PDF guide 1 Download Get the Alipay app from App Store or Google Play 2 Sign Up Register with your international phone number 3 Verify Complete real-name verification with your passport 4 Bind Card Link your Visa, Mastercard, or other international card 1 Download the Alipay App 1 Open App Store (iPhone) or Google Play (Android) 2 Search for "Alipay" — look for the blue 支 icon 3 Tap "Get" or "Install" and wait for the download 4 Open the app — the welcome screen will appear 💡 Kat's Tip Make sure you have a stable network connection. The app is about 200MB. 2 Create Your Account 1 Tap "Sign Up" on the welcome screen 2 Select your country code (e.g., +1 for USA, +44 for UK) 3 Enter your international phone number 4 Enter the SMS verification code you receive 5 Set a secure password (6–20 characters) ⚠️ Important Use a phone number you can receive SMS on. A Chinese number is NOT required — any international number works! 3 Real-Name Verification 1 Go to "Me" tab → tap your profile picture 2 Select "Identity Verification" or "Real-Name Auth" 3 Choose "Passport" as your ID type 4 Take a clear photo of your passport info page 5 Complete face recognition (follow the on-screen prompts) 🕐 Processing Time Verification usually takes a few minutes to 24 hours. You'll get a notification when approved. Don't worry if it doesn't happen instantly — it almost always goes through. 4 Link Your Bank Card 1 Go to "Me" → "Bank Cards" → "Add Card" 2 Enter your card number manually or scan it with your camera 3 Fill in your expiry date and CVV/CVC code 4 Enter the SMS verification code sent by your bank 5 Set a payment password for security 💳 Supported Cards Visa, Mastercard, Diners Club, Discover, JCB, and most major international cards are supported. AmEx sometimes has issues — Visa and Mastercard work most reliably. 📱 Before you bind Let your bank know you're travelling to China so they don't flag the Alipay verification as a suspicious transaction. A quick call or app notification takes 2 minutes. ✅ You're All Set! text: 🚌 Getting Around · Step 8 · 公交指南 How to Take a Public Bus in China The metro gets all the attention, but buses go where the metro doesn't. No English announcements, no idea where to pay — here's exactly how to ride one without panicking. ⏱ 6 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 🎫 Flat fare, usually under ¥3 💡 Kat's Tip Buses freaked my friend Max out more than anything else his first solo trip to Beijing — no announcements in English, drivers who will absolutely leave without him, so we had to do Facetime all the way. Set up your transport QR code the night before you need it, not while standing at the stop. The 10-Second Version 1. Set up your code first Activate your transport QR code in Alipay before you need it — do this from your hotel, not the bus stop. 2. Board at the front Scan your code on the reader by the driver as you get on. Flat fare, usually ¥1–3 RMB. 3. Watch your stop Track your position on Amap or Baidu Maps — don't rely on catching a Chinese-only announcement. 4. Exit at the back Press the stop-request button (although most drivers stop at every stop), then get off through the rear door — even though you boarded at the front. 1 Set Up Your Transport QR Code Before You Travel Do this from your hotel or apartment with good wifi — not standing at a bus stop with a queue behind you. Using Alipay (recommended) 1 Complete passport identity verification in Alipay if you haven't already (see our Alipay guide ). 2 Link an international Visa or Mastercard — no Chinese bank account required. 3 Tap the transport icon on the Alipay home screen, or search "公交地铁" (bus & metro). 4 Select your city and activate the transit code — you'll need to activate it separately for each city you visit. 5 Your personal QR code now generates on demand under the transport tab. Prefer WeChat? Search "乘车码" (chéngchēmǎ) inside WeChat Pay — setup is similar, though foreign card support varies more by city. ⚠️ Do This The Night Before Identity verification can occasionally take a few hours to process. Don't find this out at 8am with a bus pulling away. 2 Find Your Bus and Stop • Use Amap (高德地图) or Baidu Maps for accurate routes and real-time arrival — Google Maps does not reliably work for China transit. • Bus stop signs list every route number that stops there, with the full sequence of stops in Chinese. Match your route number carefully. • Bus numbers in big cities run into the hundreds — double check you're boarding the right one, since several routes often share a stop. 3 Board and Scan Your Code 1 Buses board through the front door only in most cities. Have your code ready before you reach the driver. 2 Open Alipay, tap the transport icon, and let your code generate. Max out your screen brightness. 3 Hold the code 5–10 cm from the reader by the driver for 1–2 seconds until it beeps green. 4 Fares are flat on almost all city routes — pay once on entry, no tapping out. ℹ️ Backup Plan If your code fails to scan, most buses still accept coins in a fare box (exact change only, no change given). Keep a few ¥1 coins on you during your first week. 4 Find a Seat (or Hold On) • Seats near the front are reserved for elderly, pregnant, and disabled passengers — marked with a special icon. • Standing is completely normal, even for long rides. Hold the overhead rail — buses brake hard and often. • Rush hour is roughly 7:30–9am and 5–7pm. Riding just outside those windows is far more comfortable. 5 Know When to Get Off • Most buses announce the next stop over a speaker and on a screen — usually Chinese only, sometimes English or pinyin in bigger cities. • Track your live location on Amap or Baidu Maps instead of relying on the announcement. • Press the red stop-request button one stop before you want to get off — buses generally don't stop unless requested. • Exit through the rear door — the norm across almost every Chinese city, even though you boarded at the front. FAQ: Things Nobody Tells You About Chinese Buses Do I need exact change if I don't have a QR code set up? ▼ Yes. Fare boxes don't give change, so you need the exact fare in coins or small notes. This is exactly why setting up your Alipay transit code in advance is worth the ten minutes. Is the same QR code used for the metro? ▼ In most cities, yes — the same Alipay transit code that opens metro gates also works scanning onto buses. One setup covers both. What if the bus is full and doesn't stop for me? ▼ This happens, especially during rush hour. Don't take it personally — just wait for the next one. Frequency on major routes is usually every 5–10 minutes. Can I use a bank card or Apple Pay instead of Alipay? ▼ Some cities — including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Chengdu — are piloting direct contactless bank card entry, but support is inconsistent station-by-station. Set up Alipay regardless. Do kids ride free? ▼ Children under 1.2 meters tall generally ride free on buses, the metro, and high-speed rail — no ticket or QR code needed for them. Are there English announcements? ▼ Sometimes, especially in Tier 1 cities on major routes, but don't count on it. This is exactly why we recommend tracking your stop visually on Amap or Baidu Maps. 🗺️ Get the Free Transit Cheat Sheet A printable one-pager: Alipay transport code setup, bus vs metro vs bike, and the Chinese characters for "next stop" and "get off here." text: 🆘 Safety & Emergency · 紧急情况 Emergency Numbers & What to Do If Something Goes Wrong in China The vast majority of trips to China go completely smoothly. But knowing this guide exists — and having it saved on your phone — means you'll travel with a calmness that actually makes your whole trip better. Read it once, save it, then forget about it and enjoy China. ⏱ 5 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Save this page offline 💡 Do This Right Now Screenshot the emergency numbers below and save them to your phone's camera roll — so you can access them even without internet. Takes 10 seconds and could save your trip. 📞 Emergency Numbers — Save These Now 110 👮 Police Theft, assault, anything threatening your safety. Text 12110 if you can't speak Mandarin. 120 🚑 Ambulance State your condition and location clearly. Get travel insurance — one ambulance ride can cost ¥500+. 119 🔥 Fire Call immediately. Give your exact address. Evacuate the building first. 122 🚗 Traffic Road accidents in cities. For expressway accidents dial 12122. 12308 🌍 Foreign Affairs Lost passport, consular emergencies, legal issues. Multilingual support available. 12367 📋 Immigration Visa questions, overstay issues, entry and exit problems. 2 What to Do in Specific Situations 🪪 Lost or Stolen Passport 1 Stay calm — this is manageable. It happens to travelers every day. 2 Call 12308 (Foreign Affairs hotline) for guidance 3 Go to the nearest police station and file a loss report (失物报案证明) — you'll need this document 4 Contact your home country's embassy or consulate in China to apply for an emergency travel document 5 Keep a photo of your passport in your cloud storage — makes the process much faster Prevention Before you travel: photograph your passport and email it to yourself + store in cloud. Done. 🏥 Getting Sick or Injured 1 For emergencies: call 120 for an ambulance or take a Didi to the nearest hospital 2 Look for 国际医院 (International Hospital) — they have English-speaking doctors 3 Show your travel insurance card and policy number at reception — saves you enormous paperwork later 4 Key hospitals with international departments: Beijing United Family Hospital , Shanghai United Family Hospital , Chengdu United Family Hospital 5 Call your travel insurer's 24/7 hotline — they can coordinate payment directly with the hospital ⚠️ Why Insurance is Non-Negotiable A standard hospital consultation costs ¥300–800. An overnight stay can be ¥3,000–10,000. Surgery? Potentially ¥100,000+. Travel insurance costs ~¥30–50/day. The math is obvious. → See our travel insurance guide 😱 Scammed or Robbed 1 Get to a safe, public location first 2 Call 110 (Police) or send SMS to 12110 if you can't speak Mandarin 3 Go to the nearest police station to file a report — you'll need this for insurance claims 4 Cancel any stolen bank cards immediately via your bank's app Common Tourist Scams in China Tea ceremony scam: "Friendly local" invites you for tea, then presents a ¥500 bill. Decline invitations from strangers leading you to private venues. Art student scam: Student asks you to see their "gallery exhibition" — overpriced prints then sold under pressure. Taxi overcharge: Always use Didi. If taking a licensed taxi, insist on the meter (打表). 🚂 Missed Train or Flight 1 Trains: Go to the ticket office immediately — you can usually switch to the next available train for a small fee (¥5–50) 2 Flights: Go to your airline's desk in the airport — policies vary. Some allow rebooking for a fee, others require buying a new ticket. 3 Trip.com has 24/7 English customer service — open the app → Help Center → chat with agent 4 Travel insurance with "missed connection" coverage pays for rebooking costs — another reason to always have it 📱 Lost Phone 1 Use Find My (iPhone) or Find My Device (Android) from another phone or computer to locate or remotely wipe 2 Report to police to get the loss report needed for insurance 3 Temporarily borrow a phone to contact your travel insurer 4 Budget Chinese smartphones are available for ¥300–600 at local phone shops if needed Prevention Enable cloud backup (iCloud or Google) before travelling. Keep your emergency contacts in your wallet on paper. Old school, but it works. 3 Key Embassy & Consulate Contacts 🇺🇸 US Embassy Beijing +86 10 8531-4000 Emergency: +86 10 8531-4000 Consulates: Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Wuhan, Shenyang 🇬🇧 UK Embassy Beijing +86 10 5192-4000 Emergency: +86 10 5192-4000 Consulates: Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chongqing, Wuhan 🇦🇺 Australian Embassy Beijing +86 10 5140-4111 Emergency: +86 10 5140-4111 Consulates: Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu 🇨🇦 Canadian Embassy Beijing +86 10 5139-4000 Emergency: +86 10 5139-4000 Consulates: Shanghai, Guangzhou 💡 Find Your Embassy Search " your country embassy Beijing China" before you travel and save the emergency number in your phone contacts. Takes 2 minutes. snippet: 30 essential chinese phrases every traveler needs. greetings, shopping, transport, emergencies, and food — with pinyin pronunciation guide. no mandarin experience needed.
text: 🗣️ After You Arrive · 实用中文 Essential Chinese Phrases Every Traveler Needs You don't need to speak Mandarin fluently to have an incredible time in China. But knowing 20 phrases will take you surprisingly far — and trying even one word in Chinese will instantly make locals warmer, more helpful, and more excited to interact with you. Effort matters more than perfection. ⏱ 10 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ With pinyin pronunciation See All Phrases → 📥 Download PDF 📖 Quick Pinyin Guide — How to Read the Pronunciation Mandarin has 4 tones — the same sound in a different tone means a completely different word. Don't worry too much about this for now. Most locals will understand you from context even if your tones are off. mā 1st tone — flat and high má 2nd tone — rising (like a question) mǎ 3rd tone — dip then rise mà 4th tone — sharp falling 👋 Greetings & Basics 你好 nǐ hǎo Hello The most important phrase. Use it everywhere. 谢谢 xiè xiè Thank you Say this constantly — Chinese people appreciate politeness enormously. 对不起 duì bu qǐ Sorry / Excuse me Use to apologise. 不客气 bú kè qì You're welcome Said after someone thanks you 谢谢. 是 / 不是 shì / bú shì Yes / No Simple but powerful. Nod for yes too. 🗺️ Getting Around 在哪里？ zài nǎ lǐ? Where is...? Point at a map then say this. Works every time. 去...怎么走？ qù... zěn me zǒu? How do I get to...? Fill in the destination name. Show on phone map. 打表 dǎ biǎo Use the meter (in a Hongkong taxi) Say this when getting in a taxi(not in Didi. You pay for Didi online). 停一下 tíng yī xià Please stop here For taxi (not Didi, you set your destination online for didi already). Point ahead too to clarify. 地铁站 dì tiě zhàn Metro station Point and say this to find the nearest metro. 🛒 Shopping & Money 多少钱？ duō shǎo qián? How much does it cost? Essential at markets. Point at the item. 太贵了 tài guì le Too expensive! Say while shaking your head. Opens negotiations. 便宜一点 pián yí yī diǎn A bit cheaper please The magic phrase at markets. Always try. 扫码 sǎo mǎ Scan (QR code to pay) Say this and open your Alipay — they'll understand. 买单 mǎi dān The bill please At restaurants. Or just show your Alipay scan icon. 🍜 Food & Dining 不辣 bù là Not spicy Critical in Sichuan, Hunan, and Yunnan provinces if you cannot handle spicy food. 好吃！ hǎo chī! Delicious! Every chef and vendor loves hearing this. Use generously. 不要香菜 bú yào xiāng cài No coriander / cilantro If you hate it like me, this phrase is your best friend in China. 这个 zhè gè This one (while pointing) The most versatile ordering phrase. Works everywhere. 一份 yī fèn One portion / one serving Hold up one finger too. 两份 (liǎng fèn) = two portions. 🆘 Emergencies 我是外国人 wǒ shì wài guó rén I am a foreigner Opens up more patience and slower speech from locals. 我需要帮助 wǒ xū yào bāng zhù I need help Chinese people are generally very willing to help tourists. 叫救护车 jiào jiù hù chē Call an ambulance Or just dial 120. Keep this saved. 我的护照丢了 wǒ de hù zhào diū le I lost my passport Show this to police or hotel staff. 我不懂 wǒ bù dǒng I don't understand Honest and helpful. Follow with phone translation. 请慢点说 qǐng màn diǎn shuō Please speak more slowly Most locals will slow down and repeat if asked politely. 💡 Kat's Honest Advice on Chinese Don't try to learn Mandarin in a week before your trip. Focus on 5–8 phrases you'll actually use (hello, thank you, not spicy, the bill, I need help) and let Google Translate + Alipay handle the rest. The goal is connection, not fluency. Locals are endlessly impressed by any effort from a foreign visitor — even one word earns you a huge smile. 🗣️ Get the Free Phrases Cheat Sheet PDF All 30 phrases in one printable card — Chinese characters, pinyin, and English. Screenshot it or print it before you fly. Send Me the PDF ✉️ ✅ On its way! No spam. I reply personally. snippet: complete guide to using the metro in china's major cities. buy tickets, use alipay qr codes, read signs, and navigate like a local. beijing, shanghai, chengdu metro tips.
text: 🚇 Getting Around · 地铁指南 How to Use the Metro in China China's city metros are modern, clean, cheap, and incredibly easy to use — even if you don't speak any Mandarin. Most stations have English signs and the ticket machines have an English option. Master the metro and you'll unlock every corner of the city for ¥3–10 per trip. ⏱ 8 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ English signs in all major cities How to Buy a Ticket → 📥 Download PDF 1 How to Buy a Metro Ticket You have three ways to pay for the metro in China. Option 2 (Alipay/WeChat QR) is fastest once you're set up: ✅ Option 1: Ticket Machine (Easiest for First Timers) Find the ticket machine in the station — they're always near the gate Press the English button (usually top right corner) Select your destination from the map on screen Choose quantity (X ticket) Pay with cash (coins or small notes) or Alipay/WeChat QR, foreign bank cards work in some station. Collect your token — a small round plastic disc ⚡ Option 2: Alipay or WeChat QR Code (I would recommend Alipay - the fastest and easiest) Open Alipay → tap Transport or scan the QR reader at the gate Select your city A QR code appears — hold it to the scanner at the gate Gate opens — fare is automatically deducted at exit No ticket machine, no queuing, no tokens. This is how locals do it.(And it also works on buses) 💡 Option 3: City Transport Card Each city has a rechargeable card (Beijing: Yikatong, Shanghai: Jiaotong Card) available at the service desk. 2 Navigating the Station 1 Look for the 地铁 (dìtiě) sign outside — red or blue depending on city 2 Security check first — put your bag through the X-ray. This is mandatory at ALL Chinese metro stations. 3 Tap or scan your token/QR at the entry gate 4 Find your line and direction on the overhead signs — always shown in Chinese and English 5 Board the train — announcements are in Mandarin and English 6 At your stop, tap out with your token (insert into the slot) or QR scan at the exit gate ⚠️ Don't Forget to Tap OUT With Alipay, the fare is calculated at exit — you must scan when leaving. If you forget, the system charges you the maximum fare (around 15 yuan/trip). 3 City-by-City Metro Tips 🏙️ Beijing Metro 27 lines, 490+ stations — huge network Line 1 and Line 10 cover most tourist sites Airport Express: Line 10 + Airport Express (¥25, 30 min to Terminal 3) Rush hours brutal: 7:30–9am, 5:30–7pm — avoid with luggage App: Beijing Metro app (English available) 🌆 Shanghai Metro 20 lines, 500+ stations — one of world's largest Line 2 connects Pudong Airport to city centre (¥7, 50 min) Line 10 is great for the Bund and French Concession Clean, well-signed, easiest for first-timers App: Metro大都会 (Shanghai Metro official) 🐼 Chengdu Metro 13 lines covering the whole city Line 10 goes directly to Tianfu Airport Line 3 for Chunxi Road shopping and food street Less crowded than Beijing/Shanghai Bilingual signs throughout ✅ 💡 All Cities Fares: ¥2–15 depending on distance All major city metros have English signs ✅ Alipay QR works in all city metros ✅ Free Wi-Fi in most stations (needs Chinese phone number to activate) Lost? 客服中心 (Customer Service) is always staffed 🚇 Get the Free Metro Cheat Sheet PDF One-page printable: how to buy tickets, key Mandarin signs translated, and metro tips for Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. As of 2026, travellers from 50 countries can enter China without applying for a visa in advance. Here's everything you need to know — updated and verified. ⏱ 5 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ 50 countries visa-free 🔴 Policy Update · August 2026 50 Countries Can Now Enter China Visa-Free China has dramatically expanded its open-door policy. As of 2026, ordinary passport holders from 50 countries can enter mainland China for up to 30 days without applying for a visa — for tourism, business, family visits, or transit. The policy is confirmed until December 31, 2026 . 🇩🇪 Germany 🇫🇷 France 🇬🇧 UK 🇮🇹 Italy 🇪🇸 Spain 🇳🇱 Netherlands 🇦🇺 Australia 🇳🇿 New Zealand 🇸🇬 Singapore 🇯🇵 Japan 🇰🇷 South Korea 🇧🇷 Brazil 🇦🇷 Argentina 🇨🇱 Chile 🇲🇾 Malaysia 🇹🇭 Thailand 🇦🇪 UAE 🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia 🇸🇪 Sweden 🇳🇴 Norway 🇨🇭 Switzerland + 29 more countries → ⚠️ US and India are NOT on the 30-day visa-free list — Canada joined in February 2026. Beijing (PEK/PKX) Shanghai (PVG/SHA) Guangzhou (CAN) Chengdu (CTU) Other major city Check My Visa Requirement → ⚠️ This tool is for general guidance only. Always verify with the official China Visa Service Centre or your nearest embassy before booking. The 3 Ways to Enter China ✅ 30-Day Visa-Free 50 countries can enter without a visa for up to 30 days. No application needed — just show up with your passport. Valid for tourism, business, family visits, and transit. ⏱️ 240-Hour Transit (10 Days) Passing through China to a third country? 55 nationalities (including the USA) can stay up to 10 days visa-free at 65 ports — perfect for a mini trip on the way somewhere else. 📋 Tourist Visa (L Visa) If your country needs a visa, apply at the Chinese Embassy before you fly. The L (tourist) visa is the standard option. Processing takes 4–7 business days. Plan ahead. How to Apply for a China Tourist Visa (L Visa) If your country isn't on the visa-free list or you plan to stay over 30 days, don't worry — the application process is straightforward. Here's exactly how to do it. 1 Check your local Chinese Embassy or Visa Application Centre Find your nearest centre at visaforchina.cn . In some countries (like the US, UK, Australia) you apply at a dedicated Visa Application Service Centre, not the embassy directly. 2 Prepare your documents You'll typically need: valid passport (6+ months remaining), completed visa application form, passport photo, flight bookings, hotel bookings, and bank statements showing you can fund your trip. Requirements vary slightly by country. 3 Submit your application Most countries require an in-person visit. Bring original documents plus photocopies. Pay the visa fee at the counter (card or cash — check in advance). 4 Wait for processing Standard processing: 4–7 business days. Express service (1–2 days) is available at extra cost. Don't book non-refundable flights until your visa is approved. 5 Collect and double-check your visa Check: your name is spelled correctly, the dates match your trip, the number of entries (single or double/multiple). Report any errors immediately. 💡 Kat's Tip Apply at least 3 weeks before your trip — not 3 days. Even if standard processing is 4–7 days, things can go wrong. Give yourself a buffer. I've seen friends scramble at the last minute and it's stressful. Official Visa Application Portal → Frequently Asked Questions Can I extend my visa-free stay inside China? ▼ No — visa-free stays cannot be extended. If you want to stay longer than 30 days, you must exit China and re-enter (this works, but check the policy for your country), or apply for a proper visa before you travel. Don't overstay — the penalties are serious. Can I enter China twice on visa-free? ▼ Yes, generally. The 30-day visa-free policy allows multiple entries. You can exit to Hong Kong, Macau, or another country and re-enter — though there's no official limit, immigration officers may question very frequent re-entries. A standard "exit → Hong Kong trip → re-enter" is totally normal and accepted. How much does a China tourist visa cost? ▼ Fees vary by country due to reciprocity policies. For US citizens: typically $185 USD for a single-entry L visa. For UK citizens: around £151. Australian citizens: approximately AUD $130. Check the current fee at your local Chinese visa centre — prices change and vary by country. What's the 240-hour transit visa-free? Can I use it even if I'm not really "in transit"? ▼ You must have a confirmed onward ticket to a third country (not back to your home country). BUT — and this is key — you can use it to genuinely explore China for up to 10 days, then continue to your "third country" destination. Many travelers use New York → Beijing → Tokyo routes and spend the full 10 days in China. Totally legitimate and very popular. Do I need to book a hotel before applying? ▼ For visa-free entry: no booking required in advance. For visa applications: yes, you typically need hotel reservations as part of your application. They don't need to be paid and non-refundable — a confirmed reservation (with free cancellation) is usually sufficient. Is Hainan different from the rest of China? ▼ Yes! Hainan island has a separate 30-day visa-free policy for citizens of 59 countries (wider than the mainland list). If your country isn't on the mainland 30-day list, check if Hainan's policy covers you — it might open the door to a China beach holiday without a visa. (The Hainan list changes periodically — always confirm with official sources before booking.) My visa application was rejected. What now? ▼ Don't panic. Rejections often happen due to incomplete documents, insufficient funds shown, or unclear travel plans. You can re-apply immediately with stronger documentation. Contact the visa centre to understand the reason. Consider using a reputable visa agency for the reapplication — they know exactly what the consulate wants to see. text: 💬 Before You Fly · 微信设置 How to Set Up WeChat as a Foreigner WeChat is not just a messaging app — it's how China works. Restaurants, taxis, shops, hotels, and even tourist attractions use WeChat for everything. Without it, life in China gets complicated fast. The good news: setup takes 10 minutes and works perfectly with your international phone number. ⏱ 10 min setup 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ No Chinese number needed Start the Guide → 📥 Download PDF 💡 Why WeChat is Different from WhatsApp WeChat has mini-programs — tiny apps inside WeChat. You can order food, book transport, pay bills, and access hundreds of services without downloading separate apps. Think of it as a smartphone inside your smartphone, specific to China. 1 Download Get WeChat from App Store or Google Play 2 Register Sign up with your international phone number 3 Verify Get verified by an existing WeChat friend 4 WeChat Pay Link your foreign card for payments 1 Download WeChat 1 Open App Store (iPhone) or Google Play (Android) 2 Search "WeChat" — the green icon with two chat bubbles 3 Tap Get / Install and wait for download (~230MB) 4 Open the app — you'll see the login screen 💡 Download at Home WeChat is available internationally but download speeds are faster at home. Don't wait until you're at the airport. 🍎 App Store ▶ Google Play 2 Register Your Account 1 Tap "Sign Up" on the welcome screen 2 Enter your name (this is your display name — you can change it later) 3 Select your country code and enter your phone number 4 Tap "Send SMS" and enter the verification code 5 Set a password (at least 8 characters with letters and numbers) 6 Agree to the terms and complete the puzzle verification ⚠️ Use a number you'll always have access to Your phone number is your WeChat ID. If you lose access to that number, recovering your account is very difficult. Use your permanent home number, not a temporary travel SIM. 3 Get Verified by a Friend This is the step most guides don't warn you about. New WeChat accounts require verification by an existing WeChat user. This is WeChat's security measure against spam accounts. 1 After registration, WeChat will ask you to have a friend verify you 2 Ask a friend or colleague who has WeChat to scan your QR code 3 They verify your account through their app — takes 10 seconds 4 Your account is now fully active 💡 No Friends on WeChat Yet? Ask in Facebook travel groups — the China travel community is very helpful. Or message me at hello@readychinatravel.com — I'm happy to verify new accounts for Ready? China! readers. 4 Set Up WeChat Pay 1 Tap Me → Pay and Services → Wallet 2 Tap "Bank Cards" → "Add a Card" 3 Select your card type (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) 4 Enter your card number, expiry, and CVV 5 Verify with SMS from your bank 6 Set a 6-digit payment PIN 💳 Supported Cards Visa and Mastercard work best. Tell your bank you're travelling to China before linking — some banks flag the WeChat verification as suspicious and temporarily block the card. ℹ️ Alipay vs WeChat Pay Both work almost everywhere in China. Most travelers use Alipay as their primary payment and WeChat Pay as backup. Set up both if you have time — it takes 20 minutes total. → Alipay setup guide 5 Essential WeChat Features to Know 🔍 Scan QR Codes Tap + (top right) → Scan Used for payments, adding contacts, restaurant menus NOT the same as your phone's camera app → Full QR scanning guide 🗺️ Mini Programs Search any service in WeChat's search bar Order food: Meituan mini-program Book trains: 12306 mini-program No extra downloads needed 💬 Translation Long-press any message → Translate Works for Chinese → English instantly Useful for restaurant menus sent via WeChat Also works in group chats 📍 Share Location Tap + → Location → Share Real-time Location Essential for meeting local friends or guides Works without Google Maps Pin drops in WeChat use Amap data (accurate in China) 💬 Get the Free WeChat Setup PDF Printable step-by-step guide with screenshots — everything you need to get WeChat running before you land in China. snippet: how locals actually decide where to eat in china — and how you can use dianping even if you don't read chinese. a practical guide for first-time visitors. updated august 2026.
text: 🍽️ Essential Apps · Step 7 · 大众点评 How to Use Dianping (大众点评) to Find Great Food in China How locals discover restaurants — and how you can use it even if you don't read Chinese. ⏱ 6 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 🍜 China's #1 restaurant discovery app 💡 Kat's Tip If you want to know where local people are actually eating — not just the spots that show up for tourists — Dianping is where I start every time, even in my own neighborhood. You don't need to read Chinese fluently to get real value from it. Photos and star ratings do most of the work. 1 What Is Dianping? Dianping (大众点评, "public review") is China's leading restaurant discovery and review app — often compared to Yelp or TripAdvisor, though it covers far more of daily life: restaurants, cafés, bars, salons, and more. It's owned by Meituan and used by hundreds of millions of people across China every month, which means its restaurant data is deep, current, and shaped by real local dining habits — not filtered for a tourist audience. 2 Why Should Travelers Use It? International platforms like Google Maps or TripAdvisor tend to only show restaurants that already cater to foreign visitors or have English listings — which is a small slice of what's actually good nearby. Dianping gives you a much bigger picture: • Find restaurants and cafés genuinely near you, not just tourist-facing ones • See real customer photos of the food and the space, not stock images • Check ratings and review volume, which is often much higher than what you'd find on international apps • See which specific dishes are popular at a given restaurant • Check the approximate price per person before you sit down • Discover small, local spots that may not appear on international platforms at all This doesn't mean Dianping is always "better" than Google or TripAdvisor — it just reflects a different, much larger pool of local reviewers, which is genuinely useful information when you're trying to eat well in a country you don't know yet. 3 How to Search for a Restaurant 1 Open the app — it should detect your location automatically (allow location access if asked). 2 Tap the search bar and type a cuisine type (like "hot pot" or "noodles"), a dish, or a restaurant name. 3 Or skip typing entirely — scroll the "Nearby" or "Recommended" feed on the home screen for a curated list of what's around you right now. 4 Results are sorted by relevance and rating by default — you can also switch to sort by distance or price. 4 How to Read a Dianping Restaurant Page This is the part that actually matters most for a foreign visitor. There is what to look for: Restaurant name — save it, even if you can't read it (more on this below) Star rating — out of 5, shown clearly at the top Number of reviews — a strong signal on its own; thousands of reviews means it's a genuinely popular local spot Photos — tap into the photo gallery for real customer shots of the food and interior Popular dishes — usually listed near the top, showing what people actually order Price per person (人均) — an average spend estimate, very useful for budgeting Location and distance from where you are Opening hours and where listed 5 How to Decide What to Order Even without reading Chinese, you can order well: • Check the "popular dishes" section — these are ranked by how often customers actually order and photograph them • Scroll customer photos to see what the food actually looks like before you order • Some listings include menu photos — screenshot the dish you want and point at it in person if the restaurant has waitstaff to take your order • Read a few recent reviews (translate with your phone's camera or a translation app if needed) for quick context on portion size or spice level 6 Useful Tips for Non-Chinese Speakers • Screenshot the restaurant's name, address, and location pin before you leave your hotel. • Use your phone's built-in camera translation (or Google Translate / Baidu Translate) to scan a menu on the spot. • Let the photos do the talking — you can judge a lot about a dish without a single word of Chinese. • Save the restaurant's Chinese name specifically — this is what you'll need to show a Didi driver or ask a local for directions. • Don't rely entirely on the English/translated version of a restaurant's name — it often won't match what's written on the sign outside or what a local recognizes. ℹ️ Also Worth Knowing: 高德扫街榜 (Amap Street Ranking)--updated 13/08/2026 Amap recently launched its own restaurant ranking feature called 扫街榜 ("street sweep ranking"), built from real visit and order data rather than written reviews. It's newer and less detailed than Dianping, but it's a handy second opinion if you're already inside Amap looking for directions and want a quick "what's good nearby" check without switching apps (personal opinion: there still are some fake rankings). FAQ Is Dianping available in English? ▼ Not fully — Dianping is primarily a Chinese-language app. You can still get real value from it using photos, star ratings, and price data without translating everything, and your phone's built-in translation tools handle the rest when needed. Do I need to create an account to browse restaurants? ▼ You can browse search results, ratings, and photos without logging in. An account is only needed if you want to save favorites, leave a review, or redeem a deal. Can I book a table or order food through Dianping? ▼ Some restaurants support in-app reservations or deals, but this is more useful once you're comfortable navigating the Chinese interface. For most first-time visitors, using Dianping to discover and vet a restaurant — then just walking in — is the simplest approach. Is Dianping better than Google Maps reviews or TripAdvisor? ▼ Not necessarily "better" — just different. Dianping reflects a much larger pool of local Chinese reviewers and covers far more restaurants across China, including places that never show up on international platforms. Both are useful; Dianping fills in what the others miss. 📱 Get the Free Apps Cheat Sheet A printable one-pager covering Amap, Dianping, Alipay, WeChat, and Didi — exactly what to set up before you land.
