snippet: how to order food in china as a foreigner. picture menus, qr code menus, translation apps, useful phrases, and how to handle dietary requirements. works without any mandarin.
text: 🍜 After You Arrive · 点餐指南 How to Order Food in China Without Speaking Mandarin Eating in China is one of the great joys of the trip — and you can eat magnificently without speaking a single word of Mandarin. Photo menus, QR code menus, translation apps, and a handful of key phrases will take you further than you think. ⏱ 7 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ No Mandarin needed 🌶️ Kat's Honest Food Warning Chinese food in China is dramatically different from Chinese food abroad — spicier, oilier, more varied, and infinitely more delicious. Sichuan food will make you cry (in a good way). Dongbei food will confuse you. Cantonese dim sum will change your weekend mornings forever. Stay open to everything. 1 Types of Menus You'll Encounter 📷 Picture Menus — Easiest Most local restaurants have photo menus Simply point at what looks good and hold up fingers for quantity Works perfectly — staff are used to foreign tourists doing this Smile and point confidently — it always works 📱 QR Code Menus — Most Common Scan the QR code on the table with WeChat or Alipay A digital menu opens — in Chinese, maybe with photos Use Google Translate camera to read text Some QR menus let you order and pay directly — no staff interaction needed 📋 Chinese Text Only — Use Translation Open Google Translate or Papago → camera mode → point at menu Instant translation — works offline with downloaded language pack Baidu Translate is a local alternative (works without VPN) Show the translated screen to staff — they understand immediately 🌐 English Menus — Tourist Areas Available in major tourist areas and international hotel restaurants Dianping app lets you filter "English menu available" Prices are often slightly higher where English menus exist Worth using on your first day while you find your footing 2 Essential Food Phrases 这个 zhè gè This one — point at the menu while saying this 不辣 bù là Not spicy — essential for people who cannot eat spicy! (my spicy level is 0/10) 少辣 shǎo là A little spicy — if you want mild heat 不要香菜 bú yào xiāng cài No coriander / no cilantro (this is very personal suggestion) 买单 mǎi dān The bill please — or just tap your Alipay scan icon 好吃！ hǎo chī! Delicious! — makes every staff and cook smile instantly 我吃素 wǒ chī sù I'm vegetarian — note: may still include fish/egg 打包 dǎ bāo To take away / doggy bag please 3 How to Find Good Restaurants ⭐ Dianping (大众点评) — China's Yelp The most trusted restaurant rating app in China. Every restaurant is reviewed by real locals. Photos show exactly what the food looks like. Filter by cuisine, price, rating, and "foreign-friendly." ✅ Sort by rating — 4.5+ stars means genuinely excellent. The photos are honest. Trust them. 💬 WeChat Mini-Programs — Order Delivery Search "Meituan" or "Eleme" in WeChat — these are China's food delivery apps. You can order from any nearby restaurant and have it delivered to your hotel or even your train seat! 💡 For hotel deliveries, give your room number. For train deliveries, give your carriage and seat number before the next stop. 💡 Kat's Restaurant Strategy Find the restaurant with the longest queue of locals outside. Queue. Order whatever the table next to you is having. This method has never failed me in 20 years of eating across China. 4 Dietary Requirements in China 🥬 Vegetarian Say "我吃素 (wǒ chī sù)" but clarify — Chinese vegetarianism may include egg and fish Buddhist vegetarian restaurants (素食 sùshí) are strictly plant-based Search "素食" on Dianping for vegetarian restaurants near you Tofu dishes, vegetable dumplings, and stir-fried greens are always safe bets 🌾 Gluten-Free Very difficult in China — soy sauce contains wheat Rice-based dishes are safest (rice noodles, steamed rice, rice porridge) Show staff a card: "我对麸质过敏 (wǒ duì fūzhì guòmǐn)" — I'm allergic to gluten Bring a printed allergy card in Chinese for serious allergies 🥜 Nut Allergies Peanuts are common in Chinese cooking — often hidden in sauces Always ask: "有花生吗？(yǒu huā shēng ma)" — Is there peanut? For serious allergies, carry a Chinese allergy card Congee (rice porridge) and plain steamed dishes are usually safest 🐷 Halal / Kosher Halal (清真 qīngzhēn) food is widely available — large Muslim communities in Northwest China Search "清真" on Dianping for certified halal restaurants Xinjiang and Gansu cuisine is predominantly halal Kosher food is very limited — research carefully before travelling 🍜 Get the Free Food Ordering Cheat Sheet Key phrases, how to read a menu with translation apps, and the best food apps — all in one printable page. Perfect for your first week in China. Send Me the Cheat Sheet ✉️ ✅ On its way! No spam. I reply personally. snippet: complete didi guide for foreigners in china 2026. how to download, register, call a didi, communicate with drivers without speaking mandarin. china's uber explained.
text: 🚗 Getting Around · 滴滴打车 How to Use Didi in China (Setup + Calling a Ride) Didi is China's Uber. It's cheaper than taxis, safer than flagging random cars, and works entirely in English. Once you have it set up, getting around any Chinese city becomes incredibly easy — even without speaking a single word of Mandarin. ⏱ 10 min setup 📅 Updated August 2026 ✅ Works in English Setup Guide → How to Call a Ride → ⚠️ Never Get Into an Unlicensed Taxi At major airports and tourist areas, people will approach you offering a "taxi" or "cheap ride." These are unlicensed drivers who charge 3–5× the normal rate and sometimes take you to the wrong place. Always use Didi — it's tracked, rated, and safe. ✈️ Part 1: Set Up Didi Before You Fly 1 Download Get Didi from App Store or Google Play 2 Register Sign up with your phone number 3 Add Payment Link Alipay or a card 4 Test Try a trip on day one 1 Download Didi China from App Store or Google Play — search "DiDi" (two capital D's) 2 Tap "Sign Up" and enter your international phone number with country code 3 Enter the SMS code you receive and create a password 4 Go to Me → Wallet → Add Payment Method 5 Add Alipay (recommended) or a foreign credit card directly 6 Set English as your app language: Me → Settings → Language → English 💡 Best Payment Setup Link your Alipay account to Didi — it's the smoothest. If you haven't set up Alipay yet, do that first . International cards also work directly in Didi but Alipay is more reliable. 🍎 App Store ▶ Google Play 🏮 Part 2: How to Call a Didi Once You're in China 1 Open Didi and tap the destination field at the top 2 Type your destination in English — Didi finds it (or paste from Amap) 3 Choose your car type — Express is cheapest, Premier is a nicer car 4 Confirm your pickup location by dragging the pin to exactly where you are 5 Tap "Confirm Booking" — a driver accepts within 1–3 minutes 6 Watch the car approach on the map. Check the plate number matches when the car arrives. 7 Payment processes automatically through Alipay when you arrive — no personal payment needed (My friend got scammed before!) 💡 The Magic Message — Copy This If your driver calls you (they sometimes do to confirm pickup location), send this WeChat or SMS message: 我是外国人，不会讲中文。请按照APP上的地址来。 (I'm a foreigner, I don't speak Chinese. Please follow the address in the app.) Copy and paste — 99% of drivers understand and simply follow the app. Works every time. 3 Didi Tips & Common Situations 📍 Pickup Problems Pin your exact location on the map or let it auto-detect (it usually shows you your nearest pickup location) At busy areas (malls, stations), walk to the Didi pickup zone marked with 网约车 signs Send your driver a photo of where you're standing if they seem confused If they cancel, just book again — it takes 30 seconds 💰 What Does Didi Cost? Short city ride (5km): ¥15–25 (~$2–4 USD) Airport to city centre: ¥60–120 (~$8–16 USD) Surge pricing applies during rain, rush hour, and public holidays The price depends, but always much cheaper than licensed taxis at airports 🚖 Didi vs Taxi Didi: tracked, rated, English app, payment automatic ✅ Taxi: can hail on street, driver may not have app, may not safe Taxi meters are honest — just harder to communicate address Screenshot your hotel address in Chinese to show taxi drivers ⭐ Rating Your Driver (optional) Rate after your trip — some drivers care about their ratings 4.8+ rating = good driver, worth selecting from the list You can also rate a bad experience — Didi platform takes complaints seriously Your passenger rating matters too — be ready on time Next Steps → 🚇 Metro Guide Cheaper than Didi for short city trips 🚄 High-Speed Train Guide Travel between cities in China 💳 Set Up Alipay Link to Didi for automatic payment 📚 All Guides → Everything you need for your China trip

title: Beijing
snippet: the honest guide to beijing for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏯 北京 Beijing History, culture, Great Wall, Chinese civilization ★☆☆☆☆ 🗓 4–6 days Foreigner-friendly English signs Must visit ✨ Why Beijing? Beijing is where China's story gets loud. For over 800 years — across six dynasties — emperors ruled from this city, and the evidence is everywhere: the world's largest palace complex, the Great Wall curling over the mountains an hour away, and temple roofs older than most countries. If you only visit one place in China, this is the one. But Beijing isn't a museum. Ancient hutong lanes sit beside world-class art districts, morning tai chi in temple parks gives way to rooftop bars in Sanlitun, and the subway carries you from a 600-year-old palace to the futuristic Bird's Nest in minutes. History, food, and modern China — all in one city. ; 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Great Wall — Mutianyu section (less crowded) UNESCO · less crowded Read the story 2 The Forbidden City World's largest palace · book ahead Read the story 3 Tiananmen Square at sunrise World's largest city square · flag ceremony Read the story 4 Temple of Heaven & morning tai chi UNESCO · locals doing tai chi at dawn Read the story 5 Summer Palace & Kunming Lake UNESCO · imperial gardens & Long Corridor The story: The Great Wall isn't one wall but 20,000+ km of fortifications built over 2,000 years (3rd century BC to 17th century) by millions of workers. Mutianyu was first built in the Northern Qi dynasty (550 AD), then rebuilt in 1368 by Ming general Xu Da as the capital's northern shield. It's the longest fully-restored section open to visitors — 5.4 km with 23 watchtowers — and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Why it's a must-see: Of all the famous sections near Beijing, Mutianyu gives you the most wall for the fewest crowds — fewer tourists than Badaling, forested mountain views, and original Ming bricks under your feet. Cable car up, wander the watchtowers, then ride the toboggan slide down. It's the most fun you'll ever have on a World Heritage site. 💡 Kat's tip: Go early (before 9am) and avoid weekends. It's about 1.5–2 hours from central Beijing — book a day tour or take the bus from Dongzhimen hub. The story: Built 1406–1420 by the Yongle Emperor with over a million laborers, the Forbidden City (Zijincheng, "Purple Forbidden City") was home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties for nearly 500 years. It's the largest palace complex in the world: 72 hectares, 980 buildings, more than 8,700 rooms, surrounded by a 10-meter wall and a 52-meter moat. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Why it's a must-see: Commoners were once forbidden to enter — now you can walk the same stones as emperors, from the Hall of Supreme Harmony with its Dragon Throne to the serene Imperial Garden. The whole complex is built around the emperor as the center of the universe: the throne is aligned with the North Star itself. 💡 Kat's tip: Tickets sell out days ahead — book online at least 7 days in advance. Enter from the Meridian Gate (south), then exit the north gate into Jingshan Park for the classic rooftop view. The story: At 440,000 m² (880m × 500m), Tiananmen Square is the largest city square in the world — big enough to hold 60 football fields. It sits on Beijing's historic central axis, flanked by the National Museum of China, the Great Hall of the People, and the Monument to the People's Heroes, with the Forbidden City rising directly behind it. Why it's a must-see: Come at sunrise for the flag-raising ceremony, timed to the sun's first light each morning. Thousands of locals gather to watch — it's a daily ritual that turns an enormous concrete square into something deeply moving, and it makes China feel real rather than postcard-perfect. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry is free, but bring your passport — security checks are strict. Arrive 30 minutes early for a good view; the ceremony on the 1st of each month is bigger with a full band. The story: Built in 1420 by the same Yongle Emperor, the Temple of Heaven is where Ming and Qing emperors came each year to pray for good harvests — the largest ritual complex of its kind in the world (273 hectares). Its layout is round in the north and square in the south, echoing the ancient belief that "heaven is round, earth is square." A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998. Why it's a must-see: The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests is a wooden masterpiece — built without a single nail, its blue-tiled roof held up by interlocking brackets. But the real magic is the park itself: come in the morning and you'll find locals doing tai chi, ballroom dancing, singing opera, and playing cards. It's Beijing's best free show. 💡 Kat's tip: Go early (6–9am) — that's when the park becomes the city's living room and the exercise culture is in full swing. The park opens at 6am. The story: Built in 1750 by Emperor Qianlong (originally as a birthday gift for his mother), the Summer Palace — Yiheyuan, "Garden of Nurtured Harmony" — was rebuilt by Empress Dowager Cixi in 1888–95 after foreign forces sacked it in 1860. It's the best-preserved imperial garden in China and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998. Why it's a must-see: A 290-hectare landscape wrapped around Kunming Lake, with the world's longest painted corridor (728 meters, 14,000+ paintings), the Marble Boat, and the Seventeen-Arch Bridge. Take a dragon boat across the lake and you'll understand how emperors relaxed — and why they called it the "summer" palace. 💡 Kat's tip: Give it half a day. Rent a boat if the weather is fine, and stay for sunset from the Seventeen-Arch Bridge — it's worth the wait. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the four bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Dongcheng / Wangfujing Best for first-timers The classic choice: walk to the Forbidden City in 10–15 minutes and Tiananmen in 20, with Metro Line 1 at Wangfujing station linking you to everything else. Shopping, restaurants, and the famous snack street are right outside your door. 🚇 Line 1 · Wangfujing 🏛 Walk to Forbidden City e.g. Happy Dragon Courtyard (budget, near Forbidden City) · The Beijing Hotel (landmark) Qianmen & Dashilan Old Beijing on a budget South of Tiananmen (15–20 minutes on foot), this was the Qing dynasty's merchant district. Restored shopping streets, hutong courtyards, and cheap eats everywhere — plus budget hotels from ¥150–300 a night. Best for budget travelers and food lovers. 🚇 Line 2 · Qianmen 🏮 Qing-era streets & snacks e.g. courtyard guesthouses behind Dashilan · ¥150–300/night Hutong courtyards (Shichahai / Nanluoguxiang) The experience splurge Sleep in a centuries-old siheyuan (courtyard home): gray brick walls, wooden lattice windows, birds in the morning. A 20–25 minute metro ride from the Forbidden City. Best for couples and anyone who wants to actually feel old Beijing. 🚇 Line 2/8 · Gulou Dajie 🌳 Lakeside hutongs e.g. The Orchid Hotel (boutique hutong stay) · ¥500–1500/night Sanlitun / Chaoyang Modern Beijing Beijing's nightlife and foodie hub — international restaurants, bars, and the Taikoo Li mall, with the 798 Art District a short ride away. Best for repeat visitors, foodies, and night owls. Trade-off: 30–35 minutes to the Forbidden City by metro. 🚇 Line 10 · Tuanjiehu 🎨 798 Art District nearby e.g. NUO Hotel Beijing (luxury near 798) 🍜 What to Eat Peking Duck 北京烤鸭 Crispy lacquered skin sliced tableside, wrapped in thin pancakes with scallion, cucumber, and sweet bean sauce. The locals' favorite — better value and less touristy than the old famous names. 🍽 Siji Minfu · ≈¥150–280 per duck · book ahead Zhajiangmian 炸酱面 Beijing's everyday bowl: thick wheat noodles tossed in fermented soybean-and-pork sauce, topped with cucumber and bean sprouts. Hearty, salty, and cheap — the taste of a hutong lunch. 🍽 Noodle shops around Qianmen & the hutongs · ¥20–45 Jianbing 煎饼 A crispy egg crêpe folded around cracker, scallion, and sauce — the city's street-breakfast ritual, cooked fresh in two minutes flat. Grab one before a day of sightseeing. 🍽 Any breakfast cart with a line of locals · ¥8–18 Copper-pot mutton hot pot 涮羊肉 Thin-sliced lamb cooked in clear broth over a copper chimney pot, dipped in rich sesame sauce. Beijing's winter soul food — warm, social, and deeply satisfying. 🍽 Dong Lai Shun · traditional spots around Niujie · ¥100–220 pp 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Book Forbidden City tickets 7 days ahead — they sell out fast! Kat Says Use the subway — English signs everywhere, super cheap (~¥3-6 per ride) Kat Says Skip the Badaling Great Wall. Go to Mutianyu — fewer crowds, better views, and there's a toboggan slide down! Explore More Cities 🏺 西安 · Xi'an Ancient history, Terracotta Army, Silk Road 🌃 上海 · Shanghai Futuristic skyline, international food, modernity ← Back to Ready? China!

title: Changxing
snippet: the honest guide to changxing for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🍵 长兴 Changxing Tea plantations, quiet lakes, local farm food ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 1–2 days Tea culture Peaceful escape ✨ Why Changxing? Changxing is the anti-tourist destination: a county of tea terraces, bamboo forests and Taihu Lake shoreline that Chinese travelers have quietly loved for centuries — and almost no foreign tourists know about. It's where China's first imperial tea factory was built in 770 AD, producing Zisun ('purple shoot') tea for the Tang court for nearly 900 years across five dynasties. And it's shockingly easy to reach: 25–35 minutes from Hangzhou and about an hour from Shanghai by high-speed rail. Come for a day of tea-picking and bamboo walks, stay overnight in a farmhouse among the terraces, and leave with the calmest photos of your whole China trip. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Guzhu Mountain tea terraces Pick tea where the Tea Sage walked Read the story 2 Xianshan Lake Wetland Park A flooded forest, straight out of a fairy tale Read the story 3 Datang Tribute Tea House China's first imperial tea factory Read the story 4 Ten-Mile Ancient Ginkgo Corridor 30,000 ginkgo trees turning gold Read the story 5 Taihu Longzhi Dream Resort A mega-resort on China's third-largest lake The story: Guzhu Mountain is where Lu Yu — the 'Tea Sage' who wrote The Classic of Tea, the world's first tea treatise — discovered Zisun tea over 1,200 years ago and recommended it to the Tang emperor. The terraced slopes still produce this prized purple-shoot tea, and you can walk the same fields, pick leaves in season, watch the pan-firing, and taste tea brewed with water from the nearby Jinsha Spring. Why it's a must-see: It's the most authentic tea-culture immersion in China: the actual birthplace of imperial tea, with the terraces cascading toward distant Taihu Lake. In spring you can pick your own leaves and have them roasted on the spot — a hands-on connection to a 1,200-year-old tradition. 💡 Kat's tip: Visit late March to mid-April for the pre-Qingming harvest. Book a tea-picking experience through a farmhouse in Guzhu village in advance (~50–80 RMB per person). Wear sensible shoes — the terraces are steep. The story: Dubbed the 'Oriental Amazon' by Chinese National Geographic, this wetland park spans 2,500 hectares of water forests, reed marshes and lotus ponds. A raised boardwalk threads through a flooded forest of dawn redwoods, where the rare reed parrotbill — nicknamed the 'panda of birds' — has been recorded, alongside egrets, wild ducks and mandarin ducks. Why it's a must-see: It's a rare chance to explore a flooded forest by boat in eastern China — drifting between tree trunks rising from still water, with lotus blooms in summer and mist in the morning. Quiet, beautiful, and almost completely unknown to foreign visitors. 💡 Kat's tip: Combine the boat tour with the boardwalk walk — they show completely different sides of the wetland. Best light for photos is 8–10am when mist still hangs over the water. The story: Built in 770 AD by order of Emperor Daizong, this was China's first imperial tea factory — at its peak staffed by over 1,000 craftsmen who produced Zisun tea rushed by fast horse to the Tang capital (modern Xi'an) in time for the Qingming festival. The current complex is a meticulous reconstruction of the Tang-style compound, with tea-making exhibits, a Lu Yu pavilion and authentic Tang-era cliff inscriptions behind it. Why it's a must-see: This is ground zero for Chinese tea history — no other site in China connects you so directly to the Tang dynasty and to Lu Yu, who wrote The Classic of Tea while living on this very mountain. For anyone who loves tea, it's a pilgrimage. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry 60 RMB; budget 2 hours. Don't miss the cliff inscriptions (moya shike) on the trail behind the complex — they're genuine Tang and Song carvings. The teahouse on site serves fresh Zisun tea with the view. The story: This 12.5-km valley in Xiaopu town holds over 30,000 ginkgo trees, including a 1,300-year-old 'Ginkgo King' and an 1,800-year-old 'Ginkgo Queen', threading through ancient villages and a Buddhist temple. A glass-bottom skybridge offers a panoramic view of the golden canopy. Why it's a must-see: When the ginkgoes turn in November, this becomes one of the most photographed landscapes in eastern China — a 12-kilometer tunnel of yellow that rivals Kyoto's autumn temples, with a tiny fraction of the tourists. It's the single best reason to time your trip to autumn. 💡 Kat's tip: Peak color is mid-to-late November. Take the sightseeing mini-train (included in the 80 RMB ticket) to cover the length, then walk back through your favorite section. Stay overnight in a village minsu to see the corridor empty at dawn. The story: Opened in stages from 2018, this 23-billion-RMB resort on Taihu Lake's southern shore bills itself as the world's largest comprehensive tourism complex: an animal world with 200+ species, a water park, an indoor snow world, a circus, and a recreated Tang-style 'ancient town' with nightly light shows and fireworks. Why it's a must-see: Even if theme parks aren't your thing, the free nightly water-and-light show on the lakefront is the best free evening entertainment in the region. And it's the closest you'll get to luxury accommodation with a Taihu Lake view. 💡 Kat's tip: The light show starts around 8:20pm and is free to watch from the lakefront. With kids, the animal world (100 RMB) is excellent value. Avoid summer weekends unless you like crowds. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Shuikou tea valley (Guzhu village) Tea lovers & slow travelers Dozens of family guesthouses sit among the tea fields and bamboo groves, ~20 minutes from the high-speed rail station. Many offer full-board packages — room + 3 home-cooked meals for 150–200 RMB per person per day. The best base for the Tribute Tea House and Guzhu Mountain. 🚇 No metro — taxi from Changxing HSR Station (~25 RMB) 🏛 Datang Tribute Tea House, Guzhu tea terraces e.g. Changxing Qinghe Minsu (~150 RMB) · Tea Language Farmhouse (~200 RMB full board) Taihu Lake resort area Families & resort lovers The Longzhi Dream complex offers the widest range of accommodation — from a panda-themed family hotel to lakeside resort rooms — with the water park, animal world and nightly shows steps away. 15 minutes from the county center. 🚇 No metro — resort shuttle from the HSR station 🏛 Taihu Lake, Longzhi Dream, nightly light show e.g. Longzhi Dream Joy World Hotel (400–700 RMB) · Animal World Panda Hotel (family, from 600 RMB) Changxing county center Convenience & transit The compact downtown near the HSR station has the usual reliable mid-range chains and the best local restaurants, with buses to all the scenic areas. The practical choice for a one-night stopover. 🚇 No metro — local buses and taxis 🏛 HSR station, downtown dining streets e.g. Atour Hotel Changxing (~300 RMB) · New Century Grand (~450 RMB) 🍜 What to Eat Taihu 'Three Whites' 太湖三白 The signature lake harvest: white fish, white shrimp and silver fish from Taihu Lake, steamed simply with ginger and scallion to highlight their delicate sweetness. 🍽 🍽 Lakeside farmhouse restaurants · ~60 RMB per dish Silver Fish & Eggs 银鱼炒蛋 Tiny translucent silver fish scrambled with farm eggs — light, fluffy and impossibly fresh. The taste of the lake in every bite. 🍽 🍽 Most farmhouse restaurants in Guzhu village · ¥30–40 Changxing Dry-Tossed Noodles 长兴干挑面 Hand-pulled noodles tossed in soy and lard oil, topped with crispy fish or braised pork — a beloved local breakfast, and some say the best in northern Zhejiang. 🍽 🍽 Shixiong Noodle Shop (downtown) · ~15 RMB Bamboo Shoot Braised Pork 笋干烧肉 Dried bamboo shoots from the Guzhu forests slow-braised with pork belly until the shoots soak up the rich sauce and the meat melts — a farmhouse classic. 🍽 🍽 Tea Language Farmhouse & Shuikou nongjiale · ~45 RMB 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Changxing is 25–35 minutes from Hangzhou East by high-speed rail (from ~40 RMB) — doable as a day trip, but staying overnight in a tea-field farmhouse is the real magic. Kat Says Best times: March–April for tea-picking and bamboo shoots; mid-to-late November for the ginkgo corridor; October for golden autumn hills. Kat Says Book a full-board farmhouse package (150–200 RMB/person/day including 3 meals) — better value than hotels, and the farmhouse cooking is how you taste Taihu fish and bamboo shoots properly. title: Chengdu
snippet: the honest guide to chengdu for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🐼 成都 Chengdu Pandas, hotpot, chill vibes, authentic local life ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3–5 days Pandas! Best food city Laid-back ✨ Why Chengdu? Chengdu is the only place on earth where you can watch giant pandas eating bamboo 20 meters away, then sit in a 100-year-old teahouse and sip jasmine tea for the entire afternoon — and nobody will think you're lazy. This city invented the concept of 'slow living': a laid-back rhythm, 8,000 teahouses, and a food scene that's officially recognized by UNESCO as a City of Gastronomy. It's also the gateway to western Sichuan — the mountains, monasteries and gorges that make this one of China's most scenic provinces. But the city itself is the star: giant pandas at dawn, Sichuan opera at dusk, and a hotpot dinner in between that will test your spice tolerance and steal your heart. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Giant Panda Breeding Base Watch pandas at their most active — 8am Read the story 2 Jinli Street & Wuhou Shrine Three Kingdoms history + lantern-lit lanes Read the story 3 A real Chengdu hotpot dinner The meal you came for Read the story 4 People's Park teahouse Tea, mahjong & the art of doing nothing Read the story 5 Wide & Narrow Alleys (Kuanzhai Xiangzi) Old lanes, new chic The story: Opened in 1987, this 100-hectare research base has grown from six rescued pandas to a population of over 200 — the most successful panda breeding program on earth, and the model for panda conservation worldwide. Red pandas roam the same park, and the base has also released captive pandas successfully into the wild. Why it's a must-see: Nowhere else gives you this access to giant pandas: you can watch them munch bamboo, climb trees and (in breeding season) cuddle their cubs, just meters away. The 8am feeding time is when they're most active — by 10am most are asleep and the tour buses have arrived. 💡 Kat's tip: Arrive at 7:30am opening and head straight to the Moonlight Nursery to see the cubs. Allow 3 hours. It's 20 minutes by taxi or metro Line 3 (Panda Avenue station) + shuttle. Entry 55 RMB. The story: Wuhou Shrine was built in 223 AD to honor Zhuge Liang, the legendary strategist of the Three Kingdoms era, and Liu Bei, the Shu Han emperor — the only temple in China housing both a ruler and his minister. Next door, Jinli Street re-creates the old Shu kingdom's marketplace: lanterns, snack stalls, folk crafts, and nightly Sichuan opera with face-changing performances. Why it's a must-see: This is the most atmospheric introduction to Sichuan's history and culture in one stop: a 1,800-year-old story told through temples, teahouses and street theater. The face-changing (bianlian) opera performers who swap masks in a blink are a genuine art form you'll see nowhere else. 💡 Kat's tip: Visit Wuhou Shrine in the afternoon (50 RMB), then walk into Jinli as the sun sets — the lanterns make it magical. Catch the opera/face-changing show inside Jinli (from 60 RMB) in the evening. The story: Hotpot began as a working-class dish in Chongqing's docks and became Sichuan's culinary religion. The broth is a deep-red cauldron of chili, Sichuan peppercorns and dozens of spices, bubbling over a gas flame while you cook your own meat, vegetables and noodles. The numbing 'ma' of the peppercorn is what makes it addictive — and uniquely Sichuan. Why it's a must-see: A Chengdu hotpot dinner is not a meal, it's a ceremony: the boiling pot, the dipping sauces, the cold beer, the hours of conversation. It's the definitive way to taste Sichuan food culture — and the spice level is adjustable, so don't be scared. 💡 Kat's tip: Order the 'yuanyang' (鸳鸯) pot — half spicy, half mild — if you're nervous. Go with locals if you can; they'll order the good stuff (tripe, pig brain, lotus root). Book ahead for dinner, especially on weekends. The story: People's Park has been Chengdu's living room since 1911. Its centerpiece is the Heming Teahouse (鹤鸣茶社), founded in 1923 — one of the oldest teahouses in China — where locals sit for hours over a 15–30 RMB pot of tea, reading, gossiping, playing mahjong and getting ear-cleaned by wandering barbers with silver tools. Why it's a must-see: This is the real Chengdu lifestyle, preserved in a public park: an entire city that has perfected the art of doing nothing in public. Watch the old men play chess, listen to the tea-water hawkers, get an ear massage — it's the cheapest, most authentic cultural experience in China. 💡 Kat's tip: Pay for your tea (¥15–30, jasmine or green), find a bamboo chair, and stay as long as you like — nobody rushes you. The ear-cleaning service (采耳) is 30–60 RMB and a surreal, wonderful experience. Afternoon is liveliest. The story: These three parallel alleys — Kuan (Wide), Zhai (Narrow) and Jing (Well) — preserve the courtyard houses (siheyuan) of Qing-dynasty Chengdu. Restored in 2008, they now mix traditional teahouses and puppet shows with designer shops, craft beer bars and Sichuan snacks, all under the city's best-preserved old roofs. Why it's a must-see: It's Chengdu in miniature: ancient lanes, modern energy, and a perfect spot to taste the city's snacks in one walk. The side courtyards hide some of Chengdu's loveliest teahouses and courtyard restaurants, far quieter than the main alleys. 💡 Kat's tip: Come in the late afternoon for golden light on the grey-brick lanes, then stay for dinner and drinks. Free entry. Try the 'san da pao' (三大炮) dessert — glutinous rice balls with a theatrical bounce. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Taikoo Li / Chunxi Road Best for first-timers Chengdu's fashionable center: the open-air Taikoo Li mall (glass pavilions around a Tang-dynasty temple) and the Chunxi Road shopping street, with metro Lines 2 and 3 crossing here. Most sights are 10–20 minutes by taxi or metro. 🚇 Lines 2/3 · Chunxi Road 🏛 Taikoo Li, Daci Temple, Chunxi Road e.g. The Temple House (iconic luxury inside Taikoo Li) · Buddha Zen Hotel (traditional courtyard, great value) Wide & Narrow Alleys Atmosphere & food lovers Sleep among the old lanes: courtyard hotels and guesthouses tucked behind the Kuanzhai alley walls, minutes from People's Park's teahouses and the city's best snack streets. Quieter and more charming than the shopping center. 🚇 Lines 2/4 · People's Park 🏛 Kuanzhai Xiangzi, People's Park, Wenshu Monastery e.g. Courtyard hotels inside the alleys · Wenshu Monastery-area guesthouses Wenshu Monastery area Budget & local life Around the 1,400-year-old Wenshu Monastery, this older quarter has street markets, vegetarian restaurants, and Chengdu's famous Wenshu snack street — plus the cheapest decent hotels in the center. More authentic, less polished. 🚇 Line 1 · Wenshu Monastery 🏛 Wenshu Monastery, Wenshu snack street e.g. Lazybones Hostel (backpacker favorite) · budget hotels along the monastery wall South High-tech District Modern & transit-savvy The modern business district south of the center: sleek hotels, international restaurants, and a direct metro link (Line 1) to the train stations and airport. Choose this if you prefer comfort and quiet over old-town charm. 🚇 Lines 1 · Century City / Financial City 🏛 Global Center (world's largest building), Century City e.g. InterContinental Century City · international chains 🍜 What to Eat Hotpot (Huoguo) 火锅 The bubbling cauldron of chili oil and Sichuan peppercorns — Chengdu's culinary religion. Cook your own meat and veg in the broth, dip in sesame-oil sauce, repeat until happy. 🍽 🍽 Shu Daxia (蜀大侠) · Xiaolongkan · ¥80–150 pp · book ahead Dan Dan Noodles 担担面 The taste of Chengdu in one bowl: springy noodles in a spicy, numbing, peanut-flecked sauce with minced pork — street food elevated to legend. 🍽 🍽 Chengdu snack chains (Long Chao Shou, 龙抄手) · ¥12–18 Sweet Water Noodles 甜水面 Thick, chewy noodles coated in a sweet-spicy sauce of brown sugar and chili — uniquely Chengdu, and the perfect palate cleanser after the numbing stuff. 🍽 🍽 Snack shops in Kuanzhai & Jinli · ¥12–15 Mapo Tofu 麻婆豆腐 Silken tofu in a fiery, numbing sauce of minced beef and fermented bean paste — named after the pockmarked ('mapo') woman who invented it in 1860s Chengdu. A certified classic. 🍽 🍽 Chen Mapo Tofu (陈麻婆豆腐, original since 1862) · ¥30–45 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Panda Base opens at 7:30am — be there at opening. Pandas are most active during breakfast and asleep by 10am; the tour buses arrive at 9:30am. Kat Says Sichuan's famous 'ma' (麻) numbness comes from the Sichuan peppercorn — embrace it. And learn one word: 'wei-la' (微辣) = mild, your hotpot safety word. Kat Says Teahouse etiquette: one pot of tea (15–30 RMB) buys you a seat for hours. People's Park's Heming Teahouse is the classic — arrive after 3pm for the liveliest scene. title: Chongqing
snippet: the honest guide to chongqing for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🔥 重庆 Chongqing Cyberpunk city, hotpot capital, mountain drama ★★★☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Unique architecture Best hotpot Spicy! ✨ Why Chongqing? Chongqing is China's most surreal city — a mega-city of 32 million people built on mountains where two rivers meet, and the trains run through apartment buildings. Photographers call it cyberpunk: buildings stacked on buildings, neon-lit bridges layered over the Yangtze, and an elevator ride that feels like a mountain hike. It's also the birthplace of Chinese hotpot — the original, dangerously spicy broth — and it's famous for one of China's friendliest street-food scenes. Come for the impossible architecture, stay for the food, and leave wondering how any of it was built. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Hongya Cave at night The most photographed spot in Chongqing Read the story 2 Jiefangbei & the CBD The city's beating heart Read the story 3 Original Chongqing hotpot The spiciest broth on earth Read the story 4 Liziba — the train through a building A metro line runs right through an apartment block Read the story 5 Ciqikou Ancient Town A thousand-year-old porcelain town The story: Hongya Cave ('Red Cliff Cave') is an 11-story complex of traditional stilted houses built into the cliff above the Jialing River, completed in 2006. Its stacked wooden pavilions — styled after the old riverside dwellings that once filled Chongqing — light up at night into a glowing, multi-tiered pagoda-like structure that everyone compares to the movie Spirited Away. Why it's a must-see: At night it's pure magic: golden lanterns, balconies full of teahouses and snack shops, and the Jialing River reflecting the whole glowing stack below. It's the definitive Chongqing photo — and inside, the fourth-floor food street is a full local snack market. 💡 Kat's tip: Come after 7pm when it's fully lit. The classic view is from across the river on the Hongya Cave side; from the Jiefangbei side walk down to the riverfront for the postcard shot. Free entry, busy on weekends. The story: Jiefangbei ('Liberation Monument') is a 27.5-meter obelisk built in 1947 to mark victory in the War of Resistance, standing in the middle of Chongqing's busiest shopping district. Around it, the CBD mixes brand malls, street markets, and the city's famous '8D' pedestrian network of elevated walkways and underground passages. Why it's a must-see: This is Chongqing's downtown — the place to feel the city's relentless energy, shop, and watch the crowds. Just steps away you'll find the Ronghui and Shibati old streets climbing the hillside, and the best rooftop bars with skyline views. 💡 Kat's tip: Stand at the monument at sunset, then follow the downhill stair-streets toward the river — the walk down Jiefangbei's hillside alleys is a mini-adventure in itself. Free. The story: Chongqing hotpot was born in the 1920s when dock workers boiled cheap beef offal in a shared pot of spiced broth on the riverside. From that pot grew a culinary empire: today the city has over 30,000 hotpot restaurants, and the local saying goes 'a good hotpot is 80% oil' — a churning, blood-red cauldron of chili, peppercorn and butter that's the spiciest in China. Why it's a must-see: This isn't just a meal, it's the city's identity — and it's genuinely different from the Sichuan hotpot next door: heavier, oilier, fiercer. Order the classic 'jiuge' (nine-grid) pot to divide your ingredients, and brace yourself for the legendary 'wei' (numbing) that follows. 💡 Kat's tip: Get the yuanyang (鸳鸯) half-mild pot if you're not a veteran. Locals swear by dipping everything in sesame oil (it cuts the spice). Top spots: Qiuzui Hotpot, Xiao Longkan — ¥80–150 pp. The story: At Liziba station, Chongqing's Line 2 monorail passes directly through the 19th floor of an ordinary apartment building. The station and the building were designed together in 2004 — the residents get soundproofing, and the train gets one of the world's most famous commuter routes, gliding out of a wall over the Jialing River. Why it's a must-see: It's the purest example of Chongqing's impossible architecture — a city where a train is your upstairs neighbor. Watch from the observation platform below as the monorail disappears into the building, and ride the line yourself for the river-and-cliff views. 💡 Kat's tip: Take Line 2 and ride a couple of stops — the river crossing is beautiful. The best photo spot is the plaza across the street from Liziba station. Free; metro ride ~3 RMB. The story: Ciqikou ('Porcelain Port') is a hilltop town that has stood above the Jialing River for over 1,000 years, thriving as a porcelain-making and shipping port since the Ming dynasty. Its stone lanes, teahouses and riverside cliff paths survived the 20th century largely intact, and it's now Chongqing's best-preserved old town. Why it's a must-see: It's a glimpse of the river-trade Chongqing that existed before the skyscrapers: Ming-style gateways, Sichuan opera stages, teahouses on the cliff edge, and the best place in the city to shop for handmade porcelain and watch calligraphers work. 💡 Kat's tip: Go on a weekday morning before the tour groups. Walk downhill to the river for the old ferry view, then climb back up for lunch at one of the cliffside teahouses. Free entry. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Jiefangbei CBD Best for first-timers Chongqing's center: the Liberation Monument, shopping, the metro hub and Hongya Cave are all within walking distance (or a 10-minute taxi). Everything on your list is 15–30 minutes away by metro or taxi. 🚇 Lines 1/2/6 · Xiaoshizi / Jiefangbei 🏛 Jiefangbei, Hongya Cave, Yangtze cable car e.g. Niccolo Chongqing (sky-high luxury in IFS Tower) · JI Hotel (great value near Jiefangbei) Nanbin Road (South Bank) Skyline views Across the Yangtze, the Nanbin Road waterfront looks directly at the downtown skyline — the best night views in the city, plus riverside restaurants and bars. Slightly less convenient, considerably more romantic. 🚇 Line 6/环线 · Nanbin Road 🏛 Yangtze cable car, Danzishi old street e.g. Chongqing Marriott (river-view rooms) · mid-range riverside hotels Guanyinqiao Foodies & shoppers Chongqing's second downtown and unofficial food capital: the Guanyinqiao night market and the surrounding streets hold some of the city's best hotpot and snacks, with direct metro access to the center in 15 minutes. 🚇 Lines 3/9 · Guanyinqiao 🏛 Guanyinqiao night market, 9 Streets food alley e.g. Holiday Inn Express · local chains (very good value) Ciqikou area Old-town atmosphere Stay near the ancient town for riverside teahouses and cliff paths in the morning before the crowds. It's a 30–40 minute metro ride to the CBD, but you wake up in old Chongqing. 🚇 Line 1 · Ciqikou 🏛 Ciqikou old town, Jialing River e.g. boutique guesthouses near the old town gate 🍜 What to Eat Chongqing Hotpot 重庆火锅 The original — a churning cauldron of chili oil and peppercorns born on the docks. Fiercer, oilier and more addictive than anywhere else on earth. 🍽 🍽 Qiuzui Hotpot (秋咀) · Xiao Longkan · ¥80–150 pp Xiaomian (little noodles) 小面 Chongqing's street breakfast: simple noodles in chili oil, vinegar and crushed peanuts — deceptively plain, devastatingly good. The city's answer to 'how to start the day'. 🍽 🍽 Any xiaomian shop with a queue · ¥8–15 Suanlafen 酸辣粉 Hot and sour glass noodles with peanuts, pickled vegetables and chili — street food perfection, usually eaten standing up from a paper bowl. 🍽 🍽 Jiefangbei & Ciqikou street stalls · ¥10–15 Maoxuewang 毛血旺 A fiery Sichuan-Chongqing classic: duck blood, tripe and vegetables swimming in a vast bowl of chili and peppercorn oil. Adventurous, and unforgettable. 🍽 🍽 Sichuan restaurants citywide · ¥60–100 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Chongqing is built on mountains — you WILL get lost. Google Maps doesn't work well here; use Amap (高德) or Baidu Maps, and remember that 'two blocks away' might mean a 20-story climb. Kat Says The Yangtze River cable car (2 RMB) across the river is a working commuter line, not a tourist ride — do it at sunset for the best skyline approach. Kat Says Order hotpot with 'weila' (微辣) if you're not a spice veteran, and always get the sesame-oil dip — it's not optional, it's survival.
