title: Huangshan
snippet: the honest guide to huangshan for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back ⛰️ 黄山 Huangshan Granite peaks, sea of clouds, Hongcun village, UNESCO ★★★☆☆ 🗓 3–4 days Hiking Sea of clouds UNESCO ✨ Why Huangshan? "No mountain is worth seeing after Huangshan," says the Chinese proverb. The Yellow Mountains are where China's painters found their style — granite pillars that punch through a sea of clouds, pines that grow sideways off cliffs, and light that changes every five minutes. It's the landscape you've already seen in every Chinese ink painting; it just happens to be real. But Huangshan is a two-part story. Below the peaks lies the Huizhou countryside — villages with white walls and black-tiled roofs, the most beautiful of which is Hongcun, UNESCO-listed and the film set of "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon." Three or four days lets you catch a sunrise on the mountain and a slow sunset in a village. Both are essential. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Hongcun Village UNESCO · "Village in Chinese paintings" · water-mirror streets Read the story 2 Welcoming Pine (Yingke Song) The 800-year-old pine that welcomes the world Read the story 3 Bright Summit & Sea of Clouds Sunrise spot · clouds below your feet Read the story 4 Xihai Grand Canyon The most dramatic hiking loop on the mountain Read the story 5 Tunxi Old Street (Laojie) Ming-dynasty shopping street · ink brushes & Huizhou snacks The story: Hongcun was founded in 1131 by a family descended from the Song dynasty general Wang Yan, and for nine centuries the villagers have lived by a genius water system — a stream diverted from the hills that flows past every doorstep, a design that keeps the lanes clean and the houses cool. The Moon Pond at the village center mirrors the houses so perfectly that Hongcun is called "the village in Chinese paintings." Why it's a must-see: This is the iconic Huizhou landscape — white walls, black tiles, horseshoe-shaped gables — and the film set of "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon" (the flying-over-water duel was shot here). Unlike Disneyfied tourist towns, Hongcun is a living village: grandparents pickle vegetables in doorways, students sketch on the canal banks. 💡 Kat's tip: Sleep inside the village — after 5pm the day-trippers leave and you get the Moon Pond to yourself at dawn. Hire a local guide for two hours; the stories behind the carvings are half the experience. The story: Growing out of a granite ledge at 1,670 meters, this pine has been bending toward visitors for 800 years, its branches extended like an open arm. It's so beloved that it appeared on Chinese currency, and when one of its branches broke in a storm, the news made national headlines. Why it's a must-see: It's the most famous tree in China and the visual shorthand for Huangshan itself. The pines of Huangshan are famous for growing in impossible places — out of bare rock, sideways, upside-down — surviving winds that would kill any other tree. 💡 Kat's tip: The Welcoming Pine is near the Yuping cable car station, making it the easiest famous thing on the mountain to reach. Go at opening time before tour groups arrive. The story: Bright Summit is Huangshan's third-highest peak at 1,860 meters, a broad rocky dome that's the mountain's most famous sunrise viewpoint. Below it stretches the "sea of clouds" — a weather phenomenon where a layer of mist fills the valleys and the granite peaks rise through it like islands, which is exactly how Huangshan got its nickname, "the mountain of the sea of clouds." Why it's a must-see: Sunrise here is the moment people climb Huangshan for. As the sun hits the clouds, the peaks turn gold, and the famous "Guangming Top" — the brightest summit — lives up to its name. The "Monkey Gazing at the Sea" rock nearby is the classic photo of a stone monkey looking out over the clouds. 💡 Kat's tip: Check the sunrise forecast the night before and leave your hotel 40 minutes early — the path gets crowded. The sea of clouds is most likely after rain or in late autumn. Bring a headlamp for the pre-dawn walk. The story: The West Sea Grand Canyon is Huangshan's deepest and most spectacular gorge — a 15-km slash in the mountain where granite spires and ridgelines drop hundreds of meters into mist. A walkway clings to the cliffs, crossing suspension bridges and passing through tunnels carved in the rock. Why it's a must-see: It's the most dramatic hiking loop on the mountain and where the "two tourists a minute" crowds of the main summits thin out. You'll feel properly small — standing on a cliff path with the canyon falling away on both sides. 💡 Kat's tip: The full loop takes 4–5 hours with serious stairs — do it if you're fit, the small loop (via the "Flying-over Stone" path) if not. Go in the morning before the clouds burn off. The canyon can close in bad weather; check at your hotel. The story: Tunxi Old Street, the gateway town below Huangshan, was built in the Ming dynasty as the trading heart of the Huizhou merchants — some of the richest traders in imperial China. The street runs 1.3 km under dark, carved wooden shopfronts that have stood for 600 years. Why it's a must-see: It's where you'll find the region's traditional crafts: ink brushes, inkstones, and she ink (ink-sticks) made here for a millennium, plus carved woodwork and sesame cakes baking in stone ovens. It's touristy, but the architecture is real and the food is excellent. 💡 Kat's tip: Stay in Tunxi the night before climbing Huangshan — it's 50 minutes from the mountain's cable car base. Try the stinky mandarin fish here; done properly it's surprisingly delicate. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. On the Mountain (North/West) Best for sunrise Hotels at the summit area let you see sunrise and sunset without an impossible 4am start. Rooms are basic and expensive, but the view from the window is why you came. Best for serious sunrise hunters. ⏰ Watch sunrise from bed 🎒 Pack light — everything is carried up e.g. Huangshan Baiyun Hotel · Xihai Hotel (book months ahead) Tangkou Town Best for logistics The small town at the mountain's base, where the shuttle buses to both cable cars depart. Hotels are reasonable, food is hearty, and you can start climbing at 7am. Best for practical travelers. 🚌 10 min to cable car 🍜 Local dinner options e.g. hotels along the main road in Tangkou · mountain-view rooms Hongcun Village Best for atmosphere Sleep inside the 900-year-old village: guesthouses converted from ancestral halls, moonlight on the Moon Pond, and mornings before the tour buses arrive. Best for culture and photography. 🏮 Dawn at the Moon Pond 🚕 1 hr to the mountain base e.g. courtyard guesthouses inside Hongcun's lanes 🍜 What to Eat Stinky mandarin fish 臭鳜鱼 Huizhou's legendary dish: mandarin fish cured in a light brine until it develops a famously funky aroma, then braised with chilies, ginger, and bamboo shoots. The smell is alarming; the flesh is surprisingly delicate and clean. Order it once, for the story. 🍽 Huizhou restaurants in Tunxi · ¥80–120 Mao tofu 毛豆腐 Tofu left to ferment until it grows a white "fur" of mycelium, then pan-fried until golden. The coating becomes creamy and nutty — it tastes far better than it looks, especially with chili oil. 🍽 Street stalls in Tunxi Old Street · ¥15–25 Huangshan sesame cakes 黄山烧饼 Small round pastries baked against the walls of a stone oven — flaky layers, a filling of dried pork and sesame, and a sweet-savory crunch. The perfect hiking fuel for the mountain. 🍽 Lao Jie shops · ¥1–3 each Mountain chicken soup 徽州土鸡汤 Free-range village chicken simmered for hours with bamboo shoots and mountain herbs into a golden, restorative broth — the traditional post-hike reward. Served in clay pots across the Huizhou countryside. 🍽 Farmhouse restaurants near Hongcun · ¥60–100 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Sunrise is the whole point of Huangshan — book a night on the mountain, or you'll regret the 3:30am shuttle. Kat Says Sea of clouds chance is highest right after rain. If it rained yesterday, climb today — and bring waterproofs. Kat Says Do the mountain first, then Hongcun to recover. A night in the village fixes everything the hiking broke. Explore More Cities 🍃 杭州 · Hangzhou West Lake, tea plantations, Buddhist temples, poetry 🏞️ 张家界 · Zhangjiajie Avatar mountains, glass bridges, forested pillars ← Back to Ready? China!

title: Kashgar
snippet: the honest guide to kashgar for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏛️ 喀什古城 Kashgar Uyghur craft bazaar, Silk Road living museum ★★★★★ 🗓 2–3 days Silk Road bazaar Ethnic culture Off the beaten path ✨ Why Kashgar? Kashgar is the farthest west you can go in China — a Silk Road city on the edge of the Taklamakan Desert where Uyghur culture, Central Asian bazaars and 2,000 years of trade history still fill the streets. It's the most different place in China from anything you've seen: adobe alleyways, mosques, melons piled high, and a Sunday livestock market that hasn't changed in centuries. This is ★★★★★ difficulty — very little English, an overnight flight from the east, and a culture that rewards patience. But for travelers who make it, Kashgar is the single most memorable stop in the country: a living Silk Road museum that feels a world away from Beijing or Shanghai. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Kashgar Old City A 2,000-year-old adobe maze Read the story 2 Id Kah Mosque & the Sunday livestock market The heart of Uyghur Kashgar Read the story 3 Handicraft Street Copper, carpets & centuries-old crafts Read the story 4 Fresh naan & a Uyghur tea house The best bread on the Silk Road Read the story 5 Lamb kebabs & hand-pulled noodles Silk Road food, grilled over charcoal The story: The old city of Kashgar has stood for over 2,000 years as a trading post on the Silk Road, its maze of adobe alleyways and wooden balconies barely changed since the days when caravans rested here between China and Central Asia. Today some 70,000 people live inside its walls, in homes built like a honeycomb — flat-roofed, mud-brick, and connected by lanes so narrow that two people can barely pass. Why it's a must-see: This is not a museum or a film set — it's a living neighborhood where children play in the alleys, craftsmen hammer copper in their doorways, and the smell of naan bread fills the air. Wandering without a plan is the whole point; every turn reveals a workshop, a courtyard, or a group of elders playing chess under a grape trellis. 💡 Kat's tip: Enter through the East Gate (the grand opening ceremony happens at 10am) and just walk. Greet people with 'salam' and a smile — locals are famously warm. Allow a full half day; the alleys are endless. The story: Id Kah Mosque, founded in 1442 and enlarged over centuries, is the largest mosque in China — its courtyard can hold over 20,000 worshippers for Friday prayers. On Sundays, the square around it and the nearby livestock market fill with farmers selling sheep, donkeys, horses and camels in a scene that looks straight out of the 19th century. Why it's a must-see: The Sunday livestock market is one of the great street spectacles of Asia: thousands of animals, traders slapping hands to seal deals, and food stalls cooking the morning's catch. And the mosque — with its yellow-tiled gateway and vast courtyard — is the architectural heart of Uyghur Kashgar. 💡 Kat's tip: The livestock market peaks before 10am on Sundays — go early, it's at the town's west edge (taxi ~15 RMB). The mosque is open to visitors outside prayer times (entry 30 RMB); dress modestly. The story: Kashgar's craft quarter is a street-long workshop where Uyghur artisans practice trades their families have held for generations: hammering copper pots, weaving carpets, forging knives, embroidering hats and carving wooden instruments. Many workshops have been here since before the Silk Road caravans stopped using camels. Why it's a must-see: You can watch a copper pot being born from a flat sheet of metal, smell the wool of fresh carpets, and buy directly from the makers — no middlemen, no factory replicas. It's the closest thing left to a genuine Silk Road bazaar, and the craftsmanship is extraordinary. 💡 Kat's tip: Bargain politely but fairly — these are working artisans, and the quality justifies the price. Copper teapots (~100–300 RMB) and embroidered caps (~30–80 RMB) make the best gifts. Ask before photographing the craftsmen. The story: Naan — flatbread baked on the walls of a clay oven — is the staff of life in Kashgar, and every neighborhood has its bakery. The classic round naan is stamped with a pattern, brushed with sesame and baked in seconds at 300°C. Karim's Bakery in the old city is locally famous for the freshest loaves; pair one with salted milk tea or a Uyghur fruit-and-nut tea in a traditional tea house. Why it's a must-see: There's nothing like naan straight from a clay oven at 7am in an adobe alley — crisp-edged, chewy-centered, dusted with sesame. And the tea houses of the old city, where men gather all day over melon seeds and endless refills of tea, are the social heart of Kashgar. 💡 Kat's tip: Naan costs 3–5 RMB — buy a few for the day. For the tea-house scene, look for one with carpets on the platforms and locals playing dap (drum); the Uyghur tea with almonds, raisins and rock sugar is the classic order. The story: Kashgar's food is Central Asian to the core: lamb kebabs grilled over charcoal with cumin and chili, hand-pulled noodles (laghman) tossed with lamb and peppers, polo (pilaf) cooked with carrots and raisins, and grilled whole fish from nearby rivers. This is the food the Silk Road traded — and it's still cooked the same way. Why it's a must-see: After weeks of Chinese food, Kashgar's meat-and-noodle cooking hits completely differently: smoky kebabs, fragrant pilaf, and the best bread in Asia. The night market near the old city's east gate is the place to graze from stall to stall. 💡 Kat's tip: Kebab stalls with long queues are the good ones — order 10 skewers and stand there eating them. Try polo (5–15 RMB) and laghman (10–20 RMB) from the old-city kitchens. Finish with a bowl of local yogurt. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Inside the Old City Immersive experience Boutique guesthouses tucked into the adobe lanes — Uyghur courtyard houses with carved wooden balconies, where you wake up to the call to prayer and the sound of naan baking. The most atmospheric stay in China, full stop. 🚇 No metro — old city is walkable; taxis cheap 🏛 Old City East Gate, Handicraft Street e.g. Kashgar Old City boutique guesthouses (traditional Uyghur courtyards) · from ~250 RMB City center (People's Square) Comfort & convenience The modern center around People's Square and the Id Kah area: international-standard hotels, English-speaking staff at the better ones, and easy taxi access to the old city (10 minutes). Best choice if you want comfort after intense days. 🚇 No metro — taxis across town ~10–20 RMB 🏛 Id Kah Mosque, People's Square, night market e.g. Radisson Blu Kashgar (international comfort) · local 3–4 star hotels Seminary / old city west edge Budget & backpackers A cluster of budget hostels and guesthouses around the old city's western lanes — atmospheric, central and cheap. Shared bathrooms at the cheapest places, but you're right in the action. 🚇 No metro — walk to the old city 🏛 Seminary area, old city west gates, bazaar e.g. Seminary Hostel (converted madrasa, atmospheric) · budget guesthouses from ~100 RMB 🍜 What to Eat Lamb Kebabs 烤肉 Chargrilled over charcoal with cumin and chili — you'll smell them three blocks away. The definitive Kashgar street food, eaten standing up. 🍽 🍽 Night market & old city stalls · ¥3–5 per skewer Hand-Pulled Noodles (Laghman) 拉条子 Thick, chewy noodles hand-ripped and tossed with lamb, peppers and tomatoes ��� a Uyghur staple you'll dream about after you leave. 🍽 🍽 Old city noodle kitchens · ¥10–20 Polo (Pilaf) 抓饭 Fragrant rice slow-cooked with lamb, carrots and raisins — Central Asia on a plate. Often topped with a piece of melt-tender lamb. 🍽 🍽 Polo houses near the bazaar · ¥10–25 Naan & Salted Milk Tea 馕与奶茶 Fresh clay-oven naan dipped in salty, buttery milk tea — the breakfast (and lunch, and snack) of the Silk Road. 🍽 🍽 Karim's Bakery & old city tea houses · ¥3–10 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Kashgar is ★★★★★ difficulty: English is rare, Uyghur and Mandarin dominate. Download Pleco + an offline translation app before you go, and learn 'salam' (hello) and 'rahmat' (thanks). Kat Says Bring cash! Many old-city shops and stalls don't accept cards or foreign WeChat Pay — RMB cash is still king in the bazaar. Kat Says The Sunday livestock market is the single greatest street spectacle in China — go before 10am. And fly in/out (5+ hour flights); there's no easy train from the east. title: Kunming
snippet: the honest guide to kunming for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌸 昆明 Kunming Spring weather, lakes, minority cultures, flowers ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3–4 days Spring city Flower markets Gateway to Yunnan ✨ Why Kunming? Kunming is the city that makes you understand why Yunnan is called China's rainbow province. The weather stays mild almost year-round — locals joke there are only two seasons here — and the streets are lined with magnolias and bougainvillea. It's the perfect first stop before heading to Dali, Lijiang, or Shangri-La. But Kunming is more than a transit hub. Dianchi Lake, China's sixth-largest freshwater lake, sits right at the city's edge; the flower markets here sell roses by the kilo at midnight; and the food is some of the most varied in China, thanks to the 25 ethnic minorities that call Yunnan home. If Beijing is China's history book, Kunming is its front porch — relaxed, colorful, and unexpectedly delicious. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Stone Forest (Shilin) UNESCO · karst landscape · 270 million years old Read the story 2 Dianchi Lake & Haigeng Park City lake · seagulls in winter · waterfront walks Read the story 3 Green Lake Park (Cuihu) Local life · tai chi · winter seagulls Read the story 4 Yunnan Nationalities Village 25 ethnic groups · dance shows · architecture Read the story 5 Dounan Flower Market Asia's largest flower market · roses by the kilo The story: The Stone Forest is a 270-million-year-old karst landscape of grey limestone pillars, caves, and underground rivers. Once an ancient seabed, tectonic shifts lifted the stone and water carved it into the maze you see today. The local Sani people, a branch of the Yi ethnic group, have legends that say the stones were once a girl turned to stone while waiting for her lover. Why it's a must-see: It's the single most famous day trip from Kunming and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. You can wander narrow passages between towers up to 30 meters tall, visit a traditional Sani village, and catch minority song-and-dance performances. It's touristy but genuinely spectacular. 💡 Kat's tip: Go early (before 9am) to beat the crowds and the midday heat. The park is 90 km from Kunming — book a tour bus or hire a driver for the day. Wear comfortable shoes; the stone paths are slippery. The story: Dianchi is the largest lake in Yunnan and the sixth-largest freshwater lake in China, stretching 40 km from north to south. For centuries it has been Kunming's water garden, pleasure boat destination, and — unfortunately — industrial dumping ground. Major cleanup projects since the 1990s have brought back birds, boardwalks, and blue skies. Why it's a must-see: On clear days the lake is backed by the Western Hills (Sleeping Beauty Mountain), and in winter thousands of red-billed gulls migrate from Siberia to Haigeng Dam, where locals sell bread for feeding them. It's a 20-minute taxi ride from downtown and a great place to catch sunset. 💡 Kat's tip: Visit Haigeng Dam in the late afternoon for the best light. Winter (November–March) is prime seagull season. Combine it with the Yunnan Nationalities Village, which sits right on the lake's north shore. The story: Green Lake has been Kunming's favorite public park since the 17th century, when the Qing dynasty connected nine springs into a single lake. The banks are lined with willows and teahouses, and the central pavilions host musicians, dancers, and retirees playing mahjong almost every day of the week. Why it's a must-see: This is where Kunming comes to breathe. Morning tai chi, elderly couples dancing to old songs, and parents showing kids how to feed gulls — it's the city's living room. Best of all, it's completely free and right in the city center. 💡 Kat's tip: Go before 9am to see the park at its liveliest. In winter, buy a bag of bread and feed the black-headed gulls that migrate here. The surrounding streets have excellent local breakfast spots. The story: Yunnan is home to 25 of China's 56 recognized ethnic minorities, and this open-air museum attempts to introduce visitors to as many as possible. Each village is built in traditional style — Dai bamboo houses, Bai marble courtyards, Tibetan prayer wheels — and staffed by people from those communities. Why it's a must-see: It's a little theme-park-ish, but if you only have a day in Kunming and want a crash course in Yunnan's ethnic diversity, this is the easiest place to do it. The dance shows are lively, and the lakeside setting makes for pleasant walking. 💡 Kat's tip: Go on a weekday to avoid school groups. Check the show schedule at the entrance and time your visit around the performances. It's right next to Dianchi Lake, so pair the two stops. The story: Dounan Flower Market is the largest fresh-cut flower trading center in Asia. More than 70% of China's cut flowers pass through here, and the market operates like a stock exchange — prices flash on screens and roses, lilies, and carnations move by the truckload. Why it's a must-see: Even if you don't buy anything, the sensory overload is unforgettable: rooms filled with roses, hallways of dried flowers, and bouquets wrapped at lightning speed. It's also the cheapest place on Earth to feel like you should buy 100 roses. 💡 Kat's tip: The real action happens after 8pm, when wholesale buyers arrive. Visit the main trading hall late evening for the full chaos. It's about 30 minutes from downtown by metro — take Line 1 to Dounan Station. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Green Lake / Wuyi Road Best for first-timers The classic choice: walk to Green Lake Park in minutes, surrounded by restaurants, cafés, and old bookstores. Metro Line 3 links you to the train station and the rest of the city. Best for travelers who want a green, walkable base. 🚇 Line 3 · Panjiawan 🌳 Walk to Green Lake e.g. Green Lake Hotel (classic) · boutique guesthouses on Wuyi Road Nanping Street / Jinbi Square City center & metro hub Kunming's commercial heart: shopping malls, pedestrian streets, and the Jinbi Archway. Plenty of hotels at every price and easy metro access to both train stations. Best for convenience and nightlife. 🚇 Line 1/3 · Dongfeng Square 🛍 Shopping & food streets e.g. Holiday Inn Kunming City Centre · budget hotels around Dongfeng Road Guandu Ancient Town Old-town atmosphere A restored ancient town on the Dianchi Lake shore, with pagodas, temples, and old streets. Quieter than downtown and closer to the airport. Best for travelers who want history without leaving the city. 🚕 30 min to airport 🏛 Temples & old streets e.g. Guandu boutique inns · mid-range courtyard guesthouses 🍜 What to Eat Crossing-the-bridge noodles 过桥米线 Yunnan's most famous dish: a steaming bowl of rich chicken broth, thin rice noodles, and a dozen small plates of raw meat, vegetables, and quail egg that cook in the broth at your table. 🍽 Jianxin Yuan · Qiao Xiang Yuan · ¥25–60 per set Steam pot chicken 汽锅鸡 Chicken steamed for hours in a clay pot with a hollow central chimney, producing a clear, intensely flavored soup. The clay pot is the secret — it condenses steam back into the broth. 🍽 Fu Zhao Lou · old Yunnan restaurants around Jinbi Road · ¥60–120 Grilled tofu & erkuai 烤豆腐 / 饵块 Street-side snacks: tiny cubes of firm tofu grilled over charcoal and eaten with chili-dusted soy sauce, plus erkuai (pressed rice cakes) wrapped around pickled vegetables or sausage. 🍽 Night markets around Guandu Old Town · street carts near Green Lake · ¥10–25 Wild mushroom hot pot 野生菌火锅 Yunnan's rainy season (June–September) brings hundreds of wild mushrooms to market. A mushroom hot pot is the safest way to try them — restaurants are licensed and the broth is legendary. 🍽 Specialty mushroom restaurants on Guanxing Road · ¥80–180 pp 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Kunming sits at 1,900 m altitude. Take it easy on day one — alcohol and intense exercise hit harder here. Kat Says The temperature swings between day and night. Carry a light jacket even in summer. Kat Says Dounan Flower Market is best after 8pm. Roses by the kilo are real, and ridiculously cheap. Explore More Cities 🌊 大理 · Dali Ancient town, Erhai Lake, Bai culture, Cangshan mountains 🏔️ 丽江 · Lijiang Cobblestone old town, Naxi culture, Jade Dragon Snow Mountain ← Back to Ready? China!

title: Lhasa
snippet: the honest guide to lhasa for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏔️ 拉萨 Lhasa Potala Palace, Tibetan Buddhism, high-altitude magic ★★★★☆ 🗓 4–5 days High altitude Tibetan culture Monasteries ✨ Why Lhasa? At 3,650 meters above sea level, Lhasa — "the Place of the Gods" in Tibetan — is one of the highest cities on Earth and the beating heart of Tibetan Buddhism. The Potala Palace crowns the skyline like nothing else in China, and the air itself seems thinner, clearer, and more alive. This is a city you feel in your lungs and your soul. Time moves differently here. Pilgrims walk the Barkhor circuit spinning prayer wheels, monks argue philosophy in monastery courtyards, and buttery incense drifts from every shrine. The Qinghai–Tibet railway and a new high-altitude airport make it reachable, but nothing about Lhasa feels easy or ordinary. Come for the once-in-a-lifetime views; stay for the quiet awe. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Potala Palace UNESCO · 1,000 rooms · symbol of Tibet Read the story 2 Jokhang Temple & Barkhor Street The holiest temple in Tibet · pilgrim circuit Read the story 3 Sera Monastery Famous monk debates · clapping, shouting, philosophy Read the story 4 Drepung Monastery Once the world's largest monastery · white-washed hillside Read the story 5 Namtso Lake (Tian Hu) Sky lake at 4,718 m · turquoise holy water The story: The Potala rises 13 storeys and 117 meters above Lhasa, built from 1645 onward as the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas. It holds more than 1,000 rooms, 10,000 shrines, and the gilded tombs of eight Dalai Lamas. For 300 years it was the seat of Tibetan government and the most recognizable building on the Tibetan plateau. Why it's a must-see: Because there is nothing else on Earth like it. The white walls are palaces and offices, the red center is the sacred halls, and inside, corridors of butter lamps and tapestries lead to jewel-encrusted stupas. The view of the city from the roof is unforgettable. 💡 Kat's tip: Book tickets online two days ahead — numbers are strictly limited and it sells out fast. Go early (morning slots) when the light hits the white walls. Give it 3 hours; the interior is a maze. The story: The Jokhang, built in the 7th century, houses the Jowo Shakyamuni — a statue of Buddha at age 12 that Tibetans believe is the most sacred object in the world. Since it was placed here, pilgrims have walked the Barkhor circuit around the temple clockwise, spinning prayer wheels and touching foreheads to the stones. Why it's a must-see: This is Tibet's spiritual core, more profound than any sight. Join the flow of pilgrims on Barkhor Street at dawn — some in fur hats, some prostrating full-length in the dust. The incense, the murmur of prayers, the golden rooftops: it's overwhelming in the best way. 💡 Kat's tip: Walk the Barkhor circuit clockwise — it's a sacred rule, never counter-clockwise. Enter the Jokhang early (8am) to avoid queues. Dress modestly and remove hats indoors. The story: Founded in 1419, Sera is one of the "Big Three" Gelug monasteries of Lhasa. Its fame today rests on a daily ritual that looks like an argument — from 3pm, monks gather in a gravel courtyard and debate Buddhist philosophy with dramatic claps, slaps, and shouts of "Dhi!" Why it's a must-see: The debates are genuinely fascinating theater: one monk sits, one stands and attacks his logic with physical gestures, and the clap is meant to "wake the mind." You don't need to understand Tibetan to feel the energy. The monastery's rooftop views over the valley are a bonus. 💡 Kat's tip: Time your visit for the 3pm debates (daily except Sundays in winter). It's 20 minutes by taxi from central Lhasa. Combine with a walk through the old quarters below the monastery. The story: In its 17th-century heyday, Drepung — "Rice Heap" — housed 10,000 monks and was the largest monastery on Earth, ranking above the Potala as the seat of the Dalai Lamas' government. Its whitewashed buildings sprawl across the hillside like a small white city. Why it's a must-see: It's the grandest monastery complex in Tibet and largely untouristed compared to the Potala. Climb through silent lanes, butter-lamp halls, and courtyards where monks still live and study. The main assembly hall holds 5,000 seated monks at once. 💡 Kat's tip: Combine it with Sera for a full monastery day — Drepung in the morning, Sera in the afternoon. The hike up the hill is steep; take the shuttle or a taxi if the altitude bothers you. The story: Namtso means "Heavenly Lake" in Tibetan. At 4,718 meters and 1,920 square kilometers, it's the highest large saltwater lake in the world — a sheet of impossibly turquoise water under the Nyenchen Tanglha snow range. Tibetans revere it as a holy lake; pilgrims circle its 280-km shore on foot. Why it's a must-see: This is the classic full-day trip from Lhasa and the most dramatic scenery you can reach in one day. The lake shifts from sapphire to jade with the clouds, yaks graze on the shore, and prayer flags snap in the wind. Sunset here is a religious experience. 💡 Kat's tip: The altitude is brutal — acclimatize in Lhasa for at least two days first. Go with a driver or day tour (4 hours each way). Bring layers; it's freezing even in summer. Don't stay overnight if you're sensitive to altitude. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Barkhor / Old Town Best for atmosphere Lhasa's old Tibetan quarter: narrow lanes, courtyards, and the pilgrim circuit outside your door. Traditional guesthouses with courtyards and rooftop views of the Potala. Best for culture and atmosphere. 🚶 Walk to Jokhang Temple 🏮 Traditional guesthouses e.g. heritage courtyard inns near Barkhor · Shambhala Guesthouse Potala View / West Best for first-timers Modern hotels facing the Potala Palace, many with rooftop or window views of the red-and-white icon. Quieter, more comfortable, and a short walk to the palace entrance. Best for comfort and views. 🚶 Walk to Potala Palace 🏔 Palace-facing rooms e.g. St. Regis Lhasa · Himalaya Hotel (palace views) North / Lhasa River Modern & quiet The newer northern quarter along the Lhasa River: wider streets, modern cafés, and fewer tourists. Best for longer stays, remote work, or travelers who want oxygen bars and modern amenities. 🚕 10 min to Old Town ☕ Modern cafés & shops e.g. modern chain hotels along the river north 🍜 What to Eat Sweet tea 甜茶 Milk tea brewed with black tea, sugar, and yak milk — served in thermos bottles at every teahouse. Tibetans sit for hours over sweet tea, chatting and watching the street. It's also the best cure for altitude headaches (caffeine + hydration). 🍽 Teahouses on Barkhor Street · ¥3–5 per cup Tibetan noodles 藏面 Hand-pulled wheat noodles in a simple broth with minced yak meat and scallions, eaten for breakfast with a side of pickled vegetables. Hearty, warming, and cheap. 🍽 Morning noodle shops near Barkhor · ¥10–20 Momo dumplings 藏式饺子 Tibet's answer to dumplings: thick-skinned, steamed or fried, stuffed with yak meat, vegetables, or cheese. Served with a fierce chili sauce. Steamed momo with sweet tea is the classic Tibetan lunch. 🍽 Restaurants across the Old Town · ¥15–30 Yak hot pot 牦牛火锅 Thin-sliced yak meat cooked in a bubbling broth with mushrooms and greens — the classic high-altitude dinner. Yak meat is lean, rich, and tastes like nowhere else. Finish with butter tea if you're brave. 🍽 Hot pot restaurants near Beijing Road · ¥80–150 pp 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Altitude is the whole game. Rest on day one, drink sweet tea, avoid alcohol and hot showers, and don't fly straight to Namtso. Kat Says Book the Potala ticket online days in advance and visit early — it's strictly limited and worth every minute. Kat Says Walk the Barkhor circuit clockwise, dress modestly at temples, and ask before photographing pilgrims. Respect makes the city open up. title: Lijiang
snippet: the honest guide to lijiang for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏔️ 丽江 Lijiang Naxi culture, cobblestone old town, Jade Dragon Snow Mountain ★★★☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Old town charm Nightlife Snow mountain ✨ Why Lijiang? Lijiang is where China's old town charm meets its highest drama: a 800-year-old cobblestone town of canals and wooden houses (UNESCO World Heritage since 1997), set against the 5,596-meter Jade Dragon Snow Mountain rising right behind it. It's the home of the Naxi people and their Dongba culture — the last living pictographic script on earth. By day you can ride a cable car to 4,506 meters and stand on a glacier; by night the old town's bars and bonfires take over. It's the perfect blend of culture, mountain adventure and nightlife — and one of the most photographed corners of China. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Lijiang Old Town An 800-year-old cobblestone maze Read the story 2 Jade Dragon Snow Mountain Cable car to 4,506 meters Read the story 3 Black Dragon Pool The classic reflection of the snow mountain Read the story 4 Naxi Dongba culture show A 1,000-year-old pictographic script Read the story 5 Old town bar street at night Live music, bonfires & dancing The story: Lijiang Old Town was founded in the late Song dynasty (13th century) and built without walls — a Naxi tradition, since a city with walls 'traps' good fortune. Its cobblestone lanes follow the canals of the Jade River, which flows through every street (the Naxi used to wash the town's stone by opening sluice gates). It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, the first old town in China to be listed. Why it's a must-see: There's no other old town quite like it: waterways threading every lane, stone bridges every few dozen meters, and a layout designed to be walked without ever feeling lost. It's also genuinely alive — residents still live and trade here, and the surrounding Naxi courtyards (with their 'three rooms one screen wall' architecture) are beautiful. 💡 Kat's tip: Wander off the main tourist lanes (Sifang Street) into the quieter northern alleys, especially at 7am when the town is empty and the canals sing. Entry is free, but there's a 50 RMB 'maintenance fee' collected at some gates — it's included if you stay in a licensed guesthouse. The story: Jade Dragon Snow Mountain (Yulong Xueshan) is a 13-peak range whose highest summit reaches 5,596 meters, permanently snow-capped and towering 4,000 meters above Lijiang's valley floor. The Glacier Park cable car climbs to 4,506 meters — among the highest cable car stations in Asia — putting you on a real glacier at the edge of the clouds. Why it's a must-see: The contrast is the magic: subtropical valley one moment, glacier and thin air the next. The ride up is a show of its own, and at the top you can walk a boardwalk onto the glacier itself. Below, the Impression Lijiang show (by the director of Avatar's sound designer, Zhang Yimou's team) sets 500 performers against the mountain. 💡 Kat's tip: Book the cable car ticket online (peak season sells out days ahead; ~140 RMB + entrance 100 RMB). Bring oxygen (30 RMB at the base) even if you feel fine — altitude hits fast. Go early; clouds roll in by noon. The story: Black Dragon Pool (Heilongtan) is a spring-fed lake at the north edge of the old town, designed as a Ming-dynasty park with the Jade Dragon Snow Mountain as its backdrop. The five-arch Jade Dragon Bridge and the Deyue Tower pagoda sit in the middle of the pool, and on clear days the entire snow mountain range is reflected in the still water — the most photographed view in Yunnan. Why it's a must-see: It's the postcard shot: pagoda, bridge and snow mountain in a single frame of mirror-still water. The park is also home to the Dongba Museum, where you can see the Naxi's pictographic script — the world's last living pictographic writing system — up close. 💡 Kat's tip: Go in the early morning for the calmest water and the clearest reflection; by 10am the wind picks up and the mirror ripples. Entry 50 RMB (some hotels include it). The Dongba Museum inside is worth 30 minutes. The story: The Naxi people's Dongba culture is one of the world's great survivals: a religion and script — over 1,400 pictographic characters — that has been passed down by Dongba priests for over 1,000 years and is still in use today. The Dongba Culture Research Institute in Lijiang preserves it, and cultural shows around the old town stage the songs, dances and rituals that go with it. Why it's a must-see: You can watch an actual living pictographic script being read, and see ritual dance and music that descend from shamanic traditions older than the town itself. It's a rare chance to meet a culture that has no equivalent anywhere else on earth. 💡 Kat's tip: Visit the Dongba Museum at Black Dragon Pool first (free with the 50 RMB park entry), then catch an evening Naxi music and dance show in the old town (from ~100 RMB). The ancient music ensemble — with 500-year-old instruments — is the unmissable one. The story: When the sun sets, the old town's riverside lanes turn into Yunnan's most famous nightlife strip: bars with live bands playing everything from folk to rock, bonfires where locals and travelers join hands to dance, and the canal reflections doubling every light. The main 'Bar Street' along the river is the energetic core; the side lanes hide quieter, cooler spots. Why it's a must-see: It's the yin to the mountain's yang: after a day of glaciers and temples, Lijiang lets loose. The bonfire circle dances (everyone holding hands, stepping in a circle to Naxi music) are joyful and unpretentious — you'll be pulled in whether you like it or not. 💡 Kat's tip: Drinks cost double on the main Bar Street — follow the music into the side lanes for the same scene at half the price. The bonfire dance starts around 8:30pm in the main square. Be careful with the cobblestones after a couple of drinks! 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Inside the Old Town Atmosphere & romance Stay in a restored Naxi courtyard house — wooden balconies, fish ponds and moon gates — right in the cobblestone maze. Magical at night when the crowds thin, but pack light: luggage has to be carried over cobblestones (some guesthouses offer pickup). 🚇 No metro — walk or taxi to the old town edge 🏛 Sifang Street, canals, Bar Street e.g. Blossom Hill Lijiang (boutique courtyard) · hundreds of courtyard guesthouses from ¥200 Shuhe Ancient Town Quieter & more authentic A smaller, quieter old town 20 minutes north of Lijiang — the same cobblestone-and-canal charm without the crowds, plus better-value guesthouses. Perfect for travelers who want the old-town experience without the party. 🚇 No metro — bus or taxi from Lijiang (20 min) 🏛 Shuhe old town, Green Dragon Bridge, Jade Dragon views e.g. boutique courtyard hotels in Shuhe from ¥250 New town (around the old town) Convenience & budget The modern city ring around the old town: standard hotels, easy luggage access and cheaper prices, 10 minutes' walk from the old town gates. Best if you're on a budget or arriving by plane with big bags. 🚇 No metro — walking distance to old town 🏛 Old town gates, bus station, restaurants e.g. InterContinental Lijiang (luxury at the mountain foot) · budget chains in the new town Ganhaizi / Jade Dragon foothills Mountain views Hotels and resorts on the meadow at the foot of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain — waking up to the full mountain wall outside your window. 30 minutes from the old town; you'll taxi for meals and nightlife. 🚇 No metro — taxi to old town ~30 min 🏛 Jade Dragon Snow Mountain, Impression Lijiang show e.g. Banyan Tree Lijiang (mountain-view villas, splurge) 🍜 What to Eat Crossing-the-Bridge Noodles 过桥米线 Yunnan's most famous dish: a bowl of boiling-hot broth you cook raw toppings in at the table — sliced meat, vegetables, quail egg, and rice noodles. Named for the legend of a wife crossing a bridge to deliver it to her husband. 🍽 🍽 Old town noodle houses · ¥30–60 per set Naxi Baba 纳西粑粑 Pan-fried flatbread — sweet (with sugar and nuts) or savory (with ham and scallion) — the classic Naxi street snack, crisp on the outside, soft within. 🍽 🍽 Street stalls across the old town · ¥10–15 Yak Meat Hotpot 牦牛肉火锅 Tender highland yak slices simmered in a spicy broth with mushrooms and greens — hearty, warming, and perfect after a cold mountain day. 🍽 🍽 Old town hotpot restaurants · ¥80–120 pp Lijiang Mushroom Hotpot 野生菌火锅 Yunnan is China's mushroom kingdom — a hotpot of foraged wild mushrooms (porcini, matsutake and more) in chicken broth. Seasonal (June–Oct) and unforgettable. 🍽 🍽 Mushroom restaurants in the old town · ¥100–150 pp 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Lijiang sits at 2,400m — give yourself a day to adjust: drink lots of water, walk slowly, and skip the first-night bar crawl. The mountain cable car is another 2,000m up, so bring oxygen if you're prone to altitude sickness. Kat Says The old town is packed during Chinese holidays (Golden Week, Spring Festival). Go in April, May or October for the best balance of weather and crowds. Kat Says Wear proper walking shoes — it's all cobblestones, and you'll walk a LOT. High heels = regret. And carry your guesthouse's card with you; the lanes look identical after dark. title: Nanjing
snippet: the honest guide to nanjing for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏛️ 南京 Nanjing Ancient capitals, Ming history, Qinhuai River, museums ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3 days History Museums Food scene ✨ Why Nanjing? Nanjing is China's forgotten capital. Six dynasties ruled from here before Beijing, the first Ming emperor built his tomb on its Purple Mountain, and in the 20th century it served as the Republic of China's capital. Few Chinese cities pack so much history into such a walkable, leafy, and surprisingly relaxed package. Today the city walls still circle the old center — one of the best-preserved city walls anywhere — while the Qinhuai River glitters with lantern-lit boats every night. Add one of China's greatest museums, the most photogenic weeping-cherry tunnel in spring, and a duck-obsessed food culture, and you have a city that rewards slow exploration. Nanjing is history you can actually touch. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum (Zhongshan Ling) 392 steps · the founding father of modern China Read the story 2 Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum UNESCO · tomb of the first Ming emperor Read the story 3 Confucius Temple & Qinhuai River (Fuzimiao) Lantern-lit night boats · food street · old Nanjing Read the story 4 Zhonghua Gate & the City Wall The longest city wall ever built · 600 years old Read the story 5 Nanjing Museum (Nanjing Boyuyuan) One of China's top three museums · free The story: Sun Yat-sen is the father of modern China — the doctor turned revolutionary who ended 2,000 years of imperial rule in 1911. He chose Purple Mountain in Nanjing for his burial site in 1925. The mausoleum's 392 steps are said to echo the 391 million people of China at the time, plus Sun himself. Why it's a must-see: The approach is the spectacle: a forested avenue of plane trees, a white-and-blue memorial rising on the hillside, and a climb that builds to one of the best views over Nanjing. It's a place of genuine reverence, not just sightseeing. 💡 Kat's tip: Book a free ticket on the official WeChat account in advance — entry is by time slot. Go early to avoid the tour groups, and pair it with Ming Xiaoling next door for a full Purple Mountain day. The story: In 1398, the Hongwu Emperor — a beggar who rose to found the Ming dynasty — was buried here under Purple Mountain with 40 concubines and, legend says, 13 treasures. His tomb has never been opened. What visitors see is the Sacred Way: a 2-km avenue lined with giant stone elephants, camels, horses, and mythical beasts standing guard. Why it's a must-see: The stone animals are ancient, weathered, and wonderful to walk among — China's own petrified parade. The architecture established the blueprint that later Ming tombs in Beijing (like the Thirteen Ming Tombs) copied. 💡 Kat's tip: Autumn is magical — the Sacred Way's maple and ginkgo trees turn gold and red in November. Budget two hours and wear walking shoes; the grounds are large. The story: The Qinhuai River has been Nanjing's pleasure quarter for a thousand years — where scholars took exams at the Confucius Temple, courtesans performed on painted boats, and poets wrote about the lanterns reflecting on the water. The neighborhood was rebuilt in the 1980s but kept the old layout and spirit. Why it's a must-see: It's the soul of old Nanjing nightlife. At dusk the riverfront buildings light up in gold and red, boats glide under stone bridges, and a massive food street sells everything from duck blood soup to candied hawthorns. Free to wander, endlessly entertaining. 💡 Kat's tip: Take the night boat tour along the river — 40 minutes, gorgeous lights, and very cheap. Eat at the side alleys rather than the main square; prices drop and quality rises. The story: In the 1360s the Ming founder built a city wall around Nanjing that stretched 35 km — the longest ever built anywhere. It survives almost intact, and Zhonghua Gate is its most dramatic piece: a fortress with three layers of walls, 27 hidden chambers, and enough space to hold 3,000 soldiers defending the gate. Why it's a must-see: You can climb the wall and walk for kilometers along the top, looking down at rooftops, canals, and temple bells on one side and modern Nanjing on the other. It's China's history you can literally stand on. 💡 Kat's tip: Rent a bicycle or just walk the section between Zhonghua Gate and the Confucius Temple — the views of the Qinhuai area are the best. Sunset is spectacular. The story: Nanjing Museum is one of China's "Big Three" national museums, holding over 400,000 artifacts that trace Chinese civilization from the Stone Age to modern times. Its greatest treasure: the "Bronze Ox Lamp," a Western Han dynasty lamp where smoke rises through the ox's neck into the body's water chamber — ancient engineering disguised as art. Why it's a must-see: It's free, air-conditioned, world-class, and (unlike Beijing's Forbidden City) rarely overwhelming in crowds. The Ming and Qing furniture halls, jade collection, and the art of the Republic period are particular highlights. 💡 Kat's tip: Reserve a free ticket on WeChat the day before. Give it half a day — it's huge. The museum café is decent for a lunch break between halls. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Xinjiekou Best for first-timers Nanjing's central hub: a giant pedestrian square ringed by malls, restaurants, and a metro interchange that reaches everything in 20 minutes. Best for logistics, food, and first-time visitors. 🚇 Lines 1/2 · Xinjiekou 🛍 Malls & food streets e.g. Jinling Hotel (landmark) · international chains on Zhongshan Road Confucius Temple / Qinhuai Old-town atmosphere Stay where the lanterns are: river views, night boats, and street food right outside your door. Livelier at night than anywhere else in the city. Best for atmosphere and night owls. 🚇 Line 3 · Fuzimiao 🏮 River views & nightlife e.g. riverside boutique hotels near the Confucius Temple Purple Mountain / East Gate Nature & quiet A green, upmarket area at the foot of Purple Mountain, close to Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum and Ming Xiaoling. Leafy streets, fewer crowds, and easy access to the Nanjing Museum. Best for walkers and families. 🚇 Line 2 · Minggugong 🌳 Forested parkland e.g. Purple Mountain resorts · university guesthouses 🍜 What to Eat Salt-brined duck 盐水鸭 "No duck survives Nanjing" goes the saying. The signature version is poached in salt brine until the meat stays pink, tender, and clean-tasting. Eaten cold, it's the taste of every Nanjing family table. 🍽 Han Fu Tang · Shui Xi Men duck shops · ¥30–60 Duck blood vermicelli soup 鸭血粉丝汤 Nanjing's beloved breakfast: silky duck-blood cubes, glass noodles, fried tofu, and duck offal in a rich broth, finished with chopped cilantro and a spoonful of chili oil. 🍽 Lao Ye Yong · Ya Du Lao · ¥15–30 Beef potstickers 牛肉锅贴 Golden half-moons of pastry stuffed with juicy beef and scallion, fried until the bottoms crackle. Served with vinegar — a snack that defines Nanjing's morning streets. 🍽 Jin Xiu Wei · Lian Biao Su · ¥8–15 Red bean & osmanthus sweets 赤豆元宵 / 糖芋苗 Sweet red-bean soup with soft rice balls, and taro chunks in a silky osmanthus-scented broth. Nanjingers end many meals with one of these warm, comforting desserts. 🍽 Old dessert shops near Confucius Temple · ¥10–20 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Summer in Nanjing is famously brutal — visit in spring (cherry blossoms on Purple Mountain) or crisp autumn instead. Kat Says The night boat on the Qinhuai River is the best-value experience in the city. Go after 7pm for full lights. Kat Says High-speed rail makes Nanjing an easy 1.5-hour day trip from Shanghai — but give it a full 2–3 days if you can. title: Ordos
snippet: the honest guide to ordos for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🐎 鄂尔多斯 Ordos Grasslands, Mongolian culture, futuristic Ordos city ★★★☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Grasslands Mongolian culture ✨ Why Ordos? Ordos is Mongolia-meets-the-21st-century: a city of futuristic architecture that was once dubbed the world's most famous 'ghost city', surrounded by singing-sand deserts, green grasslands and the spiritual heart of Mongolian culture — the Genghis Khan Mausoleum. It's the easiest place in China to experience the nomadic world: yurt stays, horse riding, roast lamb and a night sky full of stars. It's also a photographer's playground. Kangbashi district — built from scratch for a million people, home to a fraction of that — is a surreal museum of bold modern design with almost nobody around. Come for the desert and grassland, stay for the strangest, most photogenic cityscape in China. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Xiangshawan — Singing Sand Bay The desert that sings when you slide Read the story 2 Genghis Khan Mausoleum The spiritual heart of Mongolia Read the story 3 Ordos Grassland — horses & yurts Sleep like a nomad under the stars Read the story 4 Kangbashi — the 'ghost city' A futuristic city with almost nobody in it Read the story 5 Naadam festival Wrestling, horse racing & archery The story: Xiangshawan sits on the eastern edge of the Kubuqi Desert, China's seventh-largest desert. Its centerpiece is a crescent dune 110 meters high and 400 meters wide that 'sings': when the dry sand shifts under your feet or you slide down its 45-degree slope, it produces a deep humming roar — one of only three such 'singing sand' sites in China. Why it's a must-see: Where else can you slide down a dune that literally plays music? Beyond the sand itself, the resort offers camel treks, dune buggies, a cable car over the dunes and two themed areas — adventure on one island, relaxation on the other. Stay until sunset and the desert puts on a light show. 💡 Kat's tip: The singing effect only works on dry, windless days — skip it after rain. Buy the combo ticket (240 RMB with cable car + one island) rather than entry-only. Go at 4pm for golden light and cooler sand. The story: This is not a tomb but a cenotaph — Genghis Khan's real burial site remains unknown, as he wished. Since his death in 1227, the Mongolian people have maintained a mobile shrine of 'Eight White Yurts' in his honor, and the current complex was built in 1954 on the Gandel Grassland. It hosts over 60 ceremonial sacrifices a year and remains the most sacred site for Mongolians worldwide. Why it's a must-see: It's the emotional and cultural core of the Mongolian world — golden domes, white yurt-inspired halls, and a 4-km 'Sacred Path' lined with banners. The architecture is unlike anything else in China, and the annual ceremonies (with wrestling, horse racing and offerings) are a living tradition, not a show. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry 90 RMB; go in the morning when ceremonies are more likely. The site is huge — take the internal shuttle. It's 70 km from the city, so combine it with grassland stops on a full-day tour. The story: The Ordos Plateau rolls at 1,300–1,500 meters with cool summers, and its grasslands still hold working herder communities. At the tourist yurt camps you can ride horses across the steppe, try archery and milking, and sleep in a traditional felt ger — waking at dawn to horses grazing outside your door. Why it's a must-see: A yurt night on the grassland is the quintessential Inner Mongolia experience: horseback riding, mutton boiled over a campfire, and a night sky so clear the Milky Way looks fake. It's far less commercialized than Inner Mongolia's famous Hulunbuir — you'll often have the steppe to yourself. 💡 Kat's tip: Best June–September when the grass is green. Nights drop to 10–15°C even in summer — bring warm layers. Book a yurt with a private bathroom if you can; the shared-facility ones are more rustic. The story: Construction of Kangbashi began in 2004 on empty grassland. Planned for nearly a million people, it had only 28,600 residents by 2010 — earning it global fame as the 'ghost city' of China. By 2024 the population reached 131,300, and the district became China's first national 4A urban scenic area, with 18 parks, the Grand Theater shaped like two open books, and the Ulan Moron River running through the middle. Why it's a must-see: It's a surreal urban laboratory: a city built from scratch with bold Mongolian-cultural architecture — the museum inspired by desert stones, the library like a giant stack of books — and almost no traffic. Summer averages a perfect 21°C, and the evening fountain-and-fireworks show on the river is free. 💡 Kat's tip: Walk the Central Square at dusk, then watch the riverside fountain show (check times at the visitor center). Don't expect crowds — that's the whole point. Kangbashi is 25 km from the old city; taxis between the two take 30 minutes. The story: Naadam is the Mongolian 'festival of three manly sports' — wrestling, horse racing and archery — held across Inner Mongolia every summer. In Ordos, celebrations run through July–August with camel racing, traditional music, bonfire concerts and open-air feasts of whole roasted sheep. Why it's a must-see: It's the biggest, most authentic cultural event in Inner Mongolia: Mongolian wrestlers in traditional zodog jackets, child jockeys riding bareback at full gallop, and whole villages gathering under the sky. No museum can match standing in the middle of it. 💡 Kat's tip: Dates vary by location each year but always fall July–August — check local announcements in spring. Book accommodation months ahead; grassland hotels sell out during Naadam. Hire a local guide for the ceremonies' meanings. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Kangbashi District Architecture & cool summers The modern center with the city's best hotels, the museum and theater, and the riverfront. Summer averages 21°C — one of the coolest city centers in China. All the bold architecture is walkable from central hotels. 🚇 No metro — taxis cheap (10–20 RMB within the district) 🏛 Ordos Museum, Grand Theater, Ulan Moron Lake e.g. Shangri-La Ordos (luxury) · Crowne Plaza Ordos (upscale) Dongsheng (old city) Budget & transit hub The original city center: more affordable hotels, local restaurants and the main bus station for trips to Xiangshawan (55 km) and the grasslands. Grittier and more lived-in than Kangbashi. 🚇 No metro — intercity buses to all scenic areas 🏛 Dongsheng center, bus terminal e.g. Jinjiang Inn Dongsheng (budget) · Ordos Hotel (mid-range) Ejin Horo Banner Culture & self-driving Stay near the Genghis Khan Mausoleum and the surrounding Gandel Grassland — walk to the sacred site at dawn, then ride out to the grassland. Ideal for self-drivers; 70 km from Dongsheng. 🚇 No metro — 40 km from Kangbashi airport 🏛 Genghis Khan Mausoleum, Gandel Grassland e.g. mausoleum-area hotel (mid-range) · seasonal yurt camps (~400 RMB with meals) Grassland yurt camps Nomad experience Yurt stays on the working grasslands — felt gers with modern bedding, bonfires and morning horse rides. Basic by hotel standards, unforgettable by every other measure. 🚇 No metro — tour transport or self-drive 🏛 Open grassland, herder families e.g. yurt camps on the Ordos Grassland (~300–500 RMB with meals) 🍜 What to Eat Whole Roasted Sheep 烤全羊 A whole sheep roasted over open fire for 3–4 hours until the skin is golden-crisp and the meat falls off the bone — the centerpiece of every Mongolian celebration. 🍽 🍽 Grassland yurt camps & Kangbashi Mongolian restaurants · 800–1500 RMB per sheep (serves 8–10) Hand-Grabbed Mutton 手扒肉 Fresh lamb boiled with just salt and a few spices, eaten with your hands and dipped in garlic-vinegar sauce — the purest possible taste of grassland lamb. 🍽 🍽 Mongolian restaurants across Ordos · ¥60–80 per portion Mongolian Milk Tea & Cheese 奶茶与奶制品 Salty milk tea brewed with brick tea, milk and a pinch of salt, served with fried dough twists, dried milk skin and milk tofu — a herder's breakfast, a meal in itself. 🍽 🍽 Yurt camps & Mongolian teahouses · ¥15–25 per pot Oat Noodles (Youmian) 莜面 A northern staple: oat dough rolled into thin strips or tubes, steamed and dipped in savory mutton or tomato sauce — hearty, healthy and utterly different from southern noodles. 🍽 🍽 Dongsheng old-city restaurants · ¥20–30 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Best window is May–October: July–August for green grasslands and Naadam, but Kangbashi stays a pleasant 21°C all summer. Bring a jacket for grassland nights year-round. Kat Says Xiangshawan is 55 km from Dongsheng — allow a full day (taxi ~1 hour each way). Don't attempt the 'singing sand' after rain; it only sings when dry. Kat Says Combine desert and grassland: base in Dongsheng for Xiangshawan day trips and in Kangbashi for city/museum days — the two districts are 30 minutes apart by car. title: Pingwu Baima
snippet: the honest guide to pingwu baima for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🦅 平武白马藏族乡 Pingwu Baima Baima Tibetan culture, mountain villages, feather headdress ★★★★☆ 🗓 2 days Hidden ethnic gem Mountain escape ✨ Why Pingwu Baima? Pingwu Baima is the most off-the-map destination on this site: a mountain valley in northern Sichuan where the Baima people — around 20,000 of them — have lived for over a thousand years, wearing white pheasant-feather hats and speaking a language of their own. A 2012 DNA study showed they descend from the ancient Di/Qiang peoples, making them one of East Asia's oldest living cultures. It's also the doorway to Wanglang, China's first giant-panda reserve — a pristine primeval forest where the wild panda population is densest on earth. Two days here means a Baima village bonfire, a panda-forest hike, and almost no other tourists. This is the real thing. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Baima villages by Tianmu Lake A living culture, not a show Read the story 2 Wanglang National Nature Reserve China's first giant-panda reserve Read the story 3 Caogai mask dance & Baima songs A Stone-Age ritual, still performed Read the story 4 Baima embroidery & costume craft Buy direct from the artisans Read the story 5 Forest hiking & waterfalls The anti-Jiuzhaigou The story: Villages like Paxijia (扒昔加古寨) hug the turquoise shore of Tianmu Lake with wooden watchtower houses that have stood for centuries. Baima women wear pleated red-and-white dresses and the white 'shaga' felt hat crowned with pheasant feathers — men wear a single straight feather (meaning honesty), women two or three curved ones (meaning beauty). Nights bring bonfires and the round dance (yuan-yuan-wu) that everyone joins. Why it's a must-see: This is a living culture: after the new expressway opened in 2024, village homestay income jumped from under 80,000 to 200,000+ RMB a year — the Baima are proud to host, not performing for tourists. The lake-and-snows setting is pure postcard, and the warmest welcome in Sichuan is here. 💡 Kat's tip: Stay overnight — the bonfire singing and the mirror-still lake at sunrise are the two moments you'll remember forever. Ask before photographing people, and accept the 'za jiu' (bamboo-straw rice wine) toast — refusing is impolite. The story: Founded in 1965 as China's very first giant-panda reserve, Wanglang covers 32,297 hectares of primeval spruce-fir forest at 2,363–4,983 meters. It protects the largest wild giant-panda population in China — the Minshan 'A' population — plus golden snub-nosed monkeys, takin and snow leopards: 62 mammal species and 271 bird species in total. Why it's a must-see: It's the best-researched wild panda habitat on the planet and deliberately stays raw: entry is quota-controlled, you ride in on a shared bus with a naturalist guide, and the forest belongs to pandas, not tour groups. You almost certainly won't see a panda — that's exactly why it's special. 💡 Kat's tip: Book online well ahead through the official Giant Panda National Park channel — spots fill fast and private cars aren't allowed inside. Bring warm layers even in summer (average 2.4°C at altitude) and good shoes for the boardwalk trails. The story: 'Tiao Caogai' (跳曹盖) — the Baima mask dance — was listed as a national intangible cultural heritage in 2011. Every lunar New Year, dancers in white sheepskin coats leap and stamp wearing heavy carved black-bear spirit masks to drive out demons. Scholars trace the dance to Stone-Age hunting and totem worship; Baima songs, sung entirely in the Baima language, became a provincial heritage in 2023. Why it's a must-see: This is one of China's most primitive surviving ritual dances — a direct line to a culture older than the Han empire itself. You will never see anything like it anywhere else, and the fact that it's still performed in the villages, not on a stage, makes it extraordinary. 💡 Kat's tip: The full ceremony runs lunar January 5–6 in the villages — plan around Chinese New Year and be a respectful observer. Outside festival season, local cultural troupes often perform shortened versions for visitors at the villages. The story: Baima costume-making is a recognized intangible heritage: pleated skirts, hand-woven flower belts, fish-bone breast plaques, and the white goat-wool 'shaga' hat — whose making is itself a provincial heritage craft. The feather on the hat honors a 6th-century legend in which golden pheasants screeched a warning that saved Baima soldiers from ambush. Why it's a must-see: Every detail carries meaning: one straight feather means honesty, curved feathers mean beauty, the fish-bone plaque wards off bad luck. Buying directly from village artisans keeps a nearly extinct craft alive — and you'll meet the makers while they work. 💡 Kat's tip: Shop at village workshops and homestay studios rather than souvenir shops — you'll see the embroidery, felting and belt-weaving live. Hats run ¥100–300 depending on detail; embroidered belts make beautiful gifts. The story: Trails from the villages wind up through old-growth forest to waterfall hollows and alpine meadows where dove trees bloom in April–May and wildflowers carpet the slopes by summer. Autumn turns larch and birch into sheets of gold against fresh snow, and summer air sits around a cool 20°C. Why it's a must-see: This is the same Minshan mountain chain as Jiuzhaigou, an hour deeper in — with none of the crowds. Just glacier-cut valleys, rushing streams and silence loud enough to hear your own heartbeat. For hikers, it's the hidden gem Sichuan forgot to advertise. 💡 Kat's tip: Pick one 2–4 hour loop (toward Wanglang's buffer forest is the classic) and wear proper grip shoes — paths get slick after rain. Download offline maps; phone signal drops in the deep valleys. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Baima village homestays (Tianmu Lake) Immersive culture Family-run guesthouses in Paxijia and Yazhe Zaozu villages on the lake shore: wood-fired dinners, za jiu toasts and a bonfire round dance most evenings. Simple rooms (countryside inn, not resort), priceless lake-and-snow views. 🚇 No metro — ~25–40 min drive from Wanglang's gate; lakeside loop roads 🏛 Tianmu Lake, Paxijia village, Wanglang gate e.g. Tianyuan Inn (天缘客栈) · Huayaodai Inn (花腰带客栈) · ¥150–350/night incl. meals Pingwu County town (Long'an) Comfort & the Ming temple The county capital holds the 'Forbidden City of the mountains' — Bao'en Temple, built 1440–1446 entirely of golden nanmu wood with 9,999 carved dragons and the only still-rotating Ming scripture case in China. Stay here for reliable hotels and a comfortable first/last night. 🚇 No metro — ~2.5h drive from Mianyang, ~3.5h from Chengdu via G8513 🏛 Bao'en Temple (4A site, ¥40), riverside morning market e.g. Jiuzhou Jindu Hotel (resort-grade) · county hotels from ¥150–300 Inside Wanglang reserve Nature immersion Overnight inside the panda reserve by prior arrangement — you wake among the primeval forest and alpine wetlands that pandas call home. Tightly capped, requires a permit, books out months ahead. 🚇 Reservation shuttle bus only; no private vehicles 🏛 Primeval spruce-fir forest, alpine wetlands, birding towers e.g. reserve guesthouse (research-station style, simple) 🍜 What to Eat Za Jiu (bamboo-straw rice wine) 咂酒 A sweet fermented grain wine sipped through hollow bamboo straws from a shared jar — the ritual drink of every Baima toast and bonfire night. 🍽 🍽 Any village homestay or festival table Buckwheat Pancakes & Wild Honey 荞麦饼蘸蜂蜜 Crisp-edged buckwheat cakes dipped in Pingwu's famous high-altitude honey — earthy, floral and addictive. The perfect mountain breakfast. 🍽 🍽 Village inns & county-town breakfast tables · ¥10–20 Cured Pork Rib & Wild Mushroom Hotpot 腊排骨汤锅 High-mountain cured ribs slow-simmered with wild mushrooms into a milky, smoky broth — the defining winter dish of the Minshan foothills. 🍽 🍽 Rustic hotpot eateries in Pingwu town · ¥50–80 pp Smoked Bacon & Sausages 老腊肉 Dry-cured and pine-smoked pork with a deep, resinous aroma — sliced thin with garlic shoots or stir-fried with mountain greens. 🍽 🍽 Family restaurants county-wide · also sold at village markets to take home 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Book your Wanglang entry online in advance — the daily quota fills quickly and private cars can't enter. Bring warm layers for 2,400–5,000m altitudes; temperature swings are huge. Kat Says Best months: late Oct–Nov for golden larches, June–Aug for 20°C forest escapes, April–May for dove flowers. Winter roads can ice up — check before driving. Kat Says Respect the people: the Baima self-identify as 'Baima people', not simply Tibetans. Ask before photographing anyone, don't touch prayer flags or mani stones, and buy crafts directly from villagers. title: Quanzhou
snippet: the honest guide to quanzhou for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌸 泉州 Quanzhou Hidden gem, Maritime Silk Road, authentic local China ★★★★☆ 🗓 2–3 days K's hometown! 🏠 UNESCO 2021 Off the beaten path ✨ Why Quanzhou? Quanzhou is the hidden gem of China's coast — a port that was one of the world's greatest cities a thousand years ago, when Arab, Persian, Indian and European traders anchored in its harbor on the Maritime Silk Road. In 2021, UNESCO added the whole historic city to the World Heritage list, and yet almost no foreign tourists come. That's your gain. It's also Kat's hometown — so this guide comes with a local's heart. You'll find China's oldest mosque, a 1,300-year-old Buddhist temple, temples where Hindu deities and Mazu (the sea goddess) share walls, and food that blends Fujian, Southeast Asian and Arab influences into something you can't get anywhere else. Come before the world discovers it. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Kaiyuan Temple & the Twin Pagodas 1,300 years of Buddhist history Read the story 2 Zhongshan Road Southern China's most beautiful old street Read the story 3 Maritime Silk Road Museum The story of China's greatest port Read the story 4 Qingjing Mosque China's oldest surviving mosque Read the story 5 Guandi Temple (Guan Yue Temple) The busiest temple in the old city The story: Founded in 686 AD during the Tang dynasty, Kaiyuan Temple is one of the largest and oldest Buddhist temples in China — its two stone pagodas, the 44.06-meter East Pagoda and 43.85-meter West Pagoda, have stood since the 13th century and are the tallest stone pagodas in China. The temple's pillars carry carvings of Hindu deities and music-loving angels, proof of Quanzhou's cosmopolitan past. Why it's a must-see: This is the heart of Quanzhou — a huge, living temple where locals still burn incense among 1,300-year-old banyan trees. The twin pagodas are the city's symbol (they appear in old sailors' charts as landmarks for approaching ships), and the temple grounds are a peaceful green oasis in the old city. 💡 Kat's tip: Free entry. Go early (opens 6:30am) to see the morning prayers, then explore the surrounding Xijie (West Street) for old-town atmosphere and snacks. The Hindu-carved pillars are on the right side of the main hall — don't miss them. The story: Zhongshan Road is a 2.5-km arcade-lined street that has been Quanzhou's commercial spine since the 1920s, built on top of the old city's Tang-dynasty street grid. Its covered walkways (qilou) — a Fujian and Southeast Asian architectural style — sheltered merchants from sun and rain, and the street remains the most beautiful pedestrian route in southern China. Why it's a must-see: This is where Quanzhou's everyday life happens: teahouses, shops selling tea and incense, old medicine halls, and families on scooters dodging between the columns. Unlike polished tourist streets elsewhere, this one is genuinely lived-in — and at night, when the awnings light up, it's stunning. 💡 Kat's tip: Walk it at dusk (around 7pm) when the lanterns come on. Branch into the side lanes — Zhongshan Road's alleys hide courtyards, temples and the city's best cheap eats. The story: Quanzhou's Maritime Silk Road Museum tells the story of the city that was, for centuries, one of the world's busiest ports — where Marco Polo sailed from in 1292 and Ibn Battuta visited in 1346. The museum's centerpiece is a 13th-century Song-dynasty ship, 24 meters long, raised from Quanzhou Bay in 1974 — the oldest Chinese trading vessel ever recovered, with 2,300 artifacts found on board. Why it's a must-see: No other museum in China tells the Maritime Silk Road story so completely: the ship, the cargo, the religious stone carvings (Christian, Islamic, Hindu, Manichaean — all found in Quanzhou), and the city's unique role as a meeting point of world religions. It explains why Quanzhou matters more than almost any other Chinese city. 💡 Kat's tip: Free entry, open Tue–Sun 9am–5pm (closed Mondays). Allow 1.5–2 hours. The Song ship in the main hall is the unmissable object; the stone-carving gallery is the second must-see. The story: Built in 1009 AD during the Northern Song dynasty, Qingjing Mosque is the oldest surviving mosque in China — founded by Arab traders who made Quanzhou their home. Its grey stone arches and courtyard carry Arabic inscriptions, and the site remained a place of worship into the Ming dynasty, when it was visited and repaired with support from the Chinese court. Why it's a must-see: It's a physical trace of the cosmopolitan world that made Quanzhou rich: a thousand years ago, this city had mosques, temples and churches standing side by side, and people of every faith traded together. Standing in the mosque's quiet courtyard, you're in one of the most important religious sites in China — and almost nobody else is there. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry 3 RMB. Modest dress expected. It's a 10-minute walk from Kaiyuan Temple — combine the two in one morning. The adjacent Peace Street (Tumen Street) has the best local snacks. The story: This temple honors Guan Yu, the deified general of the Three Kingdoms era who became China's god of loyalty and business — and Quanzhou's Guandi Temple is among the busiest in the country. Local businesspeople still come daily to burn incense and ask for fortune, shaking numbered bamboo sticks until one falls, then reading their answer from a drawer of poems. Why it's a must-see: This is Quanzhou's everyday religion, in action: a temple where the incense smoke never stops and where you'll see more genuine worship in five minutes than in a week of tourist temples elsewhere. You can even try the fortune-telling ritual yourself — a unique, immersive local experience. 💡 Kat's tip: Free entry. Learn the fortune-stick ritual (you can watch others first) — if you get a 'bad' fortune, it's customary to tie it to the tree outside. Go on the 1st or 15th of the lunar month for the fullest scene. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. West Street / Kaiyuan Temple area Best for first-timers The old city's historic heart: Kaiyuan Temple and the twin pagodas at one end of West Street, Zhongshan Road and the snack alleys at the other. Guesthouses in restored Minnan courtyard houses give you old-town atmosphere with everything walkable. 🚇 No metro — walk, bike or taxi (small city, 5–15 min rides) 🏛 Kaiyuan Temple, West Street, Zhongshan Road e.g. Wutong House (boutique B&B in a restored house) · Quanzhou Guesthouse International Zhongshan Road / Tumen Street Foodies & night owls The old commercial spine: stay above the arcades and you're in the middle of the snack streets, the night market and the Guandi Temple's incense. Quieter than West Street's tourist edge, more authentic. 🚇 No metro — everything within walking distance 🏛 Zhongshan Road, Guandi Temple, Qingjing Mosque e.g. courtyard guesthouses off Tumen Street · budget hotels on Zhongshan Donghai / coast area Modern & beach escape The newer east side near Quanzhou Bay: business hotels, the Maritime Silk Road Museum, and easy access to the coast's fishing villages and seafood restaurants. Choose it if you want modern comfort or plan a day at the bay. 🚇 No metro — 15 min taxi to old city 🏛 Maritime Silk Road Museum, Quanzhou Bay, beaches e.g. Quanzhou Bay Hotel · international business chains Jinjiang (south bank) Business & connections Across the river, the city of Jinjiang is where many of Quanzhou's factories and the airport are — a practical base if you're mixing business with tourism, 25 minutes from the old city by car. 🚇 No metro — taxi/bus to Quanzhou old city (25 min) 🏛 Jinjiang airport, Wu Dian Shi old street e.g. Marco Polo Hotel Jinjiang (business landmark) 🍜 What to Eat Oyster Omelette 蚵仔煎 Crispy-edged, gooey-centered: fresh oysters bound with sweet-potato starch and egg, fried until the edges are lacy — the ultimate Minnan street food, served with a sweet chili dip. 🍽 🍽 West Street & Tumen Street stalls · ¥15–25 Ginger Duck 姜母鸭 Quanzhou's signature comfort food: wheat noodles in a rich, savory broth of satay sauce, peanut and seafood — a taste left by the city's centuries of maritime trade. Add your choice of fish balls, squid or pork. 🍽 🍽 Local noodle shops across the old city · ¥15–30 Runbing (fresh spring rolls) 润饼 Paper-thin crepes rolled around a sweet-savory filling of shredded vegetables, peanuts, sugar and sometimes seafood — sweet, crunchy, soft and salty all at once. 🍽 🍽 Tumen Street & temple-side vendors · ¥8–15 Seaweed & seafood soup 紫菜海蛎汤 A clear, briny soup of local seaweed and small oysters — the taste of the Fujian coast, light and restorative after a day of temple-hopping. 🍽 🍽 Seafood restaurants near West Street · ¥20–40 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Quanzhou is 1 hour from Xiamen by high-speed train — pair them: Xiamen's island charm + Quanzhou's authenticity. Kat's tip: do Quanzhou first, Xiamen second, so you end on the beach. Kat Says Almost no English is spoken — download Pleco and a translation app before you come. It's part of the charm: you're visiting a city that hasn't been 'discovered' yet. Kat Says The best snack street is Tumen Street (涂门街) near the Guandi Temple, and the best time is 7–9pm. Try everything; the oyster omelette and satay noodles are non-negotiable.
