title: Sanya
snippet: the honest guide to sanya for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌴 三亚 Sanya Tropical beaches, palm trees, resorts, island escapes ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3–5 days Beaches Resorts Tropical ✨ Why Sanya? Sanya is China's Hawaii — the country's only true tropical beach destination, sitting at the southern tip of Hainan island at the same latitude as Hawaii. Coconut palms line white-sand bays, the sea stays swimmable almost year-round, and the air smells of jasmine and salt. If your China trip has been all temples and noodles, this is where you exhale. It's not just a resort bubble, though. Sanya has the 108-meter Guanyin statue on its own island, a bay where the mountains meet the sea at "the Ends of the Earth," and a local culture with deep Li and Miao minority roots. Pick your bay by mood — party, family, or quiet luxury — and let the ocean do the rest. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Yalong Bay China's best beach · 7 km of white sand Read the story 2 Nanshan Temple & the Sea Guanyin 108-meter Guanyin statue standing in the sea Read the story 3 Wuzhizhou Island Snorkeling & diving · the clearest water in Hainan Read the story 4 Tianya Haijiao (Ends of the Earth) Legendary lovers' rocks · dramatic coastline Read the story 5 Dadonghai Bay City beach · water sports · sunset bars The story: Yalong Bay ("Dragon Tooth Bay") is a crescent of white coral sand and shallow, calm water — widely rated the best beach in China. Mountains shelter it on three sides, and the resort strip behind the sand is where Sanya's luxury hotels line up like pearls. Locals say the sand here squeaks under your feet because it's almost pure ground coral. Why it's a must-see: If you came to Sanya for a beach, this is the beach. The water is clear enough to see your toes, the sunsets are long and gold, and even the most expensive hotels can't stop you walking their shoreline — in China, all beaches are public. 💡 Kat's tip: The central beach park (Yalong Bay Tropical Paradise Forest Park nearby offers a glass bridge and the famous "Bird's Nest" views). Go early morning before 10am or after 4pm for the best light and fewer people. The story: Nanshan ("South Mountain") is a vast Buddhist cultural park where the hills meet the sea. Its centerpiece is the Guanyin of the South Sea: a 108-meter-tall, three-faced statue of the Goddess of Mercy standing on an island in the bay — one of the tallest statues on Earth, visible from kilometers away. Why it's a must-see: It's genuinely awe-inspiring — a colossal white figure rising from the ocean that feels ancient even though it was completed in 2005. The park around it has temple halls, a vegetarian restaurant run by monks, and the "Dragon Boat" beach. Plan for a relaxed half-day. 💡 Kat's tip: Take the electric shuttle inside the park — it's huge. Visit in the morning when the sea breeze is gentle. The vegetarian buffet at the temple (66 yuan all-you-can-eat) is excellent and a great value. The story: Wuzhizhou ("Hedgehog Island") is a small island about 30 minutes by boat from the coast near Houhai village. Around it, protected coral reefs keep the water brilliantly clear — shades of blue-green you won't see anywhere else in Hainan. It's the island's nearest neighbor to the famed "Mermaid" diving spots. Why it's a must-see: This is where you come for the water: snorkeling, scuba diving, jet-skiing, and a glass-bottom boat over the reef. Even if you just want to swim, the beach here is dramatically prettier than the mainland bays. 💡 Kat's tip: Book the ferry and activities online a day ahead, and go early — the island caps daily visitors. The coral is sensitive: use reef-safe sunscreen and don't touch the marine life. The story: "Tianya Haijiao" literally means "sky's edge, sea's corner" — the old Chinese phrase for the end of the world. For centuries, this rocky stretch of coast was where exiled officials came to die, far from the capital's politics. Later the boulders engraved with "Tianya" and "Haijiao" became China's most romantic symbol: lovers come here to pledge that they will follow each other "to the ends of the earth." Why it's a must-see: The coastline is dramatic — weathered granite boulders, coconut palms, and waves crashing against black rock. It's also where Chinese TV taught generations to dream of Hainan. Sunset from the rocks is the classic Sanya photo. 💡 Kat's tip: It's more symbolic than spectacular — budget 2 hours, go at golden hour, and skip the touts selling "love lockets." Pair it with the nearby Nanshan Temple for a full south-coast day. The story: Dadonghai — "Big East Sea" — is the beach that put Sanya on the map in the 1980s, right in the city itself. It's the friendliest beach in Sanya: sun loungers, banana-boat rides, kite surfers, and families flying kites until the streetlights come on. Why it's a must-see: It's the most accessible slice of the tropical life — walk out of your hotel, cross the road, and you're on the sand. The evening scene is unbeatable: locals playing volleyball in the shallows, seafood grill stalls lighting up, and beach bars with the music turned toward the waves. 💡 Kat's tip: The night market just behind Dadonghai is the place for street food — try the coconut-grilled everything. For quieter water, walk to the east end of the bay where the swimmers thin out. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Yalong Bay Best for luxury Sanya's premium resort strip: five-star hotels with private beach sections, infinity pools, and the best sand in China. Slightly isolated from the city, which is exactly the point. Best for honeymoons and pure relaxation. 🏖 Private beach access 🚕 40 min from airport e.g. Ritz-Carlton, Banyan Tree, boutique resorts on the bay front Dadonghai Best value The city beach: mid-range and boutique hotels a short walk from the sand, plus the best night market and nightlife in Sanya. Best for first-timers, families, and anyone who wants the city and the beach. 🚶 Walk to the beach 🍢 Night market nearby e.g. mid-range beachfront hotels · guesthouses on the bay Sanya Bay Best for long stays The longest bay, stretching 22 km along the city's south coast, with a boardwalk, cheap seafood, and sunset views of the whole city skyline. Hotels are the most affordable in Sanya. Best for budget travelers and winter escapees. 🌅 Famous sunset boardwalk 🛫 Close to airport e.g. affordable seafront hotels along the bay boardwalk 🍜 What to Eat Qingbuliang 清补凉 The essential Hainan dessert: shaved coconut ice topped with red beans, taro, peanuts, jelly, and fresh fruit, drizzled with coconut milk. Cool, sweet, and the perfect antidote to tropical heat — you'll want one every afternoon. 🍽 Dessert shops across the city · ¥10–20 Hainan noodle soup 海南粉 Hainan's signature breakfast: thin rice noodles in a rich sauce or soup, topped with shredded pork, squid, peanuts, and a squeeze of lime. Add chili oil and a boiled egg, and you've got a proper tropical start. 🍽 Local noodle shops · ¥10–18 Seafood grill 海鲜烧烤 At the bay-front night markets, stalls grill everything the boats brought in that day — shrimp, squid, crabs, clams — with garlic and chili, plus coconut halves to drink from. Point at what you want; it'll be on your plate in ten minutes. 🍽 Dadonghai night market · ¥60–150 pp Wenchang chicken 文昌鸡 Hainan's famous poached chicken — free-range, cooked until just done, and served with a gingery chili dip. It's the dish Hainan is proudest of, and it's everywhere in Sanya. Eat it with coconut-flavored rice. 🍽 Hainanese restaurants across the city · ¥40–80 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Winter (November–March) is peak season and prices double. May–October is hot but the best value — just bring serious sunscreen. Kat Says At seafood markets, agree on the price per kilogram before the scales come out, and check that your live catch is what gets cooked. Kat Says All beaches are public — even in front of five-star resorts. Walk the shoreline anywhere; nobody can stop you. title: Shanghai
snippet: the honest guide to shanghai for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌃 上海 Shanghai Futuristic skyline, international food, modernity ★☆☆☆☆ 🗓 3–4 days Most international Easy for beginners ✨ Why Shanghai? Shanghai is the easiest place in China for a first-timer — English is everywhere, the metro runs like clockwork, and almost every app you need works here. But don't mistake easy for boring: for over a century this has been China's most international city, a place where a 1920s French villa sits around the corner from a 600-meter supertall skyscraper. The Bund gives you the world's greatest skyline show for free, the old French Concession is made for slow afternoons and coffee, and the food scene runs from street-side soup dumplings to Michelin-starred tasting menus. If you only have a week in China, spend it here — and if you have more, Shanghai is the perfect first stop before the rest of the country. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 The Bund & the Pudong skyline Colonial past meets the future Read the story 2 Yu Garden & the old city A Ming dynasty garden in the heart of town Read the story 3 French Concession Plane trees, cafés & old villas Read the story 4 Shanghai Museum One of China's best — and free Read the story 5 Tianzifang Artistic alleyways in the old lanes The story: The Bund is a 1.5-km strip of 52 colonial-era buildings from the 1920s–30s — banks and trading houses built by British, French, American and Japanese firms when Shanghai was the 'Paris of the East'. Across the Huangpu River, Pudong's skyline rose from farmland in the 1990s: the Oriental Pearl Tower (1994), the 492-m Shanghai World Financial Center (2008) and the 632-m Shanghai Tower (2015), China's tallest building. Why it's a must-see: It's the only place on earth where you can stand in front of century-old European architecture and look directly at a fully futuristic Chinese skyline — the past and the future of Shanghai in a single glance. Come at night when the towers light up, and again at dawn when it's just you, the river, and the city waking up. 💡 Kat's tip: The Bund is free and open 24/7. Go at 7pm for the full light show, then walk two blocks back into Nanjing Road for street food. For the classic postcard view of the Bund itself, cross to Pudong and look back from Lujiazui. The story: Yu Garden was built between 1559 and 1577 by Pan Yunduan, a Ming-dynasty official, as a private garden for his parents — 'Yu' means 'peace and comfort'. It's a masterpiece of classical Chinese garden design: rockeries, carp ponds, zigzag bridges and dragon walls that hide the garden's true size (about 2 hectares) behind every turn. Why it's a must-see: It's the finest example in Shanghai of a classical Chinese garden — the kind of delicate pavilions-and-ponds scene you see in paintings. Around it, the old city walls are gone but the old-city lanes survive: tiny shops selling tea, jade and calligraphy brushes, all squeezed under traditional roofs. 💡 Kat's tip: Arrive at opening (9am) to beat the crowds. Right outside the gates, the snack street Nanxiang serves the legendary xiaolongbao — get the crab-roe version. Garden entry is 40 RMB. The story: From 1849 to 1943 this leafy district was the French Concession, and it still feels European — wide avenues shaded by 100-year-old plane trees, alleys of 1920s townhouses, and some of Shanghai's most beautiful streets (Wukang Road is the star). It was home to artists, writers and spies; Sun Yat-sen and Soong Ching-ling both lived here. Why it's a must-see: This is the Shanghai locals choose for weekend strolls: coffee on every corner, tiny galleries, vintage shops and tree-dappled streets with zero skyscrapers. It's the closest China gets to a Parisian afternoon, and the best place to slow down after the Bund's sensory overload. 💡 Kat's tip: Rent a shared bike (Meituan or HelloBike, ~1.5 RMB per 30 min) and wander without a map — get lost on purpose. Wukang Road, Anfu Road and Tianzifang's alleys are the highlights. Allow half a day. The story: Founded in 1952, the Shanghai Museum moved in 1996 into a striking round-building-with-square-base design that echoes the ancient Chinese belief 'heaven is round, earth is square'. Its collection of over one million pieces is ranked among the best in China, with world-class galleries of bronzes, ceramics, calligraphy, jade and Ming-Qing furniture. Why it's a must-see: Chinese museums rarely offer this combination: world-class artifacts, English labels, free entry, and air conditioning when the summer heat hits. The bronze gallery alone — ritual vessels up to 3,000 years old — is worth the trip. It's the perfect rainy-day or escape-the-heat move. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry is free but you must reserve online (WeChat mini-program or official site) with your passport — book a few days ahead in high season. Allow 2–3 hours; the bronze and ceramic galleries are the unmissable ones. The story: Tianzifang is a warren of shikumen (stone-gate) lane houses from the 1930s that artists began moving into around 1998, turning it into Shanghai's most creative quarter. Today its alleys hide hundreds of tiny studios, galleries, craft shops, cafés and bars — a living, working neighborhood rather than a reconstructed 'old town'. Why it's a must-see: Unlike polished tourist streets elsewhere, Tianzifang feels real — residents still hang laundry above the shops, and behind every doorway is something handmade and unexpected. It's the most atmospheric place in Shanghai to shop for gifts, watch artisans work, and duck into a laneway bar at night. 💡 Kat's tip: Go on a weekday (weekends are shoulder-to-shoulder). The alleys are a maze — pick one direction and just wander. For the classic view, climb to one of the rooftop bars around the edge of the maze. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. The Bund / Nanjing Road First-timers & skyline views Wake up to the Pudong skyline from your window, stroll the Bund at dawn before the crowds, and step out your door onto Nanjing Road — Shanghai's famous shopping street. Metro Line 2 and 10 run right through, and the old city with Yu Garden is a 15-minute walk. 🚇 Line 2/10 · East Nanjing Road 🏛 The Bund, Nanjing Road e.g. Les Suites Orient (mid-range, river views) · Peace Hotel (legendary art-deco landmark) People's Square / Huangpu Central & convenient The dead-center of Shanghai: Shanghai Museum on one side, the old city and Yu Garden to the south, and the French Concession a 10-minute taxi ride away. Two major metro lines cross here, and prices are more reasonable than the Bund. 🚇 Lines 1/2/8 · People's Square 🏛 Shanghai Museum, Yu Garden, Nanjing Road e.g. JW Marriott Shanghai at Tomorrow Square (landmark) · budget chains around the square French Concession (Xuhui / Jing'an) Café & architecture lovers The most atmospheric place to stay — tree-lined streets, boutiques and coffee shops, and the city's best brunch scene. It's less central for sightseeing but perfect if you want to feel the real Shanghai rhythm. Wukang Road's historic mansions are right outside. 🚇 Lines 1/7/10/11 · Changshu Rd / Shanghai Library 🏛 Wukang Road, Tianzifang, Anfu Road e.g. The Puli Hotel (luxury, Jing'an) · Capella Shanghai (restored shikumen villas, splurge) Lujiazui (Pudong) Modern skyline & business Stay inside the skyline you came to see: the financial district where the Shanghai Tower and Oriental Pearl live. Prices are high, and crossing the river adds 20 minutes to the Bund, but the night views from a high floor are unbeatable. 🚇 Line 2 · Lujiazui 🏛 Shanghai Tower, Oriental Pearl, IFC Mall e.g. Grand Hyatt Shanghai (tower views) · Mandarin Oriental Pudong (luxury) 🍜 What to Eat Xiaolongbao 小笼包 Delicate steamed dumplings holding hot pork-and-gelatin broth inside. The Shanghai ritual: bite a small hole, slurp the soup, then eat the rest with vinegar and ginger. 🍽 🍽 Jia Jia Tang Bao (Michelin-mentioned) · Yu Garden snack street · ¥15–30 per basket Shengjianbao 生煎包 Pan-fried pork buns with a crispy golden bottom, juicy filling and a burst of hot soup — xiaolongbao's heartier, crunchier cousin, and the true local breakfast. 🍽 🍽 Da Hu Chun (legendary since 1932) · ¥12–20 per order of 4 Hairy Crab 大闸蟹 A seasonal obsession (Oct–Nov only): small lake crabs prized for their creamy roe and sweet meat. Locals plan entire dinners around them — worth scheduling your trip for. 🍽 🍽 Wang Bao He on Fuzhou Road · ¥80–200 per crab in season · book ahead Scallion Oil Noodles 葱油拌面 Springy noodles tossed with scallion-infused oil and soy — deceptively simple, deeply comforting, and the taste of a Shanghai home kitchen. 🍽 🍽 Any local canteen or noodle shop · ¥15–25 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Get a Shanghai metro card or just tap with your phone (Alipay/WeChat Pay) — the network is huge, cheap (~3–6 RMB) and fully in English. Avoid taxis during rush hour. Kat Says The Bund at night and the Bund at 7am are two completely different experiences — do both. Night for the lights, dawn for the colonial architecture and the tai chi crowd. Kat Says Almost everything in Shanghai can be paid with Alipay or WeChat Pay; for the small old-city snack stalls carry 50–100 RMB in cash as backup. title: Shenzhen
snippet: the honest guide to shenzhen for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌆 深圳 Shenzhen China's Silicon Valley, beaches, and skyscrapers ★☆☆☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Tech & modern Near Hong Kong Beaches ✨ Why Shenzhen? Shenzhen didn't exist 40 years ago. In 1980, it was a fishing village of 30,000 people. Today it's a megacity of 17 million, home to Huawei, Tencent, BYD, and DJI — the companies shaping the world's technology. If Beijing is China's history and Shanghai is its finance, Shenzhen is its future. But Shenzhen isn't just glass towers and circuit boards. It's also where young Chinese come to start businesses, make art, and surf. The city has more parks than any other in China, a thriving craft beer scene, and some of the best beaches in the Pearl River Delta. It's efficient, green, and surprisingly laid-back for a place that builds the future. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Ping An Finance Centre (599m observation deck) Tallest building in Shenzhen · skyline views Read the story 2 Dafen Oil Painting Village Artists' colony · custom portraits · quirky culture Read the story 3 OCT Loft Creative Park Street art · cafés · design studios · music Read the story 4 Window of the World Mini global landmarks · family fun · photo ops Read the story 5 Dameisha Beach City beach · boardwalk · seafood restaurants The story: Ping An Finance Centre was completed in 2017 as the headquarters of Ping An Insurance, one of the world's largest financial companies. At 599 meters, it's the second-tallest building in China and the fourth-tallest in the world. The design by Kohn Pedersen Fox features a stainless steel facade that catches the tropical light. Why it's a must-see: The Free Sky observation deck on the 116th floor (541 meters) offers a view that stretches to Hong Kong on clear days. The elevator reaches the top in 55 seconds. It's a visceral reminder of what 40 years of growth looks like — from rice paddies to clouds. 💡 Kat's tip: Book tickets online to skip the queue. Go on a clear day — tropical haze can obscure the view. Sunset is the best time. The story: In 1989, a Hong Kong art dealer named Huang Jiang moved to Dafen with 20 artists and started producing oil painting reproductions for export. Today, Dafen is home to over 8,000 painters who produce 60% of the world's oil paintings — from Van Gogh replicas to custom portraits you can commission in 48 hours. Why it's a must-see: It's the most surreal corner of Shenzhen. Narrow alleys are lined with open-air studios where artists paint Mona Lisas, Tibetan landscapes, and abstract canvases while you watch. You can commission a portrait from a photo, buy original art for under ¥200, or just wander and watch creativity happen at industrial scale. 💡 Kat's tip: Bring a photo if you want a custom portrait (48-hour turnaround). Haggle politely — prices are flexible. The best artists are in the back alleys, not the main street. The story: OCT Loft is a converted factory complex in the Nanshan district, transformed in the early 2000s into Shenzhen's creative hub. It's home to design studios, independent bookstores, craft coffee roasters, and the annual Shenzhen Design Week. The Overseas Chinese Town (OCT) company developed it as a cultural counterweight to the city's tech obsession. Why it's a must-see: This is where Shenzhen's young creatives actually hang out. The street art changes monthly, the cafés roast their own beans, and the independent music venues host bands from across China. It's the best place to understand that Shenzhen isn't just about making things — it's about imagining them too. 💡 Kat's tip: Go on a weekend afternoon when the creative market is open. Grab coffee at Something For or Trunk Coffee, then walk to the nearby Sea World plaza for dinner by the water. The story: Opened in 1994, Window of the World is a 480,000 m² theme park featuring over 130 replicas of famous global landmarks at 1:1, 1:3, or 1:15 scale. The Eiffel Tower, Pyramids, Taj Mahal, and Statue of Liberty all stand within walking distance of each other — a surreal monument to China's 1990s fascination with the outside world. Why it's a must-see: It's unapologetically kitschy and genuinely fun. The 108-meter Eiffel Tower replica has an observation deck, the nightly dance show draws huge crowds, and the "Around the World in a Day" concept is weirdly satisfying. It's also a fascinating time capsule of 1990s China's view of global culture. 💡 Kat's tip: Go in the late afternoon and stay for the 7:30pm dance show. Buy tickets online for a discount. It's busiest on weekends — weekdays are much more relaxed. The story: Dameisha ("Big Meisha") is Shenzhen's most popular public beach, a 1.8-kilometer stretch of sand on the eastern Dapeng Peninsula. It was developed in the 1990s as a weekend escape for Shenzhen's growing middle class and remains the city's default beach destination — complete with a boardwalk, seafood restaurants, and water sports. Why it's a must-see: Where else can you surf in the morning, tour a tech headquarters at noon, and eat fresh seafood by the beach at sunset? Dameisha is no Phuket, but it's real, accessible, and surprisingly lively. The water is clean(ish), the sand is decent, and the seafood restaurants along the shore are honestly good. 💡 Kat's tip: Take the metro to Yantian Port, then bus M437 or a Didi. Avoid weekends — the beach gets packed. For a quieter option, head to nearby Xiaomeisha ("Little Meisha") or Xichong. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the four bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Futian 福田 Best for first-timers Shenzhen's CBD and transport hub: the Ping An Tower, Convention Center, and direct metro to Hong Kong. Stay here for convenience, business hotels, and the best metro connections. 🚇 Metro Lines 1/2/3/4 · 🏙️ CBD & shopping malls e.g. Shangri-La Futian · Four Seasons Shenzhen · Marriott Executive Apartments Nanshan 南山 Tech & coast Home to Tencent, Huawei, and the city's best coastline. OCT Loft, Sea World, and the Bay Area promenade make this the most liveable district. Best for creatives and tech visitors. 🚇 Metro Line 2 · 🌊 Coastal promenade e.g. Hilton Shenzhen Shekou · boutique hotels near OCT Loft Luohu 罗湖 Hong Kong border The original downtown and main border crossing to Hong Kong. Older but packed with shopping, street food, and budget hotels. Best for day-trippers to HK and bargain hunters. 🚇 Metro Line 1 · 🛃 Lo Wu border crossing e.g. budget chains near the train station · older but convenient Shekou 蛇口 Expat hub Shenzhen's most international neighborhood: foreign restaurants, international schools, and the ferry terminal to Hong Kong and Macau. Best for families and anyone wanting Western comforts. 🚇 Metro Line 2 · ⛴ Ferry to HK/Macau e.g. Fraser Suites Shekou · Seaview hotels · mid-to-high range 🍜 What to Eat Fresh Seafood 海鲜 Shenzhen's coastal location means incredibly fresh seafood. Restaurants keep live tanks of fish, lobster, and crab that you pick yourself. Steamed with ginger and scallion is the Cantonese way — and it's perfect. 🍽 Shekou Seafood Street · ¥150–400 pp · pick your own live catch Chaozhou Beef Hotpot 潮汕牛肉火锅 Paper-thin slices of fresh beef, blanched for 8 seconds in a light bone broth. Different cuts have different textures — tongue, neck, brisket, tripe. Dip in shacha sauce. It's Shenzhen's most popular dinner. 🍽 Baheli · Chaoshan Beef · ¥100–200 pp · book ahead on weekends Dim Sum 点心 Shenzhen does excellent Cantonese dim sum — often with shorter queues than Guangzhou. Har gow, siu mai, char siu bao, and egg tarts are the classics. Many restaurants serve all day. 🍽 Lei Garden · Tao Tao Ju · ¥50–120 pp · go before 10am for best selection Street BBQ 烧烤 Late-night grilled skewers of lamb, eggplant, tofu, and oysters, dusted with cumin and chili. Shenzhen's street BBQ culture is thriving — find a plastic-stool joint after 10pm and eat like a local. 🍽 Any street with red-plastic stools after 10pm · ¥40–80 pp · cash or WeChat 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says The metro connects directly to Hong Kong — you can day-trip to Kowloon in under 1 hour using the Futian or Luohu checkpoints. Kat Says Book attractions in advance on weekends — Shenzhen's population swells on Saturdays and queues get long. Kat Says Download the Shenzhen Metro app or use Alipay transit code. The metro is clean, fast, and has English signs everywhere. title: Suzhou
snippet: the honest guide to suzhou for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏮 苏州 Suzhou Classical gardens, canals, silk, water towns ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3–4 days Classical gardens Canals Water towns ✨ Why Suzhou? There's an old saying in China: "In heaven there is paradise, on earth there are Suzhou and Hangzhou." Suzhou has been the country's city of gardens, silk, and scholars for 2,500 years — a place where emperors retired, poets wrote, and craftsmen perfected the art of turning a patch of land into a miniature universe. It's just 30 minutes from Shanghai by high-speed rail, yet it feels a thousand years away. This is the city that defined what "classical Chinese garden" means — nine of them are UNESCO-listed. Streets are threaded with canals, whitewashed houses hug the water, and the famous Pingjiang Road still hums with the rhythm of daily life. Come for the gardens, stay for the boat rides, the silk workshops, and the quietly exquisite food. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Humble Administrator's Garden (Zhuozheng Yuan) UNESCO · Suzhou's largest classical garden Read the story 2 Suzhou Museum I.M. Pei masterpiece · silk & Ming furniture Read the story 3 Pingjiang Road 800-year-old canal street · old houses & teahouses Read the story 4 Tiger Hill (Huqiu) China's Leaning Tower · ancient pagoda on a hill Read the story 5 Tongli Water Town Venice of the East · canals, stone bridges, gardens The story: Built in 1509 by a retired Ming dynasty official, the Humble Administrator's Garden is the largest and most famous classical garden in Suzhou. It was designed to feel like a landscape painting you can walk into — pavilions frame views, rocks become mountains, and a central lake is connected by zigzag bridges that make you slow down and notice everything. Why it's a must-see: It's the single best example of Suzhou's garden art, which UNESCO calls "the most refined garden design in the world." Spend two hours wandering the sections named after poetry — every window is a picture frame, every reflection a composition. 💡 Kat's tip: Book your timed ticket online in advance during holidays — it sells out. Go right at opening (7:30am) to see it almost empty. In spring, the azaleas and magnolias are spectacular. The story: The 2006 extension of Suzhou Museum was the last major project of legendary architect I. M. Pei, who was born in Suzhou. He used white walls, grey-tiled roofs, and rocks in a "painting wall" style that echoes the classical gardens next door — the museum building itself is the exhibit. Why it's a must-see: The collection tells the story of Suzhou: embroidered silk robes, jade carvings, Ming dynasty scholar furniture, and calligraphy. Entry is free, the building is a work of art, and it's a calm, air-conditioned escape on hot days. 💡 Kat's tip: Reserve free tickets on the official WeChat account a day ahead — walk-ins are limited. It's right next to the Humble Administrator's Garden, so combine the two and spend a full morning here. The story: Pingjiang Road is a stone-paved street running alongside a canal for over a kilometer, and it has been Suzhou's liveliest quarter since the Southern Song dynasty. Whitewashed houses crowd the water, stone bridges arch every hundred meters, and the old names of lanes — "Button Lane," "Willow Lane" — reveal the trades that once lived here. Why it's a must-see: It's the most atmospheric slice of old Suzhou and completely free. Follow it slowly: duck-egg sellers, guqin players in teahouses, silk handicraft stalls, and tiny garden courtyards hidden behind half-open doors. 💡 Kat's tip: Come at dusk — the lanterns come on and the crowds thin out. Take a 40-minute boat ride on the canal for a different angle. The eastern end is quieter than the tourist-heavy southern section. The story: Legend says a tiger guarded the tomb of King Helü of Wu here in 496 BC, and for a thousand years the Yunyan Pagoda at the hill's summit has been slowly leaning — today it tilts about 3 degrees, earning the nickname "China's Leaning Tower of Pisa." Nobody is quite sure why it hasn't fallen, which is part of the fun. Why it's a must-see: "If you haven't been to Tiger Hill, you haven't been to Suzhou," goes the local saying. The hill is a pleasant park of gardens, stone carvings, and a sword-pool well where Helü's weapons were supposedly sunk — plus the leaning pagoda, which you can't photograph without tilting your head. 💡 Kat's tip: Half a day is plenty. The entrance is about 30 minutes by taxi from the old town. In autumn the maple trees turn the whole hill red — one of Suzhou's best seasonal moments. The story: Tongli is a water town that predates the Ming dynasty, built on five lakes with fifteen rivers threaded through its lanes. Locals still live their lives over the water — deliveries by boat, washing at the canal steps, and stone bridges with names like "Long Peace" and "Great Wealth" carrying daily traffic. Why it's a must-see: It's the perfect day trip from Suzhou (about 40 minutes by metro and bus, or a quick taxi). Unlike the more touristed Zhouzhuang, Tongli feels lived-in. The Retreat and Reflection Garden, a UNESCO-listed garden, is hidden inside an ordinary-looking house. 💡 Kat's tip: Arrive before 9am to have the canals almost to yourself. Ride a boat through the smaller back canals for the real experience. Try the local "zongzi" (glutinous rice in bamboo leaves) from a street vendor. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Pingjiang Road / Old Town Best for first-timers The classic choice: canal-side lanes, gardens on your doorstep, and old teahouses everywhere. Most of the big-name gardens are within walking or short-taxi distance. Best for travelers who want atmosphere over convenience. 🚇 Line 1 · Lindun Lu 🏮 Walk to Pingjiang Road e.g. boutique courtyard guesthouses on the canals · Pan Pacific Suzhou Guanqian Street Shopping & metro hub Suzhou's commercial heart: pedestrian shopping streets, century-old snack shops, and the best metro connections. Plenty of hotels at every price. Best for easy logistics and nightlife. 🚇 Line 1/4 · Leqiao 🛍 Food street & malls e.g. Marriott Suzhou · international chains along Renmin Road Jinji Lake Modern Suzhou The gleaming modern district east of the old city: lakefront promenades, the giant "Gate of the Orient" skyscraper, and a light show at night. Best for business travelers or a modern, spacious base. 🚇 Line 1 · Times Square 🌃 Lake views & light show e.g. Shangri-La Jinji Lake · lakeside international hotels 🍜 What to Eat Squirrel-shaped mandarin fish 松鼠桂鱼 Suzhou's signature banquet dish: a whole mandarin fish scored, fried until it curls like a squirrel's tail, and doused in sweet-and-sour sauce. Crisp outside, silky white inside. 🍽 Classic Suzhou restaurants near Guanqian Street · ¥80–150 Suzhou soup noodles 苏式汤面 A proper Suzhou breakfast: thin, springy noodles in a clear broth, topped with "cap" toppings like braised pork, crab-paste, or river shrimp. The broth is the pride — every noodle shop guards its recipe. 🍽 Tong De Xing · Zhu Hong Xing · ¥20–50 Shengjian buns 生煎包 Pan-fried pork buns with a juicy, soupy filling and a crackling bottom. Bite carefully — the first bite sprays hot broth. Best eaten straight off the pan, standing at the counter. 🍽 Lao Pai Shengjian · street shops across the old town · ¥8–15 Osmanthus sweets 桂花糖芋苗 Suzhou has a famously sweet tooth. Try sticky rice balls in fermented wine, chestnut cakes, and taro porridge scented with osmanthus flowers — a perfume-like sweetness unique to this region. 🍽 Dessert shops on Pingjiang Road · ¥10–25 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Garden tickets sell out on weekends and holidays — book online a day ahead and arrive at opening time. Kat Says A canal boat ride at dusk on Pingjiang Road is one of the most romantic 40 minutes you can buy in China. Kat Says Suzhou and Shanghai are 30 minutes apart by high-speed rail — pair them for a perfect east-coast week. Explore More Cities 🌆 上海 · Shanghai Skyscrapers, The Bund, neon, and world-class dining 🍃 杭州 · Hangzhou West Lake, tea plantations, Buddhist temples, poetry ← Back to Ready? China!

title: Xiamen
snippet: the honest guide to xiamen for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🌊 厦门 Xiamen Gulangyu island, sea breeze, colonial villas, street food ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 3–4 days Coastal Islands Food ✨ Why Xiamen? Xiamen is the Chinese city that feels like a seaside town you'd find in Portugal or Greece. Palm-lined boulevards, the sea on every horizon, a mix of Chinese and colonial-era architecture, and a pace of life that's famously slow — locals call it "the garden on the sea." It's also one of China's cleanest, most walkable cities. The centerpiece is Gulangyu, a car-free island of 19th-century villas and gardens that UNESCO calls the best example of Sino-foreign architecture anywhere. But Xiamen is more than its island: a hilltop temple overlooking the campus, an art district carved from old factories, a ring road built for cycling along the ocean, and seafood that lands on the table hours after it's caught. Pair it with nearby Quanzhou for a perfect Fujian week. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Gulangyu Island UNESCO · car-free · piano museum & colonial villas Read the story 2 Nanputuo Temple 1,000-year-old seaside temple · free entry Read the story 3 Shapowei & the Arts District Old harbor turned cafés, galleries & vintage shops Read the story 4 Ring Road & the Beaches The best ocean cycling in China · sunset boardwalk Read the story 5 Zengcuoan Fishing Village Seaside village · night markets · backpacker hub The story: In the 19th century, after the Opium Wars, foreign traders and missionaries settled on Gulangyu, a small island a 5-minute ferry from Xiamen. They built hundreds of villas — British, French, Dutch, Japanese — alongside the local Fujian style, creating what UNESCO calls "the most complete and authentic example of Sino-foreign architecture in the world." The island also became China's piano capital; nearly every family owned one. Why it's a must-see: It's a car-free, traffic-light-free world of narrow lanes, hibiscus-covered walls, and sea views at every turn. Climb Sunlight Rock for the panorama, wander past the restored villas of the old foreign quarter, and visit the world's only piano museum. It's touristy, but it's genuinely beautiful. 💡 Kat's tip: Book ferry tickets online days ahead — same-day slots sell out. Go early morning, or better, stay overnight on the island after 6pm when the day-trippers vanish and the lanes belong to the cats. The story: Nanputuo — "Southern Putuo" — was founded in the Tang dynasty more than a thousand years ago and rebuilt in the Ming and Qing. Unlike most temples, it welcomes the sea: it sits on the hillside above Xiamen University, with Buddhist halls climbing toward the summit and ocean views from the top. Why it's a must-see: It's one of the few temples in China where you can be praying in a thousand-year-old hall, then step outside to a panorama of the South China Sea. The incense, the carvings, and the free vegetarian lunch (donation only) make it a peaceful, authentic counterpoint to Xiamen's beaches. 💡 Kat's tip: Entrance is free. Go on a weekday morning when the incense is strongest. Climb to the top hall for the best view, then walk down into the campus of Xiamen University next door — you need advance registration to enter the campus itself. The story: Shapowei ("sand-tail bend") was once the old harbor where Xiamen's fishing fleets landed. When the port moved, the decaying warehouses and boatyards stayed — and in the 2010s, artists, baristas, and vintage dealers moved in. Today it's a tangle of fishing boats and craft breweries, seafood stalls and indie galleries. Why it's a must-see: It's Xiamen's creative heart and the most fun district to wander. Watch fishermen mend nets in one lane, then sip pour-over coffee in a converted warehouse two blocks away. The sunset from the waterfront terrace is the best free show in the city. 💡 Kat's tip: Come in the late afternoon — it's quiet, the light is golden, and the area comes alive at night. Look for the murals on the old factory walls and the mini art gallery on the second floor of the fish market. The story: Xiamen's island ring road hugs the coastline for 43 km, and a dedicated bike lane runs right along the water — one of the most scenic urban rides in China. It passes white-sand beaches, the landmark "White City" statue, and the point where the island faces the Kinmen islands across the strait. Why it's a must-see: Cycling the ring road is how you feel Xiamen's "island city" identity: sea on one side, mountains on the other, and a salt breeze the whole way. Even a short sunset stretch from the city center to Hulishan Fortress (with its famous 100-ton German cannon) is worth it. 💡 Kat's tip: Rent a shared bike and ride the section from Pearl Bay to the Ring Road music plaza in the late afternoon. The sea breeze is strong — bring a light jacket even on hot days. The story: Zengcuoan began as a poor fishing village of stone houses and shrines, tucked into a cove on the island's southeast coast. As tourism grew, the villagers turned their front rooms into guesthouses and food stalls — and today the maze of lanes is a buzzing seaside hub that still keeps its temples and its resident fishing families. Why it's a must-see: It's the most atmospheric of Xiamen's beachfront areas: sandy beach on one side, night market with grilled oysters and peanut soup on the other, and the old village lanes winding between. It's touristy but honest — the seafood is fresh and the atmosphere is pure coast. 💡 Kat's tip: Come at night for the food market — the grilled oysters (5 yuan a dozen) are the best value in Xiamen. The beach at dawn is nearly empty and lovely for a barefoot walk. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Zhongshan Road / Old Town Best for first-timers Xiamen's historic core: the pedestrian Zhongshan Road, arcade buildings, century-old food shops, and a 10-minute walk to the Gulangyu ferry. Best for food and walking tours of the old town. 🚢 10 min to Gulangyu ferry 🍜 Historic food street e.g. arcade-style boutique hotels on Zhongshan Road Gulangyu Island Most atmospheric Sleep inside a restored colonial villa on the car-free island. After 6pm the crowds disappear and the lanes turn magical. Best for romance and slow mornings, but packing over cobblestones is real. 🚢 Ferry to island 🏡 Villa guesthouses e.g. restored villa guesthouses near the piano museum Xiamen University / Shapowei Arts & young vibe The university quarter: café-filled lanes, the arts district, and Nanputuo Temple on the doorstep. Walk to the beach or the temple in minutes. Best for creatives and younger travelers. 🏛 Walk to Nanputuo ☕ Cafés & galleries e.g. guesthouses near XMU · art-themed hostels in Shapowei 🍜 What to Eat Shacha noodles 沙茶面 Xiamen's signature bowl: chewy noodles in a rich, nutty, slightly spicy soup made with shacha sauce (a Fujian-Southeast Asian satay blend). You pick the toppings — shrimp, squid, pork, bean curd — and they're blanched at the counter. 🍽 Wujiazhai shacha noodle shops · ¥15–35 Oyster omelette 海蛎煎 Fresh oysters folded into a glossy sweet-potato-starch omelette and fried until the edges crisp. Served with sweet chili sauce — soft, briny, and wonderful. The ultimate Xiamen street snack. 🍽 Night markets · old-town snack shops · ¥15–25 Peanut soup 花生汤 A sweet, milky soup made by boiling peanuts until they soften into a golden cream — served warm with a soft-boiled egg or fried dough. A century-old Xiamen breakfast tradition. 🍽 Huang Zehe Peanut Soup (since 1907) · ¥8–15 Grilled seafood 烤生蚝 At the night markets, oysters and shellfish grill over charcoal with garlic and chili — cheap, fast, and straight off the boats. A dozen oysters and a cold beer is the classic Xiamen evening. 🍽 Zengcuoan night market · ¥20–50 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Book your Gulangyu ferry tickets days in advance — it's the single thing that books out first in Xiamen. Kat Says Avoid Chinese public holidays (especially Golden Week in October) — Gulangyu becomes a wall of umbrellas. Kat Says Combine Xiamen with Quanzhou — 20 minutes by high-speed rail and a completely different, older, richer Fujian. title: Xian
snippet: the honest guide to xi'an for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏺 西安 Xi'an Ancient history, Terracotta Army, Silk Road ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Unmissable history Street food heaven ✨ Why Xi'an? Xi'an was China's capital for over 1,000 years across 13 dynasties — the longest of any city — and it's where the Silk Road began. Emperors ruled here when London was a village, and the evidence is still standing: the world's largest ancient city wall, pagodas built by a Tang-dynasty monk, and an army of 8,000 terracotta soldiers guarding a tomb for 2,200 years. But Xi'an isn't only ancient. The Muslim Quarter is one of China's great street-food bazaars, the city wall is the best place in the country to rent a bike, and the metro now links it all together. History nerds, food lovers and first-timers alike leave impressed — it's the perfect second stop after Beijing. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Terracotta Army 8,000 warriors guard an emperor's tomb Read the story 2 Ancient City Wall Ride a bike around 14th-century ramparts Read the story 3 Muslim Quarter (Huimin Jie) China's best street-food bazaar Read the story 4 Big Wild Goose Pagoda Where a Tang monk stored his scriptures Read the story 5 Shaanxi History Museum 130,000 years of history — free entry The story: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an stumbled onto the greatest archaeological discovery of the 20th century: an underground army built around 210 BC for Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor. So far over 8,000 life-size soldiers, 130 chariots and 670 horses have been found, each warrior with a unique face — no two are alike. The entire site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, covers 56 square kilometers. Why it's a must-see: This is one of the world's true wonders — a silent army that has waited 2,200 years for visitors, built by over 700,000 laborers. Pit 1 alone holds 6,000 warriors in battle formation, and the sheer scale makes you understand why the first emperor thought he could conquer death itself. 💡 Kat's tip: Go early (opens 8:30am) and head straight to Pit 1 before the tour groups arrive. It's 1 hour from the city — take public bus 306 (游5) from the train station for 7 RMB, not the 200 RMB tourist bus. Allow 3–4 hours. The story: Xi'an's city wall was built 1370–1378 by the first Ming emperor, on foundations laid in the Tang dynasty. It's the best-preserved city wall in China — and the largest anywhere: a 13.7-km rectangle, 12–14 meters thick at the base, with a 12-meter-wide top and a moat on three sides. Four grand gates and 98 watchtowers ring the old city. Why it's a must-see: Nowhere else in China can you cycle the full circumference of an intact ancient city wall. The 13.7-km loop takes about 1.5–2 hours on a rented bike, with views over tiled old-city roofs on one side and modern Xi'an on the other — especially magical at sunset. 💡 Kat's tip: Rent a bike on the wall (45 RMB for 2 hours, or 100 RMB deposit) — bikes are available at every gate. Go 2 hours before sunset and time your loop to finish as the lights come on. Entrance is 54 RMB. The story: The Muslim Quarter has been home to Xi'an's Hui Muslim community for over a thousand years — descendants of Silk Road traders from Persia and Central Asia who married locally and stayed. Its maze of alleys behind the 14th-century Drum Tower is now China's most famous food street: lamb skewers, roujiamo, biangbiang noodles, dates, and dried fruit piled high under neon signs. Why it's a must-see: This is where Xi'an's street-food soul lives. The main strip is touristy, but one alley deeper and you're eating where locals eat — hand-pulled noodles, bubbling paomo soup, and skewers grilled over charcoal. It's the perfect evening after a day of history. 💡 Kat's tip: Skip the shops right on the main street; wander the side alleys (Xiyangshi, Beiyuanmen) for better food and prices. Go at 6pm when it's lively but not yet packed. Bring small cash for the stalls. The story: Built in 652 AD, this 64.5-meter, seven-story brick pagoda was commissioned by the great Tang-dynasty monk Xuanzang to store the Buddhist scriptures he carried back from 17 years of travel across India — the journey that later inspired the novel 'Journey to the West'. The surrounding Da Ci'en Temple was once one of the most important monasteries in China. Why it's a must-see: It's a direct link to one of history's greatest travelers — and the pagoda itself, elegant and uncluttered after 1,300 years, is a masterpiece of Tang architecture. The Daming Palace ruins nearby show how vast Tang Xi'an was: the Tang capital was once the largest city on earth, with a million residents. 💡 Kat's tip: Come in the evening: the square in front hosts the famous music fountain show (usually 7pm and 9pm, free), and the pagoda glows gold against the night sky. Entry 40 RMB for the temple; climbing the pagoda is an extra 30 RMB. The story: Xi'an's treasure vault: over 370,000 artifacts spanning from prehistoric times to the Qing dynasty, including Zhou-dynasty bronzes, Tang-dynasty gold and silver, and thousands of pieces unearthed right in the city. Its collection is so rich that only a fraction is ever on display at once. Why it's a must-see: If you want to understand why Xi'an matters — and see the actual objects behind all that history — this is the place. The Tang gold and silver gallery alone is worth the visit, and unlike many Chinese museums, the collection is world-class even by international standards. 💡 Kat's tip: Entry is FREE but quota-limited: reserve online (official WeChat mini-program) with your passport at least 3 days ahead. Go right at opening (9am). Allow 2–3 hours; the Tang galleries on the second floor are the highlights. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Inside the City Wall (Bell Tower area) Best for first-timers The historic heart: the Bell and Drum Towers, the Muslim Quarter's food alleys, and the old-city atmosphere are all within walking distance. Metro Line 2 runs along the wall's north-south axis, linking you to the train station and the Terracotta Army bus. 🚇 Lines 2/4/6 · Bell Tower 🏛 Bell Tower, Drum Tower, Muslim Quarter e.g. Sofitel Legend People's Grand (1950s landmark) · Eastern House Boutique (great value near Bell Tower) South Gate (Yongningmen) Quiet & upscale South of the Bell Tower along the wall, this area has a more refined feel — trendy cafés, galleries and boutique hotels tucked into old courtyards, with direct access to the wall's South Gate bike rental and the Yongningmen metro. 🚇 Lines 2 · Yongningmen 🏛 South Gate, Shuyuanmen old street, De Fu Xiang e.g. Somerset Xindicheng Serviced Residence (apartments) · boutique courtyard hotels Qujiang New District Sightseers & evening shows The modern cultural district around the Big Wild Goose Pagoda and the Tang Paradise park — wide avenues, night fountain shows, and the city's most impressive modern architecture. About 15–20 minutes by taxi to the old city. 🚇 Lines 3/4 · Dayanta 🏛 Big Wild Goose Pagoda, Tang Paradise, Qujiang pool e.g. Wyndham Grand Xi'an South (5-star near the pagoda) · mid-range chains along Yanta Road Xi'an North Railway Station area High-speed train transfer If you're arriving by bullet train (from Beijing 4.5h, Chengdu 3h) or flying in, the north station area is modern, cheap and convenient — though it's a 30-minute metro ride from the old city's sights. 🚇 Lines 2/4 · North Railway Station 🏛 High-speed rail hub, 3-km to airport bus e.g. Xi'an Jinhua Hotel · business chains (Holiday Inn Express) 🍜 What to Eat Roujiamo 肉夹馍 Spiced braised pork, chopped fine and stuffed into a crisp, griddled flatbread — often called the world's first hamburger. Xi'an's most iconic snack. 🍽 🍽 Muslim Quarter stalls · ¥10–15 each · order the 'lean' (纯瘦) or 'half-fat' (肥瘦) version Yangrou Paomo 羊肉泡馍 The soul food of Xi'an: you tear flatbread into crumbs, the kitchen simmers it in rich lamb broth, and you eat it with pickled garlic and chili — a ritual meal that takes patience and rewards it. 🍽 🍽 Lao Sun Jia (老孙家) or local paomo shops · ¥30–50 Biangbiang Noodles biangbiang面 Hand-ripped belt noodles as wide as your palm, tossed with chili oil, garlic and vinegar. The name's Chinese character has 58 strokes — the most complex in the language. 🍽 🍽 Muslim Quarter noodle houses · ¥15–25 Lamb Skewers 羊肉串 Charcoal-grilled lamb skewers dusted with cumin and chili — the soundtrack of the Muslim Quarter at night. Order them in tens, eat them standing up. 🍽 🍽 Beiyuanmen alley, Muslim Quarter · ¥3–5 per skewer 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says The Terracotta Army deserves 3–4 hours and an early start — take public bus 306 (游5) from the train station for 7 RMB and ignore the touts offering 'express tours'. Kat Says Ride the city wall at sunset, not midday — the 13.7 km loop takes ~2 hours and the golden light over the old city is unforgettable. Kat Says The Muslim Quarter is at its best after 6pm. Go deeper than the main street for the real food; and yes, roujiamo really is as good as everyone says. title: Yiwu
snippet: the honest guide to yiwu for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🛒 义乌 Yiwu World's small-commodities market, crazy shopping ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 1–2 days Shopping paradise Wholesale market ✨ Why Yiwu? Yiwu is the most mind-bending shopping destination on earth: a wholesale market of 75,000 booths selling 2.1 million product types across 6.4 million square meters — certified by the UN and World Bank as the world's largest small-commodity market. If you spent 3 minutes at every booth, 8 hours a day, it would take over a year to see it all. The market that started as a street-side stall line in 1982 is now the engine of global consumer goods — that $3 earring you bought anywhere in the world probably originated here. And since January 2026, a new high-speed link puts Yiwu just 33 minutes from Hangzhou. Come for the spectacle, stay for the street food, and leave with your luggage full of the world's cheapest souvenirs. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Yiwu International Trade City The world's largest wholesale market Read the story 2 District 1 — toys, jewelry & crafts 80% of China's jewelry makers under one roof Read the story 3 District 2 — bags & hardware Where Amazon sellers shop Read the story 4 Districts 3–4 — stationery, socks & daily goods The world's biggest sock hub Read the story 5 District 5 & the Digital Trade Center Imports, the future & tourist shopping The story: From a 1982 street stall market, Yiwu has grown through six generations into the world's largest wholesale market: 6.4+ million square meters across five districts plus a new Digital Trade Center (opened October 2025). The UN, World Bank and Morgan Stanley have all called it the 'world's largest small-commodity market'; in 2024 it averaged 224,000 visitors a day, including 4,000+ foreign buyers from 230+ countries. Why it's a must-see: Even if you never buy a thing, walking this market is jaw-dropping — it's a city of products, where every object on earth seems to have a booth. It's a national 4A tourist attraction, free to enter, and unlike any shopping experience you've had in your life. 💡 Kat's tip: Free entry, open 8:30am–5:30pm. Start at the tourist service center for a map. Most booths are wholesale-only (minimum orders apply), but many will sell a sample piece if you ask nicely. Bring a translator app — many vendors speak only Chinese. The story: The oldest and busiest district (opened 2002, 340,000 m², 8,000+ booths): the ground floor sells artificial flowers, the second hair accessories and jewelry, the third crafts and festive decorations. It gathers over 80% of China's jewelry manufacturers, with 5,000+ new designs released weekly. Why it's a must-see: This is where global fashion-accessory trends are born — if you've ever bought a $3 pair of earrings from a chain store anywhere in the world, they likely came from here. The sheer glittering density of merchandise is overwhelming in the best way. 💡 Kat's tip: Visit on weekday mornings for the fewest crowds. Look for booths with 'MOQ' (minimum order quantity) signs if you're actually sourcing; otherwise, it's a fascinating window-shopping spectacle. The story: The second district (600,000 m², 8,000+ booths) covers bags and luggage, umbrellas, hardware tools, locks, small electronics and small appliances. The fourth floor hosts specialty pavilions offering factory-direct supply, and the district's bags-and-luggage zone alone feeds importers worldwide. Why it's a must-see: This is where Amazon sellers and importers come to source suitcases, power tools and kitchen gadgets by the container load. Even as a casual visitor, seeing the full breadth of 'Made in China' in one building is eye-opening — and fun. 💡 Kat's tip: If you're sourcing, bring business cards and a notebook — vendors will quote MOQs and FOB prices on the spot. The fourth-floor regional pavilions are less crowded with higher-quality goods. The story: District 3 (460,000 m²) concentrates stationery, office supplies, sports goods and cosmetics — its 1,900+ stationery vendors supply 100+ countries. District 4 (1.08 million m², 16,000+ booths) is the single largest district, selling socks, underwear, shoes and daily goods; its sock zone alone exports over 3 billion RMB a year. Why it's a must-see: District 4 is so large it could be a city by itself — the world's biggest sock-trading hub, where you'll find socks printed with everything from anime characters to national flags, sold by the thousand-pair carton. It's a museum of daily life, in bulk. 💡 Kat's tip: District 4 is overwhelming — pick one category (socks on the lower floors, say) and focus. The buildings have internal elevated roads so delivery trucks drive right onto each floor; watch for vehicles in the corridors. The story: District 5 (640,000 m², 7,000+ booths) focuses on imported goods, bedding and textiles, with a first-floor Import Pavilion stocking nearly 100,000 products from dozens of countries. The brand-new Digital Trade Center (opened October 2025, 1.25 million m²) is Yiwu's sixth-generation market: AI sourcing tools, livestream studios and virtual showrooms. Why it's a must-see: District 5's Import Pavilion is the easiest place in China to buy authentic foreign products — Italian wine, Japanese cosmetics, Russian chocolate — at near-wholesale prices. The Digital Trade Center shows where the world's market is heading, and it's genuinely cool. 💡 Kat's tip: The Import Pavilion is the best place for tourist shopping — many items sell individually. The Digital Trade Center has a visitor experience zone with AI demos; 30 minutes is enough if you're not buying. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. International Trade City area (Futian) Buyers & market visitors The most practical base if the market is your goal: business hotels cluster around Futian Street, within a 5-minute walk of Districts 1–5, plus the Foreign Buyer Service Center and logistics offices. 🚇 Jin-Yi-Dong light rail — International Trade City Station 🏛 Yiwu International Trade City, Digital Trade Center e.g. Hilton Yiwu (upscale, ~600 RMB) · Yiwu Mansion (mid-range, ~350 RMB) Binwang / downtown Nightlife & food The old center around Binwang Market and Choucheng Square has the best night markets and street food — plus Yiwu's famous Korean Quarter (the city hosts a large Korean trading community). 10 minutes by taxi from the Trade City. 🚇 Jin-Yi-Dong light rail — Yiwu Station; buses to Trade City 15 min 🏛 Binwang Night Market, Korean Quarter, Jiming Pavilion e.g. Atour Hotel Binwang (~300 RMB) · Yiwu International Hotel (~280 RMB) Fotang Ancient Town Culture seekers About 35 minutes south of downtown, staying in Fotang lets you experience the ancient town at its most atmospheric — empty old streets at dawn, temple bells, river mist — with boutique guesthouses in renovated merchant houses. 🚇 No metro — bus 318 or taxi (~40 RMB) 🏛 Fotang Old Street, Wan Shan Floating Bridge, Water Street e.g. Fotang Old Street minsu (~250 RMB) · local guesthouses (~120 RMB) 🍜 What to Eat Fotang Qianzhang Noodles 佛堂千张面 Thin wheat noodles in a clear broth topped with shredded dried tofu skin and pork — a 100-year-old local breakfast staple. Simple, savory, deeply comforting. 🍽 🍽 Xinghua Noodle Shop, Fotang Old Street · ~13 RMB Brown Sugar Twists 红糖麻花 Yiwu's brown-sugar industry dates back over 700 years (a national intangible heritage) — twists and pastries drenched in freshly boiled brown-sugar syrup. Crunchy, chewy, not too sweet. 🍽 🍽 Yihong Brown Sugar Hall (Fotang) & street vendors · ¥10–15 Korean BBQ 韩式烤肉 Yiwu's large Korean merchant community created an authentic Korean dining scene — grilled marinated short ribs, stone bibimbap and cold noodles that rival Seoul. 🍽 🍽 Korean Quarter near Binwang · ¥50–80 pp Mixed Tofu Pudding 豆花 Silken tofu pudding, sweet (sugar syrup) or savory (soy sauce, chili oil, pickles) — a refreshing street snack, especially in summer. 🍽 🍽 Fotang old-street vendors & Gongshang Night Market · ¥3–5 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says The fastest train from Yiwu to Hangzhou East takes just 33 minutes (from ~45 RMB) — day-trip from Hangzhou, but the market deserves at least one full day, ideally two. Kat Says The market is not designed for retail tourists — most booths need minimum orders of 50–500 pieces. For single-item shopping, head to District 5's Import Pavilion or the tourist center on District 1's ground floor. Kat Says Download the 'Yiwu Go' (义乌购) app before visiting — it searches products and booth numbers, so you can navigate the 6.4-million-sqm complex without getting lost. Free Wi-Fi throughout. Explore More Cities 🌊 杭州 · Hangzhou West Lake, tea culture — 33 min from Yiwu by train 🌃 上海 · Shanghai Futuristic skyline, international food, modernity ← Back to Ready? China!

title: Zhangjiajie
snippet: the honest guide to zhangjiajie for first-time visitors: why go, top 5 must-sees with real history, where to stay by district, and what to eat.
text: ← Back 🏞️ 张家界 Zhangjiajie Avatar mountains, glass bridge, sandstone pillars ★★☆☆☆ 🗓 2–3 days Avatar mountains Glass bridge National park ✨ Why Zhangjiajie? Zhangjiajie is where the landscapes of Chinese paintings turn out to be real: 3,000+ quartz-sandstone pillars rising up to 200 meters out of the forest — the rock formations that inspired the floating mountains of Avatar. It's China's original national park (est. 1982) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it runs on superlatives: the world's tallest outdoor elevator, the world's longest and highest glass bridge, and a cableway to a 1,500-meter cliff-top skywalk. The scale is the thing — you need at least two full days and a good dose of patience with queues (go at 7am, trust us). Come for the pillars, the glass bridges and the mountain mist, and leave with photos that look Photoshopped — because they're not. 🏛 Top 5 Must-See click the photo to read the story Read the story 1 Zhangjiajie National Forest Park China's first national park — the Avatar mountains Read the story 2 Tianmen Mountain & the glass skywalk A cliff walk 1,430 meters up Read the story 3 Grand Canyon glass bridge Walk on air, 300 meters up Read the story 4 Bailong Elevator The world's tallest outdoor elevator — 326m Read the story 5 Ten-Mile Gallery scenic train A train ride through the pillar forest The story: Established in 1982 as China's first national forest park, this is a forest of 3,000+ quartz-sandstone pillars that rise up to 200 meters from the treetops — formed by 300 million years of erosion. The most famous is 'Hallelujah Mountain' (1,074m), the inspiration for the floating peaks in James Cameron's Avatar. The whole area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Why it's a must-see: It's the single most alien landscape in China: pillars of rock wrapped in swirling mist, reached by cliff-top walkways, park shuttle buses and the world's tallest outdoor elevator. The light changes every hour — morning mist makes the pillars float, noon burns them gold, and sunset paints them pink. It genuinely looks like another planet. 💡 Kat's tip: Enter at 7am when gates open — by 10am the tour buses arrive. Buy the 4-day park pass (¥228). The classic loop: Bailong Elevator up → Yuanjiajie (Avatar mountains) → walk to Tianzi Mountain → cable car down. The story: Tianmen ('Heaven's Gate') Mountain is a 1,519-meter peak reached by the world's longest cableway at 7.4 km — a 30-minute ride that feels like flying. The mountain's famous 131.5-meter-high natural arch ('Heaven's Gate Cave') is climbed via 999 steps, and its cliff-face walkways include glass-bottomed skywalks bolted to the sheer rock at 1,430 meters. Why it's a must-see: It's the full mountain experience in one day: the epic cableway, the 999-step climb through the heavenly gate, and a glass skywalk where you walk on air above the valley. On misty days the whole mountain becomes a sea of cloud — the most dramatic weather show in China. 💡 Kat's tip: Book the cableway + ticket online (combined ~260 RMB). Go early (before 9am) — queues can hit 2 hours. The skywalk is free with entry; the 5 RMB shoe covers are mandatory. The 999 steps are worth it going up; take the elevator down. The story: Opened in 2016, the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon glass bridge spans 430 meters across a canyon 300 meters deep — the longest and highest glass-bottomed bridge in the world when it opened, built to hold 800 people at once. The bridge sways slightly, the glass is 4 cm thick, and walking across it is exactly as terrifying as it sounds. Why it's a must-see: It's a genuine bucket-list moment: standing on clear glass above a forested chasm, with the canyon walls on either side. Even if you're scared of heights, the adrenaline is the point — and the canyon below (with its own walking trail and waterfalls) is a beautiful park in its own right. 💡 Kat's tip: Tickets are timed — book online for a specific slot and arrive 30 minutes early. Shoes with heels are banned (you get slippers). The bridge is 40 minutes from the national park; combine it with the canyon trail below for a full day. The story: The Bailong ('Hundred Dragons') Elevator rises 326 meters up a sheer cliff face — the tallest outdoor elevator on earth, built in 2002 and certified by Guinness World Records. It carries visitors from the valley floor to the top of the pillar forest in under 2 minutes, with a glass front that gives a vertical view of the mountains as they drop away beneath you. Why it's a must-see: It's the most efficient (and most thrilling) way to reach the Avatar mountains: a 326-meter vertical ride that feels like taking off. The view from the top — the entire pillar forest laid out at your feet — is the payoff, and it saves you a 2-hour mountain climb. 💡 Kat's tip: Go up at opening (7:30am) to skip the 1-hour queue — or use it DOWN at the end of the day when everyone is going up. Single ride ¥72 (plus park entry). The glass-fronted cabin is the one to wait for. The story: The Ten-Mile Gallery is a 5-km valley path through the heart of the pillar forest, where the rock formations have been named for what they resemble — the 'Old Man Gathering Herbs', the 'Three Sisters', the 'Turtle Watching the Sea'. A small scenic train runs the length of it, or you can walk the flat, easy trail in about an hour. Why it's a must-see: It's the most relaxed way to take in the pillar forest — a gentle walk or train ride with the mountains towering all around, far below the cliff-top crowds. The named formations are a fun game of imagination, and the trail is flat enough for everyone. 💡 Kat's tip: Walk in, take the train back (or vice versa) — the train is ~38 RMB one-way. Go in the late afternoon for softer light on the pillars. It's in the Wulingyuan area, easy to combine with a half-day. 🛏 Where to Stay Pick the right district and half your trip is planned. These are the bases locals actually recommend for visitors. Wulingyuan (park entrance village) Best for park days The village at the park's main gate: everything you need for park days is 5 minutes away — the entrance, the Bailong Elevator bus stop, and the Ten-Mile Gallery trailhead. Restaurants and hotels line the main street, and the morning queue is yours to win. 🚇 No metro — the village is walkable; taxis to town 40 min 🏛 National Park gate, Bailong Elevator, Ten-Mile Gallery e.g. Pullman Zhangjiajie (5-star, 5 min from gate) · National Park Inn (family-run, owner plans your route) Zhangjiajie city center Nightlife & Tianmen days The city on the Li River has the airport, the train station and the Tianmen Mountain cableway — plus the best restaurants and night markets. Stay here for Tianmen days and easy airport/train connections; 40 minutes to the national park. 🚇 No metro — bus/taxi to Wulingyuan (40 min) 🏛 Tianmen Mountain cableway, riverside, night market e.g. Neodalle Zhangjiajie Wulingyuan (boutique, rooftop terrace) · city-center chains Grand Canyon area Glass bridge focus A handful of guesthouses near the Grand Canyon glass bridge and its canyon trail — for travelers who want the bridge first thing, before the coach crowds arrive. 🚇 No metro — taxi to Wulingyuan 30 min 🏛 Glass bridge, Grand Canyon trail e.g. local guesthouses near the canyon entrance 🍜 What to Eat San Xia Guo hotpot 三下锅 Zhangjiajie's signature: three meats (usually pork, beef and lamb) in a spicy Tujia broth — the local answer to 'what's for dinner'. Order it everywhere; every restaurant claims theirs is best. 🍽 🍽 Local restaurants across Wulingyuan & the city · ¥60–100 pp Xiangxi Smoked Bacon 湘西腊肉 Hunan-style smoked pork belly — smoky, salty, slightly sweet — stir-fried with garlic shoots. The taste of the mountains, preserved the old way. 🍽 🍽 Tujia restaurants · ¥40–60 Sour Fish Soup 酸汤鱼 Tangy, spicy freshwater fish soup — a Tujia minority specialty that warms you up after a long, cold mountain day. 🍽 🍽 Tujia restaurants in Wulingyuan · ¥50–80 Gao Mountain Baba 高山粑粑 Sweet cakes made from the chestnuts that grow in the mountains around Zhangjiajie — the classic snack to carry on trail days. 🍽 🍽 Street vendors at the park gates · ¥10–20 💡 Kat's Insider Tips Kat Says Buy the 4-day park pass (¥228) — the park is huge and you need at least 2 full days. One day is not enough, trust us. Kat Says AVOID Chinese national holidays completely — Golden Week and Spring Festival turn the glass bridge into a human parking lot. Go in April, May or September. Kat Says Enter at 7am when gates open. By 10am the tour buses arrive and the queues get biblical. The morning mist between the pillars is the most magical — and most photogenic — time. title: Index
snippet: yellow, blue, or green bike? which app, how much it costs, how to unlock and return, and the rules that get you fined. everything first-timers need. updated august 2026.
text: 🚲 Getting Around · Step 8 · 共享单车指南 How to Use Shared Bikes in China The best travel hack nobody explains properly. No separate app needed — here's how to unlock, ride, and return a shared bike, plus the rules that actually get enforced. ⏱ 6 min read 📅 Updated August 2026 🪙 From ¥1.5 per ride 💡 Kat's Tip Shared bikes are how I get around my own city day to day — cheaper than a taxi, faster than walking. No deposit, no separate download if you already have Alipay or WeChat set up. The 10-Second Version 1. No new app needed Unlock bikes straight from Alipay or WeChat — they run as a mini-program inside apps you already have. 2. Scan to unlock Point your camera at the QR code on the handlebars. About ¥1.5 for the first 15–30 minutes. 3. No license needed Helmets are encouraged, and sometimes required — some cities mandate them for e-bikes. 4. Park in the zone Return inside a marked parking zone or you'll get an automatic ¥5–20 fine deducted from your card. 1 You Don't Need a Separate App This trips up a lot of first-timers. You don't need to install Meituan, Hello Bike, or Didi individually — all three run as a mini-program inside Alipay or WeChat, the apps you already have set up for payments. 1 Confirm your Alipay account is passport-verified (Settings → Account → Verification — look for the green badge). 2 Confirm you have an international card linked, or Alipay's Tour Pass activated. 3 Open Alipay, tap the transport icon on the home screen, and select the bicycle option. Prefer standalone apps? Meituan, Hello Bike (哈啰), and Didi (with Qingju/青桔 bikes) are all free downloads with English-language settings. 2 Know Your Colors Yellow — Meituan Bike Access via the Meituan app or WeChat mini-program. Widest coverage in Tier 1 cities. Blue — Hello Bike (哈啰) Access via the Alipay mini-program. Widest coverage overall — 400+ cities, including smaller ones. Green — Didi Qingju (青桔) Access via the Didi app or Alipay mini-program. Convenient if you already have Didi installed for rides. Coverage overlaps but isn't identical — if you can't find one color nearby, check the map inside another operator's app before giving up. 3 Regular Bike or E-Bike? Both exist side by side in most cities, marked separately on the in-app map: • Regular pedal bikes — the standard option, roughly ¥1.5 for the first 15–30 minutes depending on city and operator. • Electric-assist bikes — capped around 25 km/h, cost more (roughly ¥0.50/minute). Great for longer distances or hot weather. 4 Unlock, Ride, and Pay 1 Find a bike on the in-app map — available bikes show as dots near you. 2 Point your phone's camera or the app's scanner at the QR code on the handlebars or rear wheel. 3 Tap "unlock" — you'll hear a beep and the rear wheel lock releases within seconds. 4 Ride. Payment is deducted automatically from your linked card when you end the ride. ⚠️ You Need Mobile Data You need internet to unlock and to end your ride. Sort out a China eSIM before you land — see our eSIM guide . 5 Return the Bike Properly • End your ride inside a marked parking zone — an outlined box on the in-app map, or a painted zone on the sidewalk in big cities. • Push the lock closed on the rear wheel manually, then confirm the ride has ended in the app before walking away. • If you're outside a valid zone, the app usually warns you before letting you lock the bike — don't ignore that warning, you could get a fine. • Forgetting to properly end the ride keeps charging you, even after you've walked off — always confirm the app shows "ride complete." 6 The Rules That Actually Get Enforced • No license needed. Shared bikes don't require a driver's license — regular pedal bikes and e-bikes both. • Helmets are encouraged for standard shared bikes under national guidelines. A few cities — including Hainan and Shenzhen — mandate helmets specifically for e-bikes, with fines of ¥50–200 for riding without one. • Ride in the bike lane — to the right of car traffic, separated by a line or curb — not on the sidewalk. • Parking outside a designated zone gets you an automatic fine typically ¥5–20, deducted straight from your linked card. • Basic accident insurance is included in your rental fee, usually covering up to around ¥100,000 for injury — this is not a substitute for real travel insurance. See our Travel Insurance guide . 💡 Kat's Tip If you're unsure about helmet rules in your city, just wear one anyway.And remember, not passengers allowed! FAQ: Common Shared Bike Questions Is there a deposit? ▼ No deposit is required if your account is passport-verified with a linked card. This used to be a hassle for foreigners; it's largely been resolved by 2026. What if I can't find a bike from the app I opened? ▼ Check a different operator's map — Hello Bike's blue bikes often reach areas Meituan's yellow ones don't, especially in smaller cities, and vice versa. Can I use headphones or hold my phone while riding? ▼ Not recommended. Chinese urban traffic — especially e-bikes and scooters weaving between lanes — requires full attention. Keep your phone away and your ears open. What's the actual cost for a normal day of use? ▼ Most short "last mile" trips from a subway exit to your hotel run 10–20 minutes, so you're typically looking at ¥1.5–3 RMB per trip — under a dollar even with several rides a day. Do I need to worry about theft or leaving the bike unattended? ▼ Shared bikes are designed to be picked up and left anywhere within a legal zone — you're not responsible for guarding it. Just make sure the lock has engaged and the app confirms the ride ended before you walk away. 🗺️ Get the Free Transit Cheat Sheet A printable one-pager: Alipay transport code setup, bus vs metro vs bike, and the Chinese characters for "next stop" and "get off here." Budget guesthouses and small local hotels often cannot legally check in foreign passport holders. Always book hotels that explicitly say "accepts foreign guests" or stick to international chains to avoid arriving at your hotel and being turned away. 🏨 International chains — Always safe IHG (Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza), Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, and AccorHotels all operate widely across China and always accept foreign guests. text: 📰 China News · Community Free drinking fountains in Chinese parks — where they exist (and where they don't) 📅 August 2026 CHINA NEWS Good news for budget travelers: free public drinking fountains (直饮水, zhí yǐn shuǐ) are slowly appearing in Chinese parks — it's a real but still rare thing. Where they actually exist The fountains you'll find are mostly in newer municipal projects, not in the famous tourist parks. Real examples reported in Chinese media: Qingfeng Park and Zijin Park in Changzhou (Jiangsu), Binjiang Park in Shangrao (Jiangxi), Dadukou Park in Chongqing, and some parks in Meishan (Sichuan) and Rongxian (Zigong). They usually look like stainless-steel bubblers with a button — press, lean in, drink. The honest reality - Most parks in Beijing, Shanghai, and the big tourist cities do NOT have public drinking fountains. Don't plan around finding one. - Even where they exist, they're designed for locals who already trust the system. As a visitor, you can't verify the maintenance schedule. What to do instead (1) Carry your own bottle — free hot water is available at hotels, high-speed rail stations, and most airports (look for the 开水/直饮水 water station). (2) Bottled water is ¥1–2 at any convenience store (便利店, biànlì diàn). (3) Tap water in cities is chlorinated and not recommended for drinking — filter or boil if you're in a pinch. Bottom line: free park fountains are a nice-to-have trend, not a feature you can rely on yet. Pack a bottle, and use the train station water stations instead. 👍 Helpful 👎 Not Helpful ❓ Confused 💬 Got a question of your own?
